Build (phase 5, from the eval stumbles): when the backfill added or updated rows, the run's `next[]` names the skipped transforms that read what it changed, directly or not, in run order (`croft run <transforms>`, "--from skipped what reads it, which is stale until it runs"), and the skill's Backfill recipe says to run them (§9).

**A text cursor converts nothing** (D64). `--from` takes a value written like the saved cursor (`v0006` for `v0005`) and passes it through as is. A relative value or `today` is always `CURSOR_TYPE_MISMATCH`. So is a date or a timestamp, unless the saved cursor is written the same way (a date field pinned to VARCHAR, say). The error comes before the run, exits 2, and its hint shows the saved value. Before the first load there is no saved value, so only relative values and `today` are refused. The skill's backfill recipe (`--from -90d`) applies to time cursors only.

A `--from` that cannot apply is refused before the run starts: no run is recorded and no step fails. An asset named exactly refuses the whole command (exit 2, the error above); in a bare `croft run --from …` or a glob, the assets it does not apply to are skipped with the reason. Refusals that need only the plan (`BACKFILL_UNSUPPORTED`) come from the invoking process; those that need the saved cursor (`BACKFILL_WOULD_DUPLICATE`) come from the detached child before it records the run, and the parent prints them as its own result.

Why the cursor holds (D57): a `--from` later than the saved cursor used to save `greatest(saved, loaded)` like any run, which jumped the schedule over `[saved, <when>)`. Nothing ever fetched those rows again, and `--from` needs no confirmation (§6), so `croft run x --from today` lost data silently. Holding the cursor costs one wider fetch on the next run; merge makes the re-read rows a no-op.

The same flag fills a new field for old rows of a merge ingest: `croft run stripe_charges --from 2024-01-01`.

**Large first loads.** Off a TTY, a run detaches, so a long first load is never killed by the agent's shell (§5). The agent polls with `croft wait <id> --timeout 100s` or uses its own background shell.

A crash, a kill or a rate-limit failure late in a long first load must not force a refetch from zero. So cursor ingests use **monotone partial commits** (phase 4). While writing parts, the JavaScript writer checks that every cursor value in the new parts is at least every value in earlier parts. If so, every 50k rows or 5 minutes croft commits those parts, with the cursor set to their typed maximum. If the order is not monotone (newest-first APIs), the ingest keeps single-transaction behavior.

Build (phase 4, D90). Partial commits apply to every run of a `rows()` ingest with a cursor, outside a preview; file ingests and ingests without a cursor keep one transaction.

- **The order check is per value, in yield order,** a stricter form of "every value in new parts ≥ every value in earlier parts": each cursor value must be at least every value before it. A newest-first API therefore breaks it on its first page, before anything could commit. Values compare as the typed column will: integers exactly, ISO date-times as instants (with an offset) or wall clocks (without), dates as midnight among naive values, text in code-point order. Kinds whose order would depend on how the column ends up typed (dates next to zoned date-times, numbers next to text) break it, so the load falls back to one transaction rather than trust a guess.
- **Parts** end at the end of the batch that reaches 50k rows or 5 minutes; the 5 minutes are checked only when a batch arrives, so a generator stuck in one long request commits at its next batch. Each part goes through the step's own write with the blocking checks of an unfinished load (`min_rows` waits for the last commit), as a chunked TS transform's chunks do, and its catalog entry is mirrored at once. The last part is the step's ordinary write.
- **When the order breaks after parts committed,** the rows still to come may hold cursor values below the one saved, and a stop before the end would resume past them. So the saved cursor goes back at once, in its own commit and before the out-of-order rows are staged, to where the run began, and the rest of the load is saved in one transaction whose cursor is kept at least where the parts saved it. A failure in that window refetches from the earlier cursor instead of skipping rows.
- **What the step says.** Its reason says "saved in 3 commits as updated_at arrived in order", or "saved in 3 commits: updated_at stopped arriving in order at row 120001 (…), so the rest was saved in one", or, for a newest-first load large enough to have been split, "saved in one commit: created arrived out of order (…), as newest-first APIs send it, so a failure before the end fetches the whole load again". A failure after parts committed keeps them, and its effect says how many rows were saved and where the next run continues (`details.savedRows`, `savedCommits`, `cursor`). A kill is recovered as ok (§5, "Crash recovery"), and the next run resumes from the saved cursor. `CROFT_FAULT=after_partial_commit` (the first part) and `after_partial_commit_<n>` kill the process after a part's commit.

---

## 9. Claude Code integration

The agent has never seen this tool. Everything it needs ships inside the installed version, and `croft init --claude` refreshes it.

Items 1 and 2 are the full v1 texts, and `src/agent/claude-md.md` and `skill.md` are exactly them: there is no cut list and no "This version" section, and `agent/templates.test.ts` compares the shipped files with this section byte for byte. Phases 1–4 shipped them cut to their commands: lines that sent the agent to a command, flag or feature the phase lacked were left out or reworded, SKILL.md gained a "This version" section rendered from the manifest in `core/phase.ts`, and the test listed every cut line with its reason, so no rule below disappeared unnoticed. `agent/contract.test.ts` guarantees that every command named in agent-facing text exists in the build (§4.1). The paragraphs below record what each phase shipped.

**1. The `CLAUDE.md` managed block:**

```markdown
<!-- croft:start (managed by `croft init --claude`) -->
## Data pipelines (croft)
This project loads and transforms data with croft (TypeScript + DuckDB). Load the `croft` skill for any work in
assets/, lib/ or on warehouse.duckdb. Start with `croft context --json`.
Loop: edit → `croft validate --json` → `croft preview <asset>` → `croft run <asset>` → `croft query "..."`.
Never modify warehouse*.duckdb or .croft/ except through croft. Never read .env or handle secret values.
Ask the user before any command in the skill's "Ask the user first" list, including every `croft confirm`.
<!-- croft:end -->
```

**2. `.claude/skills/croft/SKILL.md`:**

```markdown
---
name: croft
description: Build and operate this project's data pipelines with the croft CLI (DuckDB). Use when adding a data
  source, writing SQL or TypeScript transforms, adding checks, scheduling, debugging a failed run, backfilling,
  renaming, or answering a question from project data.
---
<!-- croft 0.1.0 -->
croft is not dbt, dlt, SQLMesh or Dagster; do not assume their behavior. Ask the CLI: `croft docs <topic>`,
`croft docs <ERROR_CODE>`, `croft docs --list`, `croft new --list`. Every command takes `--json` →
{ok, data, problems[], next[], confirmation?}.

## Orient
croft context --json        # assets, columns, behavior, schedules, running, held, recent failures and schema changes
croft status                # failed, stale, held, never run, edited since its last run, no asset file

## Loop (always)
1. New asset: `croft new api|file|sql|transform <name>`; edit the template, don't invent APIs.
2. `croft validate --json` after EVERY edit; apply each problem's `fix`. When the edit is to a TS transform or
   an asset one reads, add `--types`: tsc then checks the columns the transform reads.
3. `croft preview <name>`: read columns, checks, diff and samples.
4. `croft run <name>`; then verify with `croft query "..."` (one SELECT, 50-row cap).

## Conventions
- One file in assets/ = one table with that name; SQL says `FROM github_issues`. Shared code goes in lib/.
- SQL assets: `-- name: value` header lines (description, key, check, warn), then ONE SELECT (a trailing `;` is fine).
  SQL transforms are always rebuilt in full; there is no incremental SQL. Only ingests have schedules.
- SQL assets read assets, never files: to use a file, make a file ingest (`croft new file x`).
- PIVOT needs an IN list: `PIVOT t ON cat IN ('a', 'b') USING sum(x)`, or use `sum(x) FILTER (WHERE cat = 'a')`.
- Avoid now()/current_date in assets (values freeze until the next rebuild); compute ages at query time.
- Set `key` whenever records have an id. Incremental API ingests need a key.
- TS transforms that call an API or LLM per row: keep `incremental: true` + `newRows()` (the template default).
  A changed input row is sent, and paid for, again; to pay once per key, write `incremental: { once: "key" }`.
  Preview them with `--rows 20`: by default a preview hands them up to 1,000 input rows, each a paid call.
- TS transforms read `newRows("x")` with no type argument: rows get x's column types, and `croft validate --types`
  catches a column renamed upstream. A BIGINT is `number | bigint`: `Number(row.x)` before arithmetic.
- Use `ctx.http` and `res.json()` (lossless numbers), never raw fetch + JSON.parse for API data.
- Nested fields are JSON: `col->>'field'`, `col->>'$[*].name'`, `json_each(col)`. `croft describe` lists keys.
  Parenthesise `->` beside AND, OR, NOT or =: `(col->'k') = 2` (without, DuckDB reads `col->('k' = 2)`). Lambdas: `lambda x: x + 1`, never `x -> x + 1`.
- Columns named like SQL keywords must be quoted: `"order"`.
- Apps read with `import { query } from "@zabaca/croft/read"`; `query<"x">(sql)` types the rows as table x's (croft docs serve). It talks to `croft serve` when one is running (found via CROFT_URL or .croft/serve.json), otherwise opens the file briefly. Never open the .duckdb files directly.
- `croft serve` runs until stopped: ask the user to start it in their own terminal instead of running it in your shell.
- A person who needs to read tables gets a key of their own (croft docs keys): the user names the tables to share in `serve.sharedTables`, then `croft serve key add <name>` prints the key once (`data.key` with `--json`; hand it to the user, never paste it elsewhere), `key list` shows who has one, `key remove <name>` takes access away at once. A key works only with `"serverMode"` on (`data.serverMode` of `key add --json` says whether it is; otherwise the key is refused until it is); with it on, `data.quack` is how their own DuckDB 2.0 attaches over Quack (croft docs quack).
- For a GUI (DuckDB UI, DBeaver), set "readCopy": true in croft.json and open warehouse.read.duckdb, never warehouse.duckdb. With `"serverMode"` on (croft docs server-mode) the copy is read-only on disk: open it read-only.

## APIs
- Keyset paging (re-query with since = newest value seen) ONLY if the API sorts ascending by that field.
  Newest-first APIs (Stripe, most list endpoints): filter by since and follow the API's own cursor
  (`croft new api x --pagination cursor`).
- Records that change after creation (payments, refunds, orders, tickets) need an updated-since field or a
  lookback: incremental: { field: "created", unit: "s", lookback: "30 days" }. Epoch cursors need `unit`.
- A status the code expects (a 404 for "not there"): `http.get(url, { okStatus: [404] })`, never
  `.catch(() => null)`, which also hides 429s and outages. Bytes (PDFs, images): `http.getBytes(url)`.
- An API with a stated quota (so many requests an hour or a day): ask the user to put it in croft.json
  `"http": {"budgets": {"<host>": {"perHour": 50}}}`. HTTP_WAIT or HTTP_BUDGET_SPENT: wait until the time it gives.

## Ask the user first (show the printed impact; wait for an explicit yes in this conversation)
- `croft confirm <token>` (every destructive action ends here: rebuild of an ingest or incremental TS transform,
  --allow-shrink, delete, restore, lossy pin changes, key conversion, large paid reprocessing).
- Adding `allowShrink: true`; changing key/write/incremental of an ingest that has data.
- Raising `confirmAbove` of a transform that makes requests (more paid calls would run without asking).
- Renaming or deleting files in assets/ (use `croft rename`); `croft schedule on|off|pause`.
- `croft serve` (it runs scheduled work unattended, and a `--host` other than 127.0.0.1 exposes data beyond this machine).
- `croft serve key add <name>` and naming tables in `serve.sharedTables`: they give a person access to data. Show which tables the key will read. `croft serve key remove` and `key list` need no asking.
- Turning `"serverMode"` on or off in croft.json (apps then read the read copy, as of the last run, or in a lake project the lake's last snapshot with no copy, and DuckDB 2.0 clients with a key can attach over Quack; turning it on makes croft fetch DuckDB's quack and httpfs extension files from DuckDB's servers once (a download of about 21 MB, about 66 MB on disk), or `croft fetch-extensions` does it ahead of time; croft docs extensions), `serverMode.acceptFullCopyCost` (disk and write time at every run), and `serverMode.quackPlaintextOnNetwork` (it lets Quack listen beyond this machine, in plaintext, behind a proxy of the user's own).
- Adding or changing a `"lake"` block in croft.json (the warehouse then lives in a catalog and a bucket folder that someone else runs, with two logins and two keys named by secret names; it makes croft fetch DuckDB's ducklake, httpfs and postgres extension files once (a download of about 34 MB, about 109 MB on disk), or `croft fetch-extensions` does it ahead of time; croft docs lake). One machine writes a lake. Never make a Postgres, a bucket or a key yourself, never put a secret's value in croft.json, never run CHECKPOINT or set an expiry on a lake, and never put anything else in its folder (DuckLake's cleanup deletes it).
- Setting `lake.maintenance.enabled` to false (the lake then grows until `croft maintain` is run by hand), and `croft maintain --orphans` (it ends in `croft confirm`: the files it lists are not the lake's own and are gone for good once deleted). `croft maintain` itself, `croft maintain --dry-run` and `croft backup` of a lake need no asking: a pass removes nothing the 30 days or 5 versions promise keeps, and croft runs one by itself (every 24 hours unless `lake.maintenance.everyHours` says otherwise).
- `croft move-to-lake`, which ends in `croft confirm`, and setting `lake.enabled` in the `lake` block by hand: `true` puts the project on the lake, `false` puts it back on the file (untouched) and leaves what was written in the lake out of it. The move is how a file project gets into a lake (croft docs lake): from then on the lake is where its data lives. Show the user the impact it prints (what moves, what stays, what does not come along, the way back) and wait for an explicit yes. Never make the lake yourself (a new, empty catalog database and bucket folder are the user's to make), never write `"enabled": true` by hand to skip the move (the lake would start empty and the next run would fetch everything again), and have croft serve stopped first.
- Deleting .croft/ or warehouse*.duckdb, or `git clean -X` (the trash and backups live in .croft/).
- Weakening or deleting a failing check.

## Recipes
- Failed run: croft status --json → croft logs <asset> --failed → fix → croft validate --json → croft preview <asset>
  → croft run <asset> → croft status.
- Held asset: it was edited and not run by hand; run it by hand once (croft run <asset>) after checking the preview.
- Schedule: add `schedule: "every hour"` to the ingest (`croft docs scheduling`); `croft validate` shows the next fires;
  run it by hand once (new code is held until then), then ask the user before `croft schedule on`.
- Backfill: croft run <asset> --dry-run --from -90d, then the same without --dry-run. Merge ingests only.
  Then run the transforms it skipped (its next[] names them), or they stay stale.
  A date works too (--from 2026-06-24); a text cursor takes a value in its own format. The saved cursor never moves back.
- Rename: croft rename <old> <new>; fix every reference it lists; validate; preview; run.
- Wrong number: croft describe <asset> --json → croft preview <asset> --rebuild (drift) → query the upstream
  with the same filter; `croft docs internals` shows how _croft.writes maps rows to runs.
- API changed: new fields appear automatically; fill them for old rows with --from (merge ingests).
  TYPE_CONFLICT: clean the value in rows()/map() first; a pin can rewrite stored values.
- Missing secret: ask the user to add NAME=... to .env (or run `croft secrets set NAME` in their terminal);
  check with `croft secrets --json`. Never read .env.
- Warehouse file missing (DB_NOT_FOUND in status): ask the user where it went before running anything; a run
  builds a new, empty one and refetches from the sources.
- Lake (croft docs lake): LAKE_CONNECTION_LOST or LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED are about the catalog or the bucket, not the project: check
  `croft doctor`, tell the user, run again when they are reachable. LAKE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN: look at `croft status` before running
  again. LAKE_OTHER_WRITER: tell the user; do not run from this machine until they decide which machine writes.
  LAKE_CATALOG_MISMATCH: the catalog database holds another lake (another format, or files in another folder); ask the user which
  database is croft's, and never migrate it or override its data path. LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES (doctor): `croft maintain` mends it.
  `croft doctor` leaves a lake's tables out of its comparison (each costs the catalog's round trips); `croft doctor --tables` compares them.
- Lake maintenance: croft runs it by itself (croft docs lake); `croft maintain --dry-run` says what a pass would expire,
  `croft maintain` runs one. LAKE_MAINTENANCE_FAILED is a warning (the lake is fine; the next croft run or scheduler tick tries again once an hour has passed).
  A version of a table in a lake older than a few days is read with `AT (VERSION => n)` or `AT (TIMESTAMP => ...)` in
  `croft query`, within the 30 days or the table's 5 newest versions.
- Move a file project into a lake: the lake block with `"enabled": false` is in croft.json and its secrets in .env; then `croft move-to-lake` (exit 5, a token), and only after the user's yes `croft confirm <token>`.
  LAKE_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED and LAKE_VALUES_INEXACT name the columns to cast (change the asset's SELECT, `croft run` the asset, move again); MOVE_LAKE_NOT_EMPTY needs a new lake from the user;
  MOVE_BLOCKED names what to change first. A move that stopped is finished by running it again; the file is never changed by it.
- Backup: croft backup (into .croft/backups/), or croft backup <folder> on another disk; safe while croft serve
  runs. A lake's backup is a pg_dump of the catalog and a mirror of the bucket folder (LAKE_BACKUP_TOOL_MISSING: ask the
  user to install the Postgres client tools). Never copy warehouse*.duckdb by hand. Putting a backup back replaces
  data: ask the user (croft docs backup).

## Output
- JSON timestamps carry the project offset; ::DATE uses the croft.json timezone.
- `query` rows are capped: check data.truncatedRows before concluding anything; aggregate in SQL.
- `query` cuts values at 80 characters, with `--json` too (data.truncatedValues counts them); add `--full-values`.

## Long work
- Off a TTY, `croft run` returns after ~100 s with exit 6 and keeps running: `croft wait <runId> --timeout 100s`.
- Never retry a non-retryable error unchanged.
```

**2a. `.claude/agents/croft.md`** (D110), written wherever the skill is, and stamped and refreshed the same way. It makes the skill an agent with one job, used two ways. The main conversation hands it the project's data work as a subagent, and its `skills` field preloads the whole skill, so it starts with its manual. Or a person starts a session as it (`claude --agent croft`, or `"agent": "croft"` in `.claude/settings.json`), and its text replaces Claude Code's system prompt; there `skills` preloads nothing, so its text has it load the skill. What it adds to the skill is who can say yes. A subagent cannot ask the user anything (Claude Code takes `AskUserQuestion` from every subagent [V: code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents, read 2026-10-19]), and a yes in the task another agent wrote came before the user saw any impact, so as a subagent every "ask the user first" becomes "stop and return the impact and the command", run only when the main conversation answers with the user's yes; in its own session it asks, as the skill says. Stopping is the same both ways, and an agent unsure which it is acts as a subagent. Its front matter must be valid YAML: Claude Code skips an agent file whose wrapped `description` holds a `: `, and lists no error (a one-line one it reads anyway) [V: Claude Code 2.1.304, 2026-10-19]; `templates.test.ts` parses it. `agent/templates.test.ts` compares the shipped file with this text byte for byte, and `agent/contract.test.ts` checks the commands it names.

```markdown
---
name: croft
description: This project's data warehouse and BI, built with croft (DuckDB). Use proactively for any work on the
  project's data, such as adding a source (an API, files, an export), building tables and reports, adding checks or
  schedules, fixing a failed run, or answering a question from the data.
skills:
  - croft
model: inherit
---
<!-- croft 0.1.0 -->
You own this project's data warehouse. croft keeps it in one folder: each file in assets/ makes one table in one
DuckDB file, ingests bring sources in, and transforms shape them into the tables people and apps read. Your job is
to make the warehouse useful: bring in the data the project needs, model it into tables a report can read, and
answer questions from it with numbers you have checked.

The croft skill is your manual. As a subagent you start with it preloaded; a session started as this agent does
not preload it, so if it is not in your context, load the `croft` skill before anything else. Start with
`croft context --json`, and make every change through the skill's loop.

You run either as a session of your own (`claude --agent croft`), where the user is talking to you, or as a
subagent, where another agent handed you a task and the user cannot answer you. Where the skill says to ask the
user first, stop either way: show the printed impact and the exact command, and end your turn.
- In your own session, run it after the user's explicit yes, as the skill says.
- As a subagent, return the impact and the command, for the main conversation to put to the user. A yes in your
  task came before the user saw the impact, so it never counts; run it only when that conversation answers what
  you returned with the user's yes. When unsure which you are, act as a subagent.
- A missing secret: the user sets it with `croft secrets set NAME` in their own terminal; tell them, or return it.
  Never read .env.

When you finish, say:
- the tables you added or changed, and what each one holds;
- the commands that verified them, and what they showed;
- for a question: the answer, the query behind it, and what it covers (dates, filters, truncated rows);
- what is left undone, and why.
```

**3. The machine-readable contract** is in §4.3. In summary:

- Every command has `--json`, with `schemaVersion: 1`, frozen by golden tests and published JSON Schemas (phase 5: `schemas/` in the package, generated from the TypeScript types, §4.3, D99).
- `run --events` streams NDJSON progress.
- Asset names are table names everywhere.
- Timestamps carry the project offset, and durations are in milliseconds.

**4. Error design.** Every problem carries:

- a stable `code` from a registry;
- a `hint`, which is the literal next command or edit;
- a machine-applicable `fix`;
- an `effect` stating what was and was not written;
- `retryable`;
- a `docs` page.

A test fails if any thrown code is unregistered or has no fix template and docs page. Build (phase 5): every registered code has its own page, `src/agent/docs/<CODE>.md` (`agent/code-pages.test.ts`, above); the summary `croft docs` generates from the registry is only a fallback. User-code stack traces are trimmed to frames in `assets/` and `lib/`. DuckDB errors are mapped to codes, with positions shifted past the header. Users never need to learn the codes; each one has `croft docs CODE`.

**The codes:**

- **Project:** `DUPLICATE_OUTPUT_COLUMN`, `DECIMAL_PRECISION_UNSUPPORTED`, `QUERY_PATH_DENIED`, `ASSET_INVALID`, `NAME_INVALID`, `NAME_RESERVED`, `NAME_CONFLICT`, `HEADER_UNKNOWN_KEY`, `SQL_SYNTAX`, `SQL_NOT_SELECT`, `SQL_NOT_ONE_STATEMENT`, `PIVOT_NEEDS_VALUES`, `LAMBDA_ARROW` (an arrow lambda, which DuckDB 2.0 refuses; D113), `CATALOG_PREFIX`, `SQL_READS_FILES`, `INPUT_NEEDS_KEY`, `UNKNOWN_TABLE`, `UNKNOWN_COLUMN`, `QUOTE_IDENTIFIER`, `UNDECLARED_INPUT`, `CYCLE`, `SCHEDULE_INVALID`, `CHECK_INVALID`, `SECRET_MISSING`, `INCREMENTAL_WITHOUT_KEY`, `CURSOR_TYPE_MISMATCH`, `ASSET_OPENS_DATABASE`, `ASSET_RENAMED`, `QUERY_NOT_SELECT`, `USAGE_ERROR` (bad flags or arguments), `PROJECT_NOT_FOUND`, `QUERY_FAILED` (DuckDB failed while binding or running a user query, §5), `CONFIG_INVALID` (`croft.json`), `DB_NOT_FOUND` (no warehouse file; worded by `runs.sqlite` as built before and now missing, runs that wrote no table yet, or nothing run yet, §3b), `SERVE_NO_SHARED_TABLES` (a key's query while `serve.sharedTables` names no table: a `403`, D122), `SERVE_KEY_EXISTS` and `SERVE_KEY_NOT_FOUND` (`croft serve key add` for a name that has a key, `key remove` for one that has none; D122), `SERVE_KEY_NEEDS_SERVER_MODE` (a valid key's query while croft serve does not run in server mode: a `403` before the body is read, D128), `LAKE_DIRECT_READ` (`@zabaca/croft/read` in direct mode was pointed at a project whose warehouse is a lake; use croft serve, D143), `LAKE_UNSUPPORTED` (a change a lake cannot make in this write: a second rewrite of a table in one write, D138, D142; moving a project in and server mode over a lake were once listed here and shipped, D167, D183), `MAINTAIN_NEEDS_LAKE` (`croft maintain` in a project that keeps a file, D152), `MOVE_NEEDS_LAKE` (`croft move-to-lake` with no lake block to move into, or in a project already in a lake, D167), `MOVE_BLOCKED` (a read copy asked for by name, a running croft serve, a rename that did not finish, no warehouse yet, or a croft.json croft cannot rewrite stands in the way of a move, D172), `MOVE_LAKE_NOT_EMPTY` (the lake a move would fill holds tables, or a copy that has been written since or is of another file; refused by type when a run writes a lake and before a move starts, nothing written, D169, D174).
- **Run:** `HTTP_ERROR`, `HTTP_BUDGET_SPENT` (a request not sent: its host's budget in `croft.json` is spent, D104), `ASSET_CODE_ERROR`, `ROW_NOT_OBJECT`, `UNSERIALIZABLE_VALUE`, `CSV_HEADER_AMBIGUOUS`, `PIN_ROUNDED`, `DDL_AFTER_DML` (an internal invariant), `KEYSET_STUCK`, `TIMEOUT`, `INTERRUPTED`, `TYPE_CONFLICT`, `TYPE_PIN_VIOLATION`, `KEY_NULL`, `CHECK_FAILED`, `SHRINK_GUARD`, `INGEST_CONFIG_CHANGED`, `PIN_CHANGES_DATA`, `UNKNOWN_INPUT_COLUMN`, `BACKFILL_UNSUPPORTED`, `BACKFILL_WOULD_DUPLICATE`, `LARGE_REPROCESS`, `INTERNAL_ERROR` (a croft bug), `RUN_CRASHED` (a step whose process died before it committed, found by `reconcile()`), `FILE_NOT_FOUND` and `FILE_UNREADABLE` (a file ingest's file or URL, §3b), `LAKE_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED` (a result has a column DuckLake cannot store, an ENUM, a UNION, a VARINT, a BIT or a fixed-size ARRAY; nothing was written; the fix is a cast, D142, D169), `LAKE_CONNECTION_LOST` (the lake's catalog or bucket could not be reached again after the retries; retryable, nothing partial, D139), `LAKE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN` (a connection died during a commit and the commit's tag could not be looked up, so whether it landed is not known; the run id to look for is in the message, D139), `LAKE_BACKUP_FAILED` (`pg_dump` or the copy of the bucket failed; no partial backup is left, D151), `MOVE_NOT_EQUAL` (the lake did not equal the file after a move's copy; the copy was taken out and the project stays on the file, D168) and `MOVE_FILE_CHANGED` (the file changed while a move ran, so its copy is of an older file; the copy was taken out, D168).
- **Coordination:** `DB_BUSY`, `DB_HELD_BY_OTHER_PROGRAM`, `ASSET_BUSY`, `SCHEDULE_HELD` (a warning with exit 0: a held asset never fails a run, D77), `HTTP_WAIT` (a warning with exit 0: a run by hand inside a known wait holds the asset, D105), `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE`, `SERVE_UNAUTHORIZED` (a `401`/`403` from `croft serve`; exit 2, never retried), `SERVE_UNSAFE_FILESYSTEM`, `QUERY_TOO_MANY_ROWS`.

retryable, nothing written, D195), `EXTENSION_LOAD_FAILED` (DuckDB refused a file that passed the checksum), `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` (the lake could not be attached; retryable except when the catalog or the store refused the login or key, which waiting does not change; no credential in the text, D118, D141), `LAKE_CATALOG_MISMATCH` (the catalog database holds another lake: another DuckLake format, older or newer, or files in another bucket folder; never retried, never migrated, no migration advice, D178), `LAKE_BACKUP_TOOL_MISSING` (`croft backup` of a lake needs `pg_dump` and none was found; `src/core/errors.ts` is the full registry: each code's category, severity and exit code.

**5. Introspection commands:**

- `context`, `status`, `describe` (columns, JSON keys, behavior in words, cursor, samples);
- `run --dry-run` (actions, reasons, windows, confirmations);
- `validate` (with output columns), `preview` (including `--rebuild` for drift);
- `logs` (`--failed`, `--runs`), `secrets`, `doctor`, `docs internals`;
- `schedule status` (each asset as the scheduler sees it: schedule, cron, next and last fire, due, held; phase 3).

All of these but `schedule status` ship from phase 2. (Phase 1, which had no `run --dry-run`, `validate` or `preview`, backfilled with `croft run <asset> --from <when>`, checking the saved cursor first with `croft describe <asset>`.)

**6. Protecting the agent's context window:**

- Row caps (50 in `query`; 3 samples in check failures, 20 in `--json`).
- Values cut to 80 characters.
- Logs default to the last 200 lines.
- `context` capped at 20 KB.
- `.env` values redacted (D54). Every `.env` value of 4 or more characters is redacted from messages, hints and logs. In command data (query rows, samples), declared secrets are always redacted, and any other `.env` value only when it looks like a credential: 8 or more characters, and not only letters or only digits. Otherwise `PORT=5432` or `LOG_LEVEL=info` would rewrite ordinary values the agent reasons from. `data` then carries `redactedValues: true` (§4.3). A declared secret set in the shell instead of `.env` is covered too: declaring the project's secret names (`ProjectEnv.declare()`) registers their shell values, so redaction hides them even when no `secret()` call handed them out. Values printed by croft.json's `secretsFrom` command (§9.8, D108) count as `.env` values from the moment it runs, in the process that ran it; a process that did not run it (`croft query`, `status`) never held them and cannot hide them in table data.
  - **A value is redacted in its renderings, not just its raw text** (D61):
    - escaped, as in JSON (including `\/`, as PHP writes it), in `util.inspect`'s quoting, and as `\xHH` or `\uHHHH`, up to three levels of escaping;
    - split over lines by `util.inspect`, which writes a multi-line string as `'…\n' +` continuation lines;
    - each line of 8 or more characters of a multi-line value (a PEM key's body), on its own;
    - URL and form encoding (space as `+`), with percent escapes in either hex case;
    - for values of 8 or more characters, base64 and base64url, including the value inside a longer encoded credential such as a Basic auth header (at most the characters of two bytes at either edge remain).
  - **Not covered:** other encodings (hex, gzip, encryption), and a value split across two writes of a stream.

**7. What `init` deliberately does not write.** Without `--with-hook` it does not write `.claude/settings.json`. Permission rules and hooks change what Claude Code may do without asking, so they stay the user's decision (D27).

- `croft docs claude-permissions` prints a suggested snippet: `"ask": ["Bash(croft confirm:*)"]`, and deny rules for reading `.env` and `.env.*` (`"Read(./.env)"`, `"Read(./.env.*)"`, plus the `./data/` variants for a project inside an app). Because every destructive action funnels into `croft confirm`, that one prefix rule gates all of them. croft never writes these rules. With a `secretsFrom` command (item 8), the page suggests denying that command too (`"Bash(sops -d:*)"` for sops), since its output is the secrets.
- `croft init --claude --with-hook` (or `croft init --with-hook` for a new project) opts into a PostToolUse hook (`agent/hook.ts`, D97), merged into `.claude/settings.json`: matcher `Edit|Write|MultiEdit`, one command handler, `timeout` 120 (seconds). The command is pinned to this form: `cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" && ./node_modules/.bin/croft validate --hook`. It runs the project's own pinned croft from the project folder, with no network and no global croft; not `bunx`, which fetches from the registry when nothing is installed (and the npm name `croft` is another package), and not a bare `croft`, whose launcher would plan from Claude's current folder, which follows its `cd`. For a project in `data/`, init writes the hook in both places the skill goes: the app's settings get `cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/data && …`, and `data/.claude/settings.json` the plain form, for sessions started there.
- The merge keeps every setting and hook already in the file, in their order, and appends croft's as a group of its own in the file's indentation; the file is written back as JSON, so other formatting (compact arrays, CRLF line ends) is not kept. A file that already runs `croft validate --hook`, in this form or another, is left as it is, so the hook is never added twice. A file croft cannot extend (not strict JSON, not an object, or `hooks` of the wrong shape) is left untouched with a `USAGE_ERROR` whose fix carries the snippet to add by hand, and a file croft cannot write is `PROJECT_NOT_WRITABLE`; the rest of init goes through either way. The settings files are listed with init's other files, and the human output adds one line saying what the hook does.
- `croft validate --hook` reads the hook's JSON on stdin (`tool_input.file_path`, or `tool_response.filePath`; a relative path is read from the input's `cwd`, and symlinked folders such as macOS's `/var` are resolved). An edit that is not a `.ts` or `.sql` file in `assets/` (a `.d.ts` excluded) or a file in `lib/` exits 0 with no output, in about 0.1 s, without resolving the project. Otherwise it validates what the edit can break: an SQL asset with everything downstream, since readers bind against its output columns; a TS asset alone; a `lib/` file, the TS assets whose bundle includes it and those that fail to load because of it. A discovery refusal of the edited file (`NAME_INVALID`, `NAME_RESERVED`, `NAME_CONFLICT`) is reported as is. Only errors and warnings of the checked assets and of the edited file count. With an error, stdout stays empty and stderr carries one line saying what was found and what else was checked, each problem in croft's usual block, and a closing line, with exit 2. Warnings alone and a clean check are silent with exit 0 (`--json` still carries them). A problem Claude can fix in the project (a `croft.json` that does not load) is reported the same way; any other failure exits with croft's own code. Asset names, `--types` and a terminal on stdin are `USAGE_ERROR`. It never opens the warehouse and never runs tsc (0.12–0.3 s for an asset edit).
- The hook's exit-code semantics are [V], with the rest of Claude Code's side (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks and /settings, read 2026-09-24, recorded in `agent/hook.ts`): a shell-form command hook runs through `sh -c` in Claude's current folder (which follows its `cd`), with `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` exported as the folder the session started in, which is where the shared `.claude/settings.json` is read; the file tools' `tool_input.file_path` is absolute; for PostToolUse, exit 2 "Shows stderr to Claude; the tool already ran", exit 0 sends stdout and stderr to the debug log only, and any other exit (127 when the command cannot start) is a non-blocking notice to the user with the first line of stderr; the default timeout is 600 s; the same handler in several settings files runs once. The e2e journey `j29` runs the hook command read from `settings.json` through a real `sh -c`, with real PostToolUse JSON, against the real bin. MultiEdit is no longer in the documented tool list and stays in the matcher for older versions; a name that matches no tool matches nothing. The handler uses no newer field (`args`, `if`, `statusMessage`), so older Claude Code versions read it. Not yet run inside a live Claude Code session [U].
- Consequences of those semantics as built: before `bun install` (or in an app whose `data/` is not installed yet), `./node_modules/.bin/croft` is missing and each edit gives the user a non-blocking hook error (exit 127). croft's environment errors exit 2 like its usage errors, so a hook whose `PATH` lacks Bun (`NEEDS_BUN`) or has an older one (`BUN_TOO_OLD`) shows that error to Claude after every edit. Warnings never reach Claude through the hook, though Claude Code could take them as `additionalContext` on exit 0: the spec asks for a silent success, and `SECRET_MISSING` would otherwise follow every edit.

**8. Secrets.** croft loads secrets itself; Bun's automatic `.env` loading is off (`bun --no-env-file`) [V]. Bun's loading depends on the working directory, so a scheduled tick started from `/` would see no secrets. It also silently lets `.env.local` override `.env`. The rules:

- croft reads `<project>/.env`. Shell environment variables take precedence over it, and `croft secrets` shows where each value came from.
- `.env.local` and `.env.*` are ignored, with the `doctor` warning `ENV_FILE_IGNORED`.
- Only declared names reach code, through `ctx.secret()`. They are not placed in `process.env`.
- `croft secrets set` writes `.env` with mode 0600.
- Every child process croft spawns gets its environment passed explicitly. Without that, Bun hands a child the environment it started with, which includes any values it loaded from `.env` [V]. The launcher strips those values for the same reason (§2).
- A `.env` line croft cannot parse is `ENV_FILE_INVALID` in `doctor`.

**Secrets from a command (D108).** A project that keeps its credentials in an encrypted store (a SOPS file, a password manager's CLI) names a command in croft.json, instead of wrapping every croft command in a script that decrypts each key and execs croft:

```json
"secretsFrom": { "command": ["sops", "-d", "--output-type", "dotenv", "secrets.enc.yaml"] }
```

- The order is the shell environment, then `.env`, then the command. A name either one sets never runs it, and `croft secrets set` (which writes `.env`) always takes effect.
- It runs lazily: when a step's `ctx.secret()` asks for a declared name the shell and `.env` lack, or `croft secrets` checks one. At most once per process (per `ProjectEnv`): the values, or the failure, are kept for the rest of it. `validate` (and so the hook), `doctor`, `status`, `query` and every other command never run it; `validate` and `doctor` report such a name as `unchecked`, not `SECRET_MISSING`. A detached run's child runs it itself.
- It is an argv, run without a shell (no `~`, `$VAR`, quoting or pipes), from the project folder, with no stdin and no terminal, and with croft's own environment passed explicitly, minus croft's credentials (`CROFT_CONFIRM_GRANT`, `CROFT_SERVE_TOKEN`) and without `.env`'s values. A bare program name is looked up on that environment's `PATH`, which is the one a scheduled run has. It has 60 s and 16 MiB of output.
- stdout is read as `.env` text (`parseDotenv`); unparseable lines are skipped. Values stay in memory, never on disk, and are redacted like `.env` values (point 6), so a declared one is always hidden in data and any other one when it looks like a credential. Its stderr is discarded on success.
- A failure is `SECRETS_COMMAND_FAILED` with how it failed (could not start, not on `PATH`, not executable, an exit status or signal, 60 s passed, no `KEY=value` line), the last 20 lines of its stderr redacted with every value known by then (including any its stdout printed before it failed), `file: "croft.json"`, and a hint for the user, not the agent: what the command prints is the secrets. It is raised for every name the command would supply, with the asset; steps that need no secret, or find theirs elsewhere, still run. A name the command ran without printing is `SECRET_MISSING`, whose message and hint name the command.
- `croft secrets` lists each such name as `set` with source `command`, `missing`, or `unchecked` when the command failed (with its error among the problems, exit 2), and says in its human output whether the command ran.
- Scheduled runs pass only `HOME`, `PATH`, `LANG` and a few more variables (§8), and their `PATH` is Bun's folder, `/opt/homebrew/bin` on macOS, `/usr/local/bin` and the system folders. A command must therefore name its program by absolute path when it lives elsewhere, and set any variable it needs in the command (`["/usr/bin/env", "SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE=…", "sops", …]`), and must not wait for a prompt. `doctor` checks the program on both `PATH`s without running it.
- The scheduler only runs a command a person has run (§6).
- croft.json is the user's own file, like asset code; nothing forbids it to name a command (D3 is about reading the config without running user code, which still holds: the launcher and the tick never run it). Its text is not redacted, so credentials do not belong in it.

**Secrets without a TTY.** Inside Claude Code the user usually has no interactive terminal, so the primary instruction is "open `.env` in your editor and add `STRIPE_KEY=…`".

- `croft secrets set NAME` is a convenience: a hidden prompt on a TTY, or `--stdin` for piping from a password manager.
- Off a TTY without `--stdin`, it exits 5 with `REQUIRES_HUMAN`.
- `croft secrets --json` returns `[{name, status: "set"|"missing"|"unchecked", source: ".env"|"env"|"command"|null, usedBy}]`, so the agent can confirm a secret exists without reading it (`unchecked` and `command` only with `secretsFrom`).

Declaring `secrets` drives `doctor`, `validate`, error messages and what `ctx.secret()` returns. It is not a hard isolation boundary, because asset code could still read the file. That is why `.env` values are redacted from output, not only declared ones (point 6 gives the rules). SQL cannot read `.env`: the sandbox blocks `read_text('.env')` [V].

---

## 10. Implementation layout

**One package**, `@zabaca/croft` on npm, with bin `croft` → `bin/croft.mjs`, which imports `src/cli/main.ts` (§2). The command is plain `croft`, just as `@zabaca/zbc` ships the command `zbc`. The package root also ships `croft.schema.json` (draft-07) and, from phase 5, `schemas/` (the JSON Schemas of every `--json` output, draft 2020-12, §4.3), and `package.json` `files` lists `bin`, `src`, `dist`, `schemas` and `croft.schema.json`, and leaves out tests, test kits and fixtures (`!src/**/*.test.ts`, `!src/**/testkit.ts`, `!src/**/*-testkit.ts`, `!src/**/fixtures`). `scripts/build-schemas.ts` (`bun run build:schemas`), which needs the `typescript` devDependency, writes `schemas/`; nothing loads it at run time. Its exports:

- `.` → `src/index.ts`
- `./read` → `dist/read.js` + `dist/read.d.ts`, built from `src/read.ts` with `bun build --target node` and code splitting at publish time. Direct mode is a separate hashed chunk (`dist/read-*.js`) that `read.js` imports only on first use, so the entry never imports `@duckdb/node-api`. The `.d.ts` is generated from `src/read-types.ts`, and a build test typechecks one consumer against both `dist/read.d.ts` and `src/read.ts` to catch drift.

**Packing.** `dist/` is git-ignored, so the build runs from `package.json`: the `prepack` and `build` scripts both run `scripts/build-read.ts`. `npm pack` or `npm publish` from a clean checkout therefore ships `dist/read.js`, `dist/read.d.ts` and their chunks. `schemas/` is committed, not built at pack time. `tests/pack.test.ts` packs a copy without `dist/` and `node_modules` and checks the tarball, `schemas/` included.

**Dependencies:**

- **Runtime:** only `@duckdb/node-api`, pinned exactly, because both the storage format and the AST shape depend on its version (2.0.0-r.1 since croft 0.4, D111).
- **Everything else is a Bun built-in:** `bun:sqlite` (`runs.sqlite`, and the scheduler registry's OS lock), `Bun.Glob`, `Bun.file`/`Bun.write`, `Bun.hash`/`Bun.CryptoHasher`, `Bun.build` (fingerprints), `fetch`, `node:util` `parseArgs`, `node:child_process` (detached runs, notifications, `croft tick` spawns, `launchctl` and `crontab`, and the `cp -c`/`cp --reflink=auto` clones behind the read copy and backups), `Bun.spawn` with its IPC channel (`croft serve`'s query workers), `node:fs` (write-intent files; `watch` only as a latency hint), `node:crypto` `timingSafeEqual` (serve tokens), `node:net`/`node:tls` (the read client's proxy-proof loopback HTTP, §5, also used for loopback webhooks), and `Bun.serve` (`croft serve` and test mocks).
- **No CLI framework and no schema library.** Validators are hand-written so their errors read well.
