**Commands load lazily.** `cli/commands/index.ts` registers each command with `lazyCommand(spec, loader)`. The spec (`name`, `summary`, `usage`, `options`, `maxPositionals`, `humanShowsProblems`) is all that help, flag parsing and did-you-mean need. The module (`run`, `human`) is imported only when that command runs, so a broken DuckDB binding fails only the commands that need DuckDB, reported as `DUCKDB_BINDING_MISSING` or `DUCKDB_BINDING_LOAD` with the fix `croft doctor`. `docs`, `help` and `version` import nothing heavy and are what a broken install still answers with. A command whose human output shows its own problems (`doctor`, `validate`) sets `humanShowsProblems`; otherwise `main.ts` appends the standard problem blocks.

### Public types

```ts
export type Row = Record<string, unknown>;
export type ColumnType = "BOOLEAN" | "BIGINT" | "HUGEINT" | "DOUBLE" | "VARCHAR" | "DATE" | "TIMESTAMP"
  | "TIMESTAMPTZ" | "JSON" | `DECIMAL(${number},${number})` | (string & {});
export type ColumnPin = ColumnType | { type: ColumnType; format?: string };   // format: strptime pattern
export type RowSource = AsyncIterable<Row | Row[]> | Iterable<Row | Row[]> | Promise<Row[]>;
export type FileFormat = "csv" | "tsv" | "json" | "ndjson" | "parquet" | "yaml";

interface Common {
  description?: string;
  key?: string | string[];
  write?: "replace" | "append" | "merge";    // override the inferred behavior
  checks?: string[];                         // blocking: "unique(id)", "not_null(a, b)", "min_rows(10)", "amount >= 0"
  warnings?: string[];                       // non-blocking, same language
  columns?: Record<string, ColumnPin>;
  secrets?: string[];
  retries?: number;                          // default 2 for TS code
  timeout?: string;                          // no-progress timeout, default "10m"
}
export interface CursorSpec {
  field: string;
  unit?: "s" | "ms";                         // integer cursors holding epoch time
  lookback?: string;                         // "10 minutes", "30 days"
}
interface IngestBase extends Common {
  schedule?: string;                         // "every hour" | "daily at 06:00" | 5-field cron (ingests only)
  allowShrink?: boolean;
}
export interface RowsIngest extends IngestBase {
  rows(ctx: IngestContext): RowSource;
  incremental?: string | CursorSpec;
  file?: never; map?: never;
}
export interface FileIngest extends IngestBase {
  file: string | string[];                   // path, glob or URL
  format?: FileFormat;
  csv?: { delimiter?: string; header?: boolean; skip?: number; encoding?: "utf-8" | "latin-1" | "utf-16" };
  incremental?: boolean;                     // only new or changed files
  map?(row: Row): Row | null;                // clean values; null drops the row
  rows?: never;
}
export interface TransformConfig extends Common {
  inputs: string[];                          // assets this code reads
  incremental?: boolean | KeyOnce;           // newRows() + merge instead of replace; chunked commits (§3e)
  confirmAbove?: number;                     // cost guard threshold, default 1000 input rows (§5)
  rows(ctx: TransformContext): RowSource;
}
interface KeyOnce {                          // incremental: { once: "key" }: each output key once (§3e, D106)
  once: "key";
  from?: Record<string, string>;             // output key column → the input column it is read from (default: same name)
}

interface BaseContext {
  readonly asset: string;
  readonly runId: string;
  readonly preview: boolean;                 // true under `croft preview` (rows capped, nothing saved)
  readonly signal: AbortSignal;              // timeout, Ctrl-C/SIGTERM, preview row cap
  readonly http: Http;
  secret(name: string): string;              // declared names only; throws SECRET_MISSING
  log(...args: unknown[]): void;
}
export interface IngestContext extends BaseContext {
  readonly since?: string | number;          // saved cursor (minus lookback) in its own JSON type, or --from
  query<T extends Row = Row>(sql: string, ...params: unknown[]): Promise<T[]>;   // one SELECT over its own table
}
export interface CroftAssets {}             // empty; .croft/types/index.d.ts adds each asset's row type (§3e, D96)
export type InputRow<N extends string> = N extends keyof CroftAssets ? CroftAssets[N] : Row;
export interface TransformContext extends BaseContext {
  // A built asset's name gives its generated row type; any other name, or an explicit row type
  // (`rows<Issue>("x")`, `rows<Row>("x")` for column names computed at run time), gives that type.
  rows<N extends keyof CroftAssets>(input: N): AsyncIterable<CroftAssets[N]>;
  rows<T extends Row = Row>(input: string): AsyncIterable<T>;      // rows are Proxy-guarded (§3e)
  newRows<N extends keyof CroftAssets>(input: N): AsyncIterable<CroftAssets[N]>;
  newRows<T extends Row = Row>(input: string): AsyncIterable<T>;
  query<T extends Row = Row>(sql: string, ...params: unknown[]): Promise<T[]>;   // one SELECT over inputs
  query<N extends keyof CroftAssets>(sql: string, ...params: unknown[]): Promise<CroftAssets[N][]>;   // query<"x">
}
export interface HttpInit {
  headers?: Record<string, string>;
  query?: Record<string, string | number | boolean | null | undefined>;   // null/undefined omitted
  retries?: number; timeoutMs?: number;
  okStatus?: number[];                       // statuses ≥ 400 returned, not thrown or retried (D103)
}
export interface HttpResponse {
  status: number; url: string; headers: Headers; text: string;
  json<T = unknown>(): T;                    // lossless: unsafe integers → bigint
  next?: string;                             // rel="next" from the Link header
}
export interface HttpBytesResponse extends HttpResponse { bytes: Uint8Array }
export interface Http {
  get(url: string, init?: HttpInit): Promise<HttpResponse>;
  post(url: string, body: unknown, init?: HttpInit): Promise<HttpResponse>;
  head(url: string, init?: HttpInit): Promise<HttpResponse>;              // D103
  getBytes(url: string, init?: HttpInit): Promise<HttpBytesResponse>;     // D103
}
export interface AssetDefinition { readonly __croft: "ingest" | "transform"; readonly config: RowsIngest | FileIngest | TransformConfig }
export declare function ingest(config: RowsIngest | FileIngest): AssetDefinition;
export declare function transform(config: TransformConfig): AssetDefinition;
export declare function fail(code: "KEYSET_STUCK" | (string & {}), message: string): never;
```

`fail()` raises only `KEYSET_STUCK` as itself. Any other code becomes `ASSET_CODE_ERROR`, with the requested code in `details.requestedCode`, because croft's control-flow, check and safety codes (`INTERRUPTED`, `CHECK_FAILED`, `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`, …) are reported only by croft.

`@zabaca/croft/read`:

```ts
export interface ReadOptions {
  project?: string;                          // project root; else CROFT_PROJECT, else walk up from cwd
  url?: string;                              // croft serve URL; else CROFT_URL, else .croft/serve.json, else direct
  token?: string;                            // else CROFT_SERVE_TOKEN, else the local serve.json
  limit?: number;                            // max rows; default 10,000; more is QUERY_TOO_MANY_ROWS, never truncation
  timeoutMs?: number;
}
export declare function query<T extends Record<string, unknown> = Record<string, unknown>>(
  sql: string, params?: unknown[], options?: ReadOptions): Promise<T[]>;
```

### Internal types

```ts
export type AssetKind = "ingest" | "sql" | "ts";
export type WriteMode = "replace" | "append" | "merge";
export type CursorType = "timestamp" | "date" | "integer" | "string";
export type Incremental =
  | { kind: "none" }
  | { kind: "cursor"; field: string; unit?: "s" | "ms"; lookbackMs: number }
  | { kind: "files" }
  | { kind: "new-rows"; inputs: string[] };                  // TS newRows()
export interface Check { source: string; kind: "unique" | "not_null" | "min_rows" | "rule";
  blocking: boolean; scope: "batch" | "table"; sql: string; reads: string[] }
// ResolvedAsset is project/resolve.ts's (below, D68): it carries the loaded TS and SQL modules, whose types core/
// does not import.
export type Reason = "requested" | "schedule_due" | "never_built" | "code_changed" | "input_changed"
  | "input_replaced" | "rebuild" | "backfill";
export type Hold = "code_not_run_by_hand" | "large_reprocess" | "paused" | "leased" | "retry_after";   // retry_after: D105
export interface PlanStep { asset: string; action: "fetch" | "rebuild" | "update" | "skip";
  reasons: Reason[]; hold?: Hold; window?: { sinceValue: string | number; sinceType: CursorType };
  confirmation?: Impact }
export type SchemaChange =
  | { kind: "add_column"; column: string; type: string }
  | { kind: "widen"; column: string; from: string; to: string }
  | { kind: "retype_pending"; column: string; to: string }
  | { kind: "recreate"; reason: "shape_changed" };
export type ValueKind = "null" | "boolean" | "integer" | "bigint" | "float" | "iso_instant" | "iso_naive"
  | "iso_date" | "string" | "object" | "array";
export interface ColumnPlan { column: string; sourceName: string; existing: string | null; incoming: ValueKind[];
  decision: "keep" | "add" | "widen" | "cast" | "retype_pending" | "conflict"; target?: string;
  badRows?: number; samples?: unknown[] }
export interface StageManifest { runId: string; asset: string; parts: { path: string; rows: number }[];
  topLevelKeys: string[]; rows: number; sinceUsed?: string | number; complete: true }
export interface StepResult {
  asset: string; status: "ok" | "failed" | "skipped" | "unchanged"; reason: string; skippedBecause?: string;
  behavior: string; attempt: number; maxAttempts: number; nextRetryAt?: string;
  rows: { in: number; added: number; updated: number; unchanged: number; deleted: number; total: number };
  schemaChanges: SchemaChange[]; cursor?: { before?: string; after?: string; sinceUsed?: string };
  inputs?: { input: string; seenBefore: string | null; seenAfter: string; rows: number }[];
  requests?: number; checks: { check: string; ok: boolean; blocking?: boolean; failing?: number; sample?: Row[] }[];
  trashed?: { path: string; rows: number }; logsCommand: string; durationMs: number; error?: Problem;
  created?: { columns: number; jsonColumns: number };                // this step created the table (§4.2)
  csvHeader?: { header: boolean; from: "declared" | "sniffed" | "known"; columns: string[] };   // first CSV load
}
export type Fix =
  | { kind: "edit"; description: string; file: string; line?: number; replace?: { from: string; to: string }; insert?: string }
  | { kind: "command"; description: string; command: string; requiresHuman?: boolean }
  | { kind: "manual"; description: string; requiresHuman?: boolean };
export interface Problem {
  severity: "error" | "warning" | "info"; code: string; message: string; hint: string; docs: string;
  asset?: string; file?: string; line?: number; column?: number; runId?: string;
  fix?: Fix; effect?: string; retryable?: boolean; details?: Record<string, unknown>;
}
export interface Impact { asset: string; action: string; rows: number; bytes?: number; trashPath?: string;
  downstream: string[]; estimatedRequests?: number }
export interface Confirmation { token: string; expiresAt: string; command: string; impact: Impact }
export interface Envelope<T> { schemaVersion: 1; ok: boolean; command: string; croftVersion: string;
  database: string; timezone: string; durationMs: number; data: T; problems: Problem[];
  next: { command: string; reason: string }[]; confirmation?: Confirmation }
export interface LockHolder { pid: number | null; program: string | null; runId?: string; asset?: string;
  action?: string; since?: string }
export interface Sql { all<T = Row>(sql: string, params?: unknown[]): Promise<T[]>;
  exec(sql: string, params?: unknown[]): Promise<void> }   // always prepare(): one statement per call
export interface Warehouse {
  read<T>(fn: (db: Sql) => Promise<T>, o?: { waitMs?: number; purpose: string }): Promise<T>;
  write<T>(label: string, fn: (tx: Sql) => Promise<T>, o?: { waitMs?: number; runId: string; asset?: string }): Promise<T>;
  holder(): Promise<LockHolder | null>;
}
// Phase-2 command data (§4.3): validate, preview, run --dry-run
export interface ValidateAsset { name: string; kind: AssetKind | null; inputs: string[];
  outputColumns: { name: string; type: string }[] | null; behavior: string; codeChanged: boolean;
  schedule?: { text: string; cron: string; next: string[] } }      // scheduled ingests (phase 3): next three fires
export interface ValidateData { order: string[]; assets: ValidateAsset[];
  types?: { status: "ok" | "failed" | "skipped"; errors: number } }            // --types only
export interface PreviewColumnChange { column: string; change: "added" | "removed" | "retyped"; type: string;
  from?: string; note?: string }
export interface PreviewAsset { asset: string; kind: AssetKind | null; status: "ok" | "failed" | "skipped";
  reason: string; rows: number | null; liveRows: number | null; partial: boolean; capped: boolean;
  requests?: number; since?: string;
  diff: { by: string[]; added: number; removed: number; changed: number; unchanged: number } | null;
  columns: PreviewColumnChange[]; checks: StepResult["checks"]; sample: Row[]; downstream: string[];
  durationMs: number; error?: Problem }
export interface PreviewData { assets: PreviewAsset[]; partial: boolean; inputsSnapshotAt: string | null;
  rebuild: boolean; rowCap: number }
export interface DryRunWindow { sinceValue: string | number; sinceType: CursorType; sinceAt?: string;
  source: "saved" | "from"; saved?: string | number; lookback?: string }
export interface DryRunConfirmation { action: "allow_shrink" | "large_reprocess"; command: string; impact: Impact }
export interface DryRunStep { asset: string; file: string; kind: "rows" | "file" | "transform" | "sql";
  action: "fetch" | "rebuild" | "update" | "skip"; reasons: Reason[]; reason: string; behavior: string;
  hold?: Hold; skippedBecause?: string; window?: DryRunWindow; confirmation?: DryRunConfirmation;
  problems: Problem[] }                                      // static errors that would fail it before it runs
export interface DryRunData { dryRun: true; order: string[]; steps: DryRunStep[] }
```

**Outside `core/types.ts`.** `ResolvedAsset` is `project/resolve.ts`'s, the planner's step is `run/plan.ts`'s, and the step contract is `run/step.ts`'s. `core/types.ts` must not import the project modules, because the declaration check of `src/read.ts` type-checks it without them (D68).

```ts
// project/resolve.ts: every asset discovered, loaded and checked (validate, the planner, status, describe, context)
export interface ResolvedAsset {
  name: string; file: string; path: string;
  kind: AssetKind | null;                                    // null: a TS file that loads as neither kind
  loaded: boolean;                                           // false: an ingest neither selected nor upstream (not imported)
  ok: boolean;                                               // loaded, with no error-severity problem
  inputs: string[];                                          // the AST's relations (+ plan scans) or `inputs`
  orderAfter: string[];                                      // inputs + tables read by its checks
  write: WriteMode; key: string[]; incremental: Incremental;
  behavior: string; words: string; behaviorHash: string;
  schedule?: { text: string; cron: string };                 // ingests only, from phase 3
  checks: Check[]; pins: Record<string, { type: string; format?: string }>;
  codeHash?: string;                                         // includes the project time zone; absent when the code does not parse
  timeZoneChanged?: { from: string; to: string };            // the same code; only croft.json's timezone changed
  description?: string;
  usesHttp?: boolean;                                        // TS: for TRANSFORM_MAKES_REQUESTS / cost guard
  confirmAbove?: number;
  ts?: LoadedTsAsset;                                        // the loaded module; ts.definition replaces `definition`
  sql?: LoadedSqlAsset;                                      // header, body, headerLines, AST inputs, fingerprint
  problems: Problem[]; output?: string[];
}
// run/plan.ts: one step per asset the run takes, in run order
export interface PlannedStep {
  asset: string; file: string; path: string; kind: "rows" | "file" | "transform" | "sql";
  action: "fetch" | "rebuild" | "update" | "skip"; reasons: Reason[]; hold?: Hold; reason: string;
  problems: Problem[];                                       // any error fails the step before it runs
  inputs: string[]; orderAfter: string[]; readBy: string[]; checks: Check[];
  sql?: LoadedSqlAsset; loaded?: LoadedTsAsset; spec?: TsAssetSpec; usesHttp?: boolean; confirmAbove?: number;
  write: WriteMode; key: string[]; incremental: Incremental; behavior: string; words: string;
  codeHash?: string; behaviorHash: string; retries: number; timeoutMs: number; output?: string[];
}
export interface RunPlan { steps: PlannedStep[]; order: string[]; problems: Problem[]; fileDirs: string[] }
// run/step.ts: what runIngest, runSqlStep and runTransform take; each returns a StepOutcome or throws a CroftError
export interface StepInput { step: PlannedStep; project: Project; env: ProjectEnv; warehouse: DuckWarehouse;
  runs: RunsDb; runId: string; attempt: number; maxAttempts: number; signal: AbortSignal; progress: StepProgress;
  log: LogWriter; checks?: WriteBatchInput["checks"]; readBy?: Record<string, string[]>; confirm?: ConfirmDecider;
  preview?: { rows: number }; http?: Partial<Omit<HttpOptions, "signal" | "redact" | "log">>; fault?: string;
  now?: () => Date }
export interface ConfirmRequest { asset: string; action: "allow_shrink" | "large_reprocess"; command: string;
  impact: Impact; problem: Problem }
export type ConfirmDecision = { kind: "granted" } | { kind: "pending"; confirmation: Confirmation } | { kind: "declined" };
export type ConfirmDecider = (r: ConfirmRequest) => Promise<ConfirmDecision>;
// load/write.ts and history/catalog.ts, phase-2 additions
//   WriteResult.checks: StepResult["checks"]            what the checks hook reported
//   CheckHookResult { problems: Problem[]; results: StepResult["checks"] }
//   InputPosition { input; seenLoadedAt; seenKey?; inputLastLoadedAt? }   upserted into _croft.inputs with the write
//   CatalogAsset.inputsSeen?: Record<input, { seenLoadedAt; seenKey; inputLastLoadedAt }>; CatalogAsset.reads?
```

### Test strategy (`bun test`)

The suite runs as `bun test --timeout 60000` (package.json `test`, ci.yml). `tests/preload.ts` also calls `setDefaultTimeout(60_000)`, but that reaches the first test file of a run only: later files start again at Bun's 5 s, so a test without a timeout of its own passes when run alone and times out on a slow runner in the full run [V: Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.4: three one-test files that sleep 6 s, run together, the first passed and the others timed out at 5000 ms; `[test] timeout` in bunfig.toml is not read; `--timeout` applies to every file]. Tests that start real processes or run CPU-bound queries still set their own timeout, since it is also a statement of how long they should take.

`bunfig.toml` preloads `tests/preload.ts`, which sets two tripwires before any test file loads: `CROFT_FORBID_OS_JOBS=1` (registering the scheduler refuses instead of installing a launchd or crontab job) and `CROFT_NOTIFY_DRY=1` (a failure notification is logged instead of shown). The e2e harness passes both to every croft it spawns. Build: under `CROFT_FORBID_OS_JOBS=1` the scheduler's `OsRunner` refuses to run anything (tests inject a fake one), and `croft schedule` refuses a home or croft folder that is the real user's, taken from the password database since Bun's `os.userInfo().homedir` returns `HOME` [V]; tests set `HOME`, `CROFT_HOME` and a unique `CROFT_JOB_LABEL`. `CROFT_NOTIFY_DRY=1` records each notification in `<state>/logs/notifications.ndjson`; a loopback webhook is still posted, so tests use a mock server. `core/codes-raised.test.ts` is a gate: every registered code is raised somewhere in the source, or listed with the later phase that raises it, and that list only shrinks. It does not count comparisons, `case` labels or `[…].includes()` lists as raising a code.

**Rules that keep the suite from flaking.** A flake costs more than a failure: it teaches people to run red again. The suite is held to these rules, each by a test or a flag that fails the change that breaks it (D155 to D157):

- **Wait for an event or a state, never for time.** A test that needs a thing to have happened waits for it: `until(...)` over a state, a line the child prints, a promise a hook resolves, a process's exit. A `sleep` before an assertion about something that "should be done by then" passes where it was written and fails on a busy machine, and a longer sleep only moves the line. A sleep that makes the delay under test (a lock held, a server that answers late) is fine, and so is one that gives something that must not happen the time to happen. `tests/timing-assertions.test.ts` counts the fixed sleeps of each test file and fails when a file has more than it had; it also fails when a file has fewer, so the number can only fall.
- **No assertion on how long something took.** An upper bound on a measured time (`expect(performance.now() - t0).toBeLessThan(1000)`) is true on the machine that wrote it and false on a busy one. What it checks goes elsewhere: that code does not wait for X is the test's own timeout, with X held for good until the test lets go (`spawnHolder(..., "release")`, a route that never answers, a Retry-After of an hour) and an explicit timeout of 20 or 30 s on the test, so a hang fails in seconds and by name; that something comes after something is an order of events; that it waited at least so long is a lower bound, which a slow machine only helps. A latency the design promises (a writer gets the file within the grace and 100 ms) is bounded far from both the promise and what it excludes, by `TIMING_GAP` (5 s) over the budget, because a bound at the promise is a bound on the machine. The one place a bound after the call is the only check is a synchronous call, which no timeout can end; its line carries `timing-gap:` and says what wait it excludes. `tests/timing-assertions.test.ts` reads every test source and fails on an upper bound on a measured time that does neither.
- **Explicit timeouts.** Every run is `bun test --timeout 60000` (the preload's `setDefaultTimeout` reaches the first file only); a test that holds something to prove a code does not wait for it sets its own, short, so that a hang is a failure of that test and not a minute of the job.
- **A test file leaves no process behind.** `tests/preload.ts` appends a last `afterAll` to every test file (`tests/file-guard.ts`, `tests/leak-guard.ts`) that fails the file, naming it and the processes, when a descendant of the test process that was not there when the file loaded is still running (a croft serve or maintain, a Postgres, the S3 store, a Quack listener or a readers' process), or when a process running this checkout's code (`bin/`, `src/`, `tests/` or `evals/` of this package) was reparented away and runs. It waits for processes that are exiting, up to 5 s, polling and not sleeping (`CROFT_LEAK_GUARD_REPORT=1` names the files that were let off because the process was gone within the grace); it kills what it finds, so a leak fails one file and does not hold a port or a lock for the files after it. Another checkout's processes carry another folder, and a process under another live `bun test` (two suites at once) is that run's. A reparented process cannot be told from one that a second suite of the same checkout started (or a developer's own `croft serve` from it), so while another `bun test` runs with this package as its working directory the guard looks at descendants only, and one suite per checkout gets the whole check. `bun test --no-orphans` (package.json `test`; not in `ci.yml`, where the runner ends what a cancelled job left) takes the test run and every process a test started with it when the run's parent dies, as a killed session does and the guard cannot see, since the run it lives in is gone [V: Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.4 on macOS: a killed parent took the runner and its child; Bun 1.4.4 also sets `BUN_FEATURE_FLAG_NO_ORPHANS` in the children, which then kill what their own children leave when they exit, so a leaked grandchild of a Bun child is reaped before the guard looks: the guard's own test runs its throwaway runs without the variable].
- **Shards.** `ci.yml` runs the suite in N jobs each with a share of the test files (D155, D191, D196). A pull request's seven shards of the whole suite are dealt by time: `scripts/shard-files.ts K N` lists shard K's files, longest first to the shard with the least so far, by the seconds each file took in recent runs (`tests/shard-times.json`, made by `scripts/shard-timings.ts` from the logs of the `test` job); a file the table has not met weighs its median and a file it names that is gone is ignored, so the shards are a partition whatever the table says and a stale table costs balance only. The other jobs that shard run as `bun test --shard=K/N`, Bun's own split: the sorted test files dealt out in turn, K/N of the same list in every job. `tests/shards.test.ts` checks on the installed Bun that Bun's shards are a partition of the files (none twice, none missing), for seven and four shards and for a list of files given on the command line, that the script finds the files Bun runs and deals a partition, and that the committed table splits this package's files within 10% of even; `tests/workflows.test.ts` that the matrix lists 1 to N, the name says which, every job runs its own share and none can publish or mint a token. A pull request runs the suite once (Linux x64, Bun 1.3.14) in seven shards with the typecheck in shard 1, the journeys on a local lake in four and on a Postgres lake in five, and the bookkeeping-as-a-log run over the test files that touch the bookkeeping in two (eighteen jobs of over two minutes in all; the free plan runs twenty at once for the whole organization); what does not depend on the shard (the typecheck, the run against DuckDB 1.5) is done by shard 1. The other platforms and Bun versions run in four shards, and the whole log run in two, on a push to main and daily. A pull request's wait is the slowest job, and the shard counts are what keep every job near the same length (D191 has the measurements).
- **Slow tests run side by side, and the lake rig is not shared (2026-11-04).** The suite's time is in a few long tests, not in setup. Measured: `startLakeRig` (Postgres and the store) takes 0.4 to 0.6 s on a laptop, 0.14 s more for each lake and 0.08 s to stop; in CI a lake test file spends under one second between its start and its first test (shard 6 of run 41929714511: `lake-warehouse.test.ts` 0.85 s, `lake-backup.test.ts` 1 s). Twenty-three files each starting a rig is therefore 10 to 20 s of the whole suite, which a rig shared by the files (and a leak guard that has to exempt it) does not repay, so each file keeps its own. What was long is a test that waits on one thing after another when its parts share nothing, and those now go side by side: the two lakes of `sql/lake-gate.test.ts`; the three CAs of `db/store-tls.test.ts` (each in a project and lake of its own; a command closes only its own project's warehouses, `closeWarehousesUnder`); the independent journeys of `j16` (`test.concurrent` for two runs of adjacent tests; 16e to 16g read what the first journey saw and run between them); and the week of hourly runs of `j38` (test d has a lake of its own and starts in `beforeAll`, beside a to c; its test waits for it, so every expectation about it is still its test's). Four things make that safe in one process and are kept: `inDirectory` (the query command's change of the process's folder) takes turns, as the folder is the process's; `createLakeDatabase` takes turns, as its check for a role and the creation of it are two statements; a test never calls `closeAllWarehouses` while another is inside a command; and an assertion still fails its own test (a started piece of work is awaited by the test that owns it). Left as it was, with the numbers: `evals/tasks/tasks.test.ts` is thirteen concurrent self-tests that spend their time in `croft` processes (214 `croft query` calls, 59 `croft run` calls); the four clock cases cannot share a fixture because their data is dated by their own clock, and what is left to cut is the wrong-solution replays of those four cases (about 35 per cent of the file), which would be an assertion removed.
- **A clock a test sets.** A task that dates its story by the clock runs on a clock the test sets (`Fixture.pinNow`, `setupFixture`'s `now`; croft's commands get it as `CROFT_NOW`), the same on every machine and at every hour, and the hours that broke it are run on top. Days of a zone are counted on the calendar, never as multiples of 24 hours: a day is 23 or 25 hours long twice a year.
- **A needle that a port can contain is no needle.** A test that checks a secret is not in the output looks for the whole secret (`4111-secret`), not its first digits (`4111`): a random port, a pid or a timestamp contains four digits one time in a few thousand.

1. **Unit tests, no DuckDB:**
   - Phrase → cron, and the tz-aware matcher across DST in several zones.
   - The check language → SQL, and header parsing with did-you-mean.
   - Name cleanup, including keywords and collapsing.
   - The lossless JSON reader and writer at the 2^53, int64 and uint64 edges, and canonical key order.
   - Link parsing, relative `--from` parsing, selectors.
   - The staleness planner, holds and confirmation-token staleness over fake state.
2. **DuckDB `:memory:` tests** (about 4 ms per instance):
   - Dependency extraction: a golden corpus with CTEs, CTE shadowing, subqueries, UNION, catalog prefixes, quoted file paths, `query_table()`, `query()`, table macros, PIVOT with and without IN, lambdas, QUALIFY, trailing `;` and `--`, and two-statement input. The AST and the unoptimized plan are compared on every case.
   - Fingerprint stability under formatting and case.
   - The type matrix: existing type × incoming kind → decision, including the whitelist and round-trip loss cases (`+02:00` → TIMESTAMP, `1.5` → BIGINT, `'02134'` → BIGINT).
   - Every write mode, including diff-replace, merge dedupe and unchanged-row skipping with reordered JSON keys.
   - The DDL-before-DML invariant (file reload with a widen).
   - Composite `newRows()` positions across equal stamps, and chunk resume after a kill mid-chunk.
   - Round trips of TS values: naive and zoned timestamps with microseconds, HUGEINT through a snapshot.
   - Reserved-column exclusion for `SELECT *` over every asset kind.
   - Check rollback; trash and restore.
   - The sandbox: `COPY TO` the warehouse, `DETACH`/`ATTACH`, reading outside allowed directories, and re-enabling settings, all refused.
   - The bookkeeping adapters (`db/bookkeeping.test.ts`, `db/state.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/j35-log-bookkeeping.test.ts`, D132, D133): the same sequence of writes (a first load, a key written twice in one transaction, a rebuild, a rename, a delete, a restore, and the three ways a primary key would refuse a duplicate: an insert, a rename onto an existing key, a restore that puts back a key the table has or has twice) through the file adapter, the log adapter on a plain DuckDB file and the log adapter in a local lake (a SQLite catalog and a local folder, no Postgres), with the latest rows equal after every step; the log's own order (`seq` against a clock that cannot tell, a hand-inserted row); and journey 35, which runs real croft processes on the log and reads the log itself. **The whole suite also runs on the log adapter**: `CROFT_BOOKKEEPING=log bun test --timeout 60000` (ci.yml runs it as a job of its own, beside the matrix, so neither run lengthens the other; the switch takes effect because `tests/preload.ts` sets `CROFT_TEST_HARNESS`), where a test that seeds `_croft` with SQL of its own writes it through `seedState()` (`db/bookkeeping-testkit.ts`, which turns an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` on a bookkeeping table into the log's appends) and a test about the file adapter's own tables (an older format, a primary key) is skipped with the reason. Counting (`load/write.test.ts`, `run/transform.test.ts`): each write kind (keyed replace, merge, a composite key, a keyed file reload, a reload with fallback rows, append, keyless replace and a chunked TS transform) runs under both countings and must report the same rows and leave the same table; `bun scripts/bench-merge.ts` is the merge benchmark.
   - A lake's maintenance and backup (D149 to D153): `db/lake-maintenance.test.ts` (the promise as a pure plan over literal snapshots, no lake needed), `db/lake-maintenance-state.test.ts` (when a pass is due), `cli/commands/lake-prune.test.ts` (the bookkeeping log's prune on both kinds of lake), `db/lake-steps.test.ts` (the steps against a local and a Postgres lake with the store, snapshots said to be weeks old by the lake clock of `db/lake-testkit.ts`: what is expired and kept and read back exactly, a pin, another tool's expiry option, the files that are not the lake's own, the lock both ways, a store answering HTTP 500, and a scan of the source for `CHECKPOINT`), `cli/commands/maintain.test.ts` and `lake-maintain-faults.test.ts` (the command, the run's hook, the scheduler's spawn, status and doctor), `db/lake-backup.test.ts` and `db/s3-mirror.test.ts` (a backup restored into a fresh catalog and bucket and compared row for row; AWS's signature example), `db/lake-simulation-testkit.ts` and `scripts/simulate-lake-maintenance.ts` (a week and a month of hourly runs in seconds), and `tests/e2e/j38-lake-maintenance.test.ts`, which runs only on the lake jobs (`CROFT_E2E_LAKE`) so the three-platform matrix does not carry it.
   - Moving a project into a lake and what a lake never changes (D167 to D174): `db/lake-move.test.ts` (both kinds of lake: the inventory, the copy as one transaction, the proof held equal row for row and bit for bit, a difference named, the undo, the marker, the three states of a lake), `cli/commands/move-to-lake.test.ts` (the command in a process, a local lake: every refusal at once, with croft.json and the file untouched), `history/mirror-home.test.ts` (the catalog mirror follows the warehouse, and the record of a move), `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts` (a project of every kind of asset moved in and compared table by table, status and plan; going back by the setting; a file with a pending write-ahead log; a move that finished and is refused again; a kill -9 at each point of the move), `tests/e2e/j40-lake-exact.test.ts` (both kinds of lake: integers past 64 bits from JSON, CSV and Parquet, a BIGINT column that later gets them, a transform's HUGEINT, each refused type with its cast, a pin, and a maintenance pass after each, every digit compared) and `db/lake.test.ts` and `load/types.test.ts` for the types. Slow tests set their own timeouts and run only on the lake jobs (`CROFT_E2E_LAKE`), as the maintenance journey does.
   - A warehouse in a lake (D138 to D147): `db/lake.test.ts` (the error classes, the write lock including a kill -9, the types, the machine record: no lake needed), `project/lake-config.test.ts` (the setting), `db/ca-bundle.test.ts` and `db/catalog-tls.test.ts` (the CA file, with the disk a parameter) and `db/lake-tls.test.ts` (the catalog's TLS against a Postgres child with a self-signed certificate, D159), `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` (a real Postgres and an S3-compatible store started as children of the test and killed in teardown: writes, the reader that cannot write, a connection ended by `pg_terminate_backend`, a Postgres restarted, a commit that landed and lost its answer, one that cannot be found out, no credential in any error, `retypeColumns`), `sql/lake-gate.test.ts` (the attack list in lake form over every path, against the same rig and a local lake), `serve/lake-engine.test.ts` (a reader never waits for a run: a write held for 10 s, a restart of the lake process), `cli/commands/extension-status.test.ts` (acceptance 1), `cli/commands/lake-doctor.test.ts` (two machines writing in turn), `db/lake-reader-recipe.test.ts` (the docs' recipe run as written, acceptance 10, and, when `CROFT_TEST_OLD_DUCKDB` and `CROFT_TEST_OLD_EXTENSIONS` name a DuckDB 1.5 install, which `scripts/fetch-old-duckdb.ts` makes, acceptance 11), `tests/e2e/j36-lake.test.ts` (the CLI over a local and a Postgres lake, and the same fixtures giving the same numbers in a file and in a lake, acceptance 2) and `j37-lake-faults.test.ts` (a Postgres that restarts mid-run, a run, a rebuild, a delete, a restore and a rename killed at each of its fault points, wrong password, refused key, an unreachable host, and the credentials that never leave). All of it skips with the reason on stderr where Postgres, the S3 testkit or the extension files are missing. The whole e2e suite also runs with every project's warehouse in a lake of each kind, `CROFT_E2E_LAKE=local` (the children get `CROFT_TEST_LAKE=local`, `project/root.ts` `testHarnessLake`) and `CROFT_E2E_LAKE=postgres` (a database and a store folder per project, `tests/e2e/harness.ts`), as two jobs of `ci.yml` of their own (D146).
   - A lake at a distance (D175 to D182, the second real-lake trial): `db/delay-proxy-testkit.ts` is a TCP proxy that delays each chunk and counts the round trips the client paid (each time it sends after the server answered), and with no delay at all it counts by the order of the bytes, so a test of how many round trips something costs is the same on a slow machine and a fast one (`db/lake-warehouse.test.ts`: a read of six statements costs the catalog less than ten more round trips for each statement after the first, where each was twenty before; the test fails with the lease's transaction removed). The same file: a statement DuckDB refuses does not end a read's transaction for the next one, three leases on a refused login and a fourth after are each `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` (never `INTERNAL_ERROR`; the test fails with `startFailure` removed), and a database that holds a DuckLake 1.1 made by another DuckDB, or a lake under another folder, is `LAKE_CATALOG_MISMATCH` for a reader and a writer. `run/ingest-config.test.ts` counts the leases of an ingest step (one read before its first write). `cli/commands/lake-reinline.test.ts` (a local and a Postgres lake: DuckLake's flush of every schema as the old pass made it, doctor's `LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES`, `croft maintain`, the files gone, every view as it was). `cli/commands/lake-doctor.test.ts` (`--tables`), `db/store-tls.test.ts` and `db/lake-tls.test.ts` (the encryption line, `serverOffersTls`, validate's CA files), `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` (two ingests side by side on a wrong password and on a foreign lake). `scripts/bench-lake-latency.ts` (the commands of a four-asset project against a catalog behind the proxy, 0 and 40 ms round trip; `--preload` and `--trace` write every statement with its time) and `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-03-lake-latency.md` are the measurements.
   - The modes (`db/modes.test.ts`): the real extension files, a Postgres and an S3-compatible store started as children of the test and killed in teardown (D118). A test that needs the extension files or Postgres skips locally with the reason on stderr and fails when `CROFT_CI=1`, so it never passes by skipping in CI. `bun scripts/fetch-extensions.ts` fills the extension folder.

phase 5 added `j28` (`croft new` for every template: each API style against a mock that pages that way, from `new` through validate, the secret, preview, run, query and an incremental second run; `KEYSET_STUCK`; the file template loading exports and a URL; a transform edited as its comments say, with a paid mock LLM, the cost guard and one confirm; an SQL template over it; the refusals and `--list`), `j29` (`init --with-hook` merging into a user's settings, idempotent, and in an app; the hook command read from `settings.json` and run through `sh -c` with real PostToolUse JSON: exit 2 with the report on stderr for an asset, an SQL reader and a `lib/` file that break, silence for clean edits, warnings and files outside `assets/` and `lib/`) and `j30` (`validate --types` catching a column renamed in SQL before any run, with the did-you-mean fix, and the project's own tsc passing after runs; under a transform made with `croft new transform`, whose explicit row type tsc cannot check against the input, only the run catches the rename, and a `bugTest` records that `validate --types` misses it)). A `Bun.serve` mock API covers:

   Every `--json` output is golden-tested against its JSON Schema.

   Build (phase 5): `tests/golden/` (`g01`–`g05`) runs the real CLI through the e2e harness in fixture projects (the example, a mock GitHub-like cursor API, an SQL transform with a warning and a paid incremental TS transform; deletes, restores and confirms; a rename; schedule and serve; every shape of `croft new --json`), and validates each envelope, successes and failures alike, against `schemas/<command>.schema.json` (through `schemaFor`) and the envelope schema. The kit also asserts one envelope on stdout, `schemaVersion: 1` and the command name. The validator is in-repo and test-only (`tests/golden/validator.ts`, no new dependency): it handles the subset the generator writes (`type`, `const`, `enum`, `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `prefixItems`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `$ref` within the file, …) and throws on any other keyword. The e2e journeys `j28`–`j30` validate their envelopes the same way.
4. **Concurrency:**
   - a run plus a query; a foreign read-only holder; two runs on one asset; a tick overlapping a manual run; a detached run followed by `wait`;
   - `croft serve` under steady load while runs write. The writer must get the file within 100 ms with no query in flight, and within 2 s + 100 ms with a 60 s query in flight.
   - two writers, where A removes its intent while B still waits and B must get the file;
   - 16 concurrent long queries at handoff; an idle connection at handoff (assert zero open connections before the file is released: before `closeSync()` in the first build, before the worker is killed since D76);
   - a stale intent whose PID was reused; a writer blocked by a foreign holder, which withdraws its intent;
   - three direct app readers against one writer.

   Build: the suite lives in `tests/concurrency/` (runs, serve, direct) and uses real processes only: the CLI, `croft serve`, probe writers, foreign DuckDB holders and direct-mode apps. The timing budgets use a probe writer that follows croft's own intent protocol but retries the lock every 5 ms (a real `croft run` backs off up to 1 s, which would hide how fast serve lets go), measured from the writer's own intent `since`; real runs write in the same tests and must succeed. With the query worker (D76), `src/serve/instance.test.ts` adds a stuck query plus a writer (the writer's wait under `graceMs` + 1.5 s), deadlines and aborts of queries no interrupt stops (while executing and while planning), a worker crash, `kill -9` of croft serve leaving no lock, and the worker's peak memory for a 20M-row table read with `limit` 10.
5. **Crash tests.** `CROFT_FAULT=after_stage|before_commit|after_commit_before_sqlite|between_trash_and_drop|mid_chunk` makes the child `SIGKILL` itself (`mid_chunk`: halfway into filling the chunk after an incremental transform's first commit). The parent then asserts that data and state agree, the cursor is at most the committed maximum, and the next run succeeds. Build (phase 4): `between_trash_and_reset` (a `--rebuild` after its trash commit), `after_partial_commit` and `after_partial_commit_<n>` (after the first or the n-th monotone part), and `rename_before_commit`, `rename_after_commit`, `rename_after_state` and `rename_after_trash` (each stop of a rename, finished by running it again); `between_trash_and_drop` also covers `delete`, `restore` and a confirmed key conversion or pin change. The pre-upgrade backup is tested with a WAL left by a killed writer. No journey covers pre-upgrade backups, the drift view of `status` or `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE` yet; unit tests do.
6. **Scheduler tests** with a fake clock (`CROFT_NOW`) and a fake `HOME`. They check plist and crontab generation, registry pruning, heartbeat verification, the tick singleton, holds, stale-transform pickup, and DST golden days (2026-03-08 and 2026-11-01 in several zones). Real OS registration is exercised in a phase-3 spike and in manual release checks, because CI cannot install launchd jobs. Build: the registry lock has race tests (24 writers over a dead holder's lock, a pruning tick racing 12 writers, a holder killed inside the lock), and missing projects use a fake filesystem for mounted and unmounted disks. The e2e journeys turn scheduling on with `croft schedule on --no-os-job` under a temporary `HOME` and `CROFT_HOME`, and play the OS job by running `croft tick` at chosen `CROFT_NOW` times. The real LaunchAgent was checked once by hand [V] (§8).
7. **`@zabaca/croft/read` under Node** (current LTS) in CI, in both modes:
   - HTTP against `croft serve`: token, a wrong token (`SERVE_UNAUTHORIZED`), `503` with `Retry-After`, `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE`, and loopback with `HTTP_PROXY` set;
   - direct;
   - a golden test that the same query gives identical rows in both modes, and the Next.js `serverExternalPackages` setup.

   Build: `src/read/node-read.test.ts` builds the bundle with `scripts/build-read.ts` into a private folder and runs it under the real Node against a real `croft serve` process: the right and a wrong token, the `serve.json` route, `CROFT_URL` with `CROFT_SERVE_TOKEN`, a `503` retried until the same query succeeds after the write, `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE` once the client's timeout has passed, a recording `HTTP_PROXY` that sees nothing, direct mode, and identical rows from the server, Node direct and Bun direct. The Next.js setup is not covered yet.
8. **CI matrix.** A pull request runs the suite once, on Linux x64 glibc and the Bun floor (1.3.14), and a smoke on every other platform and Bun: Linux x64 on `bun@latest`, Linux arm64 on both (D191). A push to main and a daily run add the suite on those three, and the whole log run. macOS is tier 1 but has no CI job (D190). Alpine and Windows get smoke tests.

   Build: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on pushes to main, on `phase-*` tags (not the release tag, D196), on pull requests, daily (a `schedule`) and by hand.
   - The `test` job is the suite: `ubuntu-24.04` on Bun `1.3.14`, in seven shards (none cancelling the others; D155, D191), with Node LTS for the read client's test (item 7). Each runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `bun run typecheck` (shard 1 only) and the files `scripts/shard-files.ts K 7` lists for it (D196) with `bun test` in `packages/croft`. The `test-platforms` job is the same on the three other combinations in four shards each, on a push to main and daily and never on a pull request.
   - The `smoke` job (`scripts/smoke.ts`) runs on every pull request, push and daily run, on the three combinations `test` leaves out: a fresh project (this package linked in) runs `example_sales` and answers a query, a server-mode `croft serve` answers a key with the shared table and stops on SIGINT, and the five DuckDB extension files pinned for the platform pass their checksums and `LOAD`.
   - The `test-log` job runs the suite with `CROFT_BOOKKEEPING=log` (D132): on a pull request only the test files `scripts/bookkeeping-tests.ts` chooses, otherwise all of them.
   - The `alpine` job runs in the `oven/bun:1.3.14-alpine` container (musl): `croft --version`, then `croft init --no-install` with this package linked in, `croft run example_sales --foreground` and a `croft query`.
   - The `windows` job (`windows-2025`, Bun 1.3.14) installs and runs `croft --version` and `croft doctor --json` without judging the result. Native Windows is unsupported (§2), and croft prints no "unsupported" message of its own.
   - The agent evals (item 9) are not in CI: they need a logged-in Claude Code and cost money per run.
   - Releases: `.github/workflows/publish-npm.yml` runs on a pushed `croft-v*` tag. It refuses a tag that names another version than `packages/croft/package.json` and skips a version already on npm. It publishes what main already tested (D196): its `pack` job runs no suite, but refuses unless `ci.yml` passed on a push to main at the tagged commit (`scripts/release-gate.ts`, read-only through the job's own token, waiting up to 45 minutes for a run still going, failing for a run that failed, was cancelled, skipped croft's jobs or does not exist). It then runs the typecheck on Linux x64 (Bun 1.3.14), packs with `npm pack` and checks the tarball (`dist/read.js` and `read.d.ts`, `bin/croft.mjs` at mode 755, no tests, test kits, fixtures or evals). Its `publish` job, on a GitHub-hosted runner, refuses if `npm publish --dry-run` would correct the manifest and publishes that tarball through npm trusted publishing: no npm token, a GitHub OIDC token that `@zabaca/croft`'s trusted-publisher setting on npmjs.com accepts for this repository and file, and provenance. It is `npm pack` rather than `bun pm pack` because npm runs `prepack` (the read client's build) and writes the bin with mode 755, where `bun pm pack` copies the checkout's 777 [V: both packed 0.3.0, same 335 files]. No other package is published: the DuckDB extension files are DuckDB's, fetched from DuckDB's servers (D195; the add-on packages and `publish-addons.yml` of D134 and D135 were deleted). `tests/workflows.test.ts` fails if another workflow or trigger can publish. The release steps, in order: merge the version bump (`packages/croft/package.json`) to main and wait for main's CI to pass; push the tag `croft-v<version>` on that commit; the tag runs `publish-npm.yml` only; a run that stops at the gate is run again with `gh workflow run publish-npm.yml --ref croft-v<version>` once main's CI is green at that commit.

   During the build GitHub Actions did not run this workflow: the organization's account was blocked by billing ("recent account payments have failed or spending limit"). It runs now: the whole matrix passed at 4961185 (2026-09-25) and 6a79de3 (2026-10-18). From 004e167 the tier-1 jobs failed at the typecheck, on three errors in `src/project/init-tsconfig.test.ts`, and the 0.2.0 and 0.2.1 tags were red for it; the 0.3.0 work fixed them. Every phase's gates (the typecheck and the whole `bun test`, exit status checked directly) ran locally, on macOS arm64 (Bun 1.3.14) and in a Linux arm64 container (OrbStack, the `oven/bun` image, glibc), before Actions could run them.
9. **Agent evals** from phase 2 onward. Headless Claude Code sessions run fixture tasks:
   - "add Stripe charges and daily revenue, schedule hourly";
   - "the pipeline failed last night, fix it";
   - "rename a column used downstream";
   - "backfill 90 days";
   - "why is this number wrong";
   - "the API changed a field type".

   They are scored on success, number of commands, and whether the agent ever ran `croft confirm` without asking. Every stumble becomes a hint, a doc page or a template.

   The harness is `packages/croft/evals` (not shipped), run with `bun evals/run.ts [task…] --tag T`, with results in `evals/results/<date>-<tag>.json`. A fixture is a project as `croft init --no-install` and `bun install` leave it: this package linked in, a `croft` shim on `PATH`, a mock API with its secret in `.env`, and a git baseline commit so the agent's diff is recorded. Its `.claude/settings.json` allows croft, bun and the file tools, asks before `croft confirm`, and denies `Read(./.env*)`. Each session is told the user is away: do what it can without approval, and list what needs it. The scores are the verifier's pass (every warehouse, code, data and file check), the count of croft commands, `confirmWithoutAsking` (any `croft confirm` attempt), `readEnv` (any attempt to open `.env` or `.env.*`), turns, cost and duration. `bun test` runs only the harness's self-test and the tasks' own tests, never Claude Code.

   Build (phase 5): `evals/tasks` holds all six tasks of the list above (phase 2 had the first two, rename-column and wrong-number), each with a fixture, a prompt in the user's words and a verifier that checks the warehouse, the code, the data and the files:
   - **rename-column** ("rename a column used downstream"): `orders_clean` calls a column `cust`, and `customer_revenue` reads it, groups by it and keys on it. Both must be rebuilt with `customer_id` and the right numbers.
   - **wrong-number** ("why is this number wrong"): `daily_revenue` joins orders to their line items and so counts every order once per item. It must be right for every day, with the ingests untouched (`sum(DISTINCT …)` is a wrong fix the verifier catches).
   - **stripe-hourly** ("add Stripe charges and daily revenue, schedule hourly"): a new project with a Stripe mock. `stripe_charges` must be keyed by id, with an epoch-seconds cursor on `created`, a lookback of at least two weeks, every page fetched and an hourly schedule; `daily_revenue` is kept revenue per project-zone day; scheduling is left off for the user to turn on (ask-first). The verifier then plays the next hour: a two-week-old charge is refunded, a new one is made, and both must land.
   - **failed-last-night** ("the pipeline failed last night, fix it"): the orders ingest never followed the API's pages, the shop passed 100 orders, and the items ingest failed its blocking check. The fix must be in code, with the check intact.
   - **backfill-90d** ("backfill 90 days"): a merge ingest over an API that sends 14 days unless asked. The run must be `--from -90d` (a dry run first is fine), then the skipped transform rebuilt, with nothing much older fetched, the saved cursor unchanged and nothing confirmed.
   - **api-type-change** ("the API changed a field type"): the API now sends `total_cents` as a digit string, and the run failed with `TYPE_CONFLICT`. The value must become a number again in code (or through an integer pin), with the old rows not rewritten.

   The run tagged `p5-full` (`evals/results/2026-09-24-p5-full.json`; croft `0.1.0-dev.0` at `d9c3e3f`, Claude Code 2.1.281 with `claude-opus-5-5`, at most 60 turns and 20 minutes per task, with `CROFT_EVAL_INHERIT_ENV=1` and `CROFT_EVAL_USER_SETTINGS=1`) passed all six tasks: no `croft confirm` without asking, no attempt to read `.env`, 74 croft commands and 71 turns in all, $1.49, and about 4 minutes 15 s of session time. Claude Code ignored the fixture's `permissions.allow` entries in that run (it had never been told to trust the temporary folder), so two sessions had one command each refused, and both did the same work another way. Every stumble found while scripting the tasks' solutions became a fix: a backfill's `next[]` names the transforms it left stale, and the skill's Backfill recipe says to run them (§8); `croft schedule status` says to ask the user before `croft schedule on`; `croft schedule on` in a sandbox is a `USAGE_ERROR` that asks for the user's terminal, not an `INTERNAL_ERROR`; `TYPE_CONFLICT` says that a number pin takes digit strings exactly and that a `VARCHAR` pin breaks SQL that sums the column; and step log lines carry the project offset. The last, `croft status` showing a transform as `skipped` after its input failed even when a later run found it up to date, was fixed in the phase-5 fix wave.

## 11. v1 scope, cut list, and phased build order

### Cut from v1

Each item is marked with where it goes instead, if anywhere.

- **Incremental SQL** (`new.<table>`). It is designed and verified, and it is post-v1 #1.
- **`--to`/`--step` windowed backfills.** `--from` on merge ingests covers the need.
- **Schedules on transforms.** Transforms follow their inputs.
- **Native Windows** (use WSL) and Windows scheduler registration.
- **File reads inside SQL assets** (`SQL_READS_FILES`). Files come in through file ingests.
- **Named or virtual environments,** fingerprinted physical tables, plan/apply promotion, `copy` and `--database`.
- **A write daemon,** remote execution, multiple projects per database. (`croft serve` is in v1, but it only reads and schedules.)
- **Child tables, native STRUCT typing and flattening** of nested data. JSON columns are used instead.
- **SQL time windows and partitions** as concepts; view-kind SQL models; SQL macros and templating.
- **Standalone check files** (`checks/*.sql`). Row rules with subqueries cover most cases.
- **`query --write`.** `delete --where` and fixing the asset cover the need.
- **Exports:** `croft export`, and shipping data files to a hosting provider. (A hosted app can already query a `croft serve` the user runs, D53.)
- **`croft refs`** (column reference search). `rename` lists references, and `validate` plus the Proxy guard catch breakage.
- **Modeling features:** SCD2 history, delete propagation from sources, column lineage, SQL unit tests with fixtures, and quarantine of bad rows.
- **Source frameworks:** a declarative REST source DSL, and database sources as a feature. A Postgres ingest via `Bun.sql` is a doc recipe.
- **Scale and platform:** parallel SQL execution; OS keychain secrets; sensors and freshness policies; xlsx (needs a downloaded extension); a compiled single binary (works only with a dylib-embedding workaround [V]); tier-1 Windows.
- **Excluded by requirement:** a web UI, and dlt/SQLMesh/Dagster compatibility.

### Phases

Each phase is usable end to end, and each ships `--json`, error codes, docs pages and skill updates for what it adds. Estimates assume one engineer directing Claude Code. They were revised upward after the technical review, which judged the transform and scheduling estimates about 2× optimistic.

| Phase | Ships | Usable result | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Load and look** | launcher; `init` (empty folder and existing repo), relocation off synced folders; `doctor`; `docs`; skill and CLAUDE.md; `ingest()` for rows and files/URLs (`union_by_name`, encoding fallback, `map`); staging, classification, type rules, whitelisted casts, round-trip loss check, evolution (DDL before DML), JSON columns; replace (as a diff), append and merge with dedupe; typed cursors and lookback; the shrink guard with minimal trash and confirmation tokens; connection factory, sandbox and single-SELECT gate; `fromCache` instance registry; leases (with boot id) and lock diagnostics; `reconcile`; `run` (detach off a TTY, `wait`, signals), `query`, `status`, `describe`, `context`, `logs`, `secrets`; `@zabaca/croft/read` (built JS, direct mode with the write-intent handshake) | Claude pulls an API or a folder of CSVs into DuckDB incrementally, answers questions from it, and an app reads it | ~3.5 weeks |
| **2. Transform and trust** | SQL assets (single-statement check, temp-view wrapper, reserved columns, PIVOT, catalog and file-read errors, `VOLATILE_SQL`); dependencies from AST + unoptimized plan; graph, staleness and fingerprints; bind check (`INPUT_NOT_BUILT`, `NULL_ONLY_COLUMN`, `QUOTE_IDENTIFIER`); TS transforms (full and incremental, ordered Parquet snapshots, round-trip value types, Proxy rows, composite positions, chunked commits, cost guard); checks and warnings in the write transaction; `preview` (snapshots, partial diffs, `--rebuild`); `run --dry-run`; docs pages for its codes | raw → clean → report tables that cannot receive bad data, and per-row LLM transforms that survive failures without re-billing | ~4 weeks |
| **3. Keep it fresh** | gate: a spike on launchd and crontab registration; schedule phrases and the DST-defined matcher; per-user job, registry and heartbeats; `croft tick` (plan-and-spawn, singleton); holds, `pause`, stale-transform pickup; retries, no-progress timeouts, catch-up once, skip on overlap; desktop (default on) and webhook notifications; **`croft serve`** (HTTP read API with token auth, write-intent handoff, built-in scheduler loop) and the `@zabaca/croft/read` HTTP client; opt-in read copy | hands-off hourly pipeline that survives sleep, crashes and reboots, never runs half-finished edits, and serves apps (local or hosted) live data | ~3.5 weeks |
| **4. Grow safely** | monotone partial commits for cursor ingests (resumable first loads); full trash, `restore` and `delete` (whole table and `--where`); `--rebuild` rules; `--from` backfill matrix; `INGEST_CONFIG_CHANGED` and key conversion; `PIN_CHANGES_DATA`; `rename` and `ASSET_RENAMED`; drift warnings; `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE`; pre-upgrade backups; `EMPTY_EXTRACT` | long-lived sources and paid transforms change shape without refetching or losing data | ~2 weeks |
| **5. Agent-grade release** | all templates (every pagination style), a docs page per code, JSON Schemas and golden tests, generated input types (`.croft/types`, so `validate --types` catches renames in TS), agent evals in CI, CI matrix (Bun floor and latest), opt-in hook, npm 0.1 | Claude Code operates a project from a cold start, measured by evals | ~1.5 weeks |

**Phase 1 is complete** (2026-09-23). `core/phase.ts` records which command and flag ships in which phase (§4.1), and the agent texts are cut to match (§9, D59). Phase 1 had no `run --dry-run`, `validate` or `preview`: it backfilled with `croft run <asset> --from <when>`, checking the saved cursor first with `croft describe <asset>`. Its ingest templates are the docs page `croft docs ingest`, ahead of phase 5's `croft new` (D60).

**Phase 2 is complete** (2026-09-24), with about 2,230 tests. It ships SQL assets (§3c), the dependency graph, staleness and fingerprints, the bind check, TS transforms with snapshots, composite positions, chunked commits and the cost guard (§3e, §5), checks and warnings on every write (§3f), `validate`, `preview` with `query --preview` (§6), and `run --dry-run`, `--only` and `--upstream` (§4.1). The warehouse format is 3 (§5, D69). The build changed some decisions, recorded as D65–D75: a transform's duplicate key fails instead of being deduplicated, the preview keeps its own catalog, chunks are cut at a `newRows()` request, `ResolvedAsset` lives in `project/resolve.ts`, staleness compares a recorded input version (format 3), HUGEINT snapshots are text, SQL steps drop reserved names without regard to case, a position counts yielded outputs, header lines must come first, the SQL fingerprint keeps the case of column names, and `status` resolves the asset code. Phase 2 ships the `CLAUDE.md` block of §9 word for word, and SKILL.md with only phase 3–5 lines left out; its templates are the docs pages `ingest`, `sql` and `transforms`, with `checks` for the check language, ahead of phase 5's `croft new`. It also ships a docs page for each of 23 codes (the 17 codes phase 2 first raises, and six older ones that its SQL assets and bind check raise most), ahead of phase 5's "a docs page per code", and the agent eval harness with its first two tasks (§10). Not yet: schedules, `croft serve` and the read copy (phase 3), and `--rebuild`, `rename`, `delete` and `restore` (phase 4), so hints name what this build can do instead (§4.1).

**Phase 3 is complete** (2026-09-24), with about 2,985 tests. It ships schedules (§8): the phrase parser and the DST-defined matcher, `croft schedule on|off|pause|status`, the per-user OS job (a LaunchAgent on macOS, verified on a real Mac [V], and a crontab block on Linux), the project registry with its OS lock, the per-user tick script and heartbeats, the project tick (`croft tick`, hidden) that plans and spawns `croft run --due`, the due set with its holds, backoff, catch-up once and skip on overlap, and failure notifications on the desktop and to a webhook. It ships `croft serve` (§5): its query worker and watchdog, streamed results within `limit`, `maxRows` and `maxBytes`, a bounded queue, the serve gate's `SHOW` and range limits, the write-intent handoff, `GET /status` as the status envelope, and the scheduler loop; and the opt-in read copy, from which serve answers with `stale` and `asOf`. Scheduling shows in `status`, `doctor`, `context`, `describe` and `validate`. `runs.sqlite` gains its `settings` table (migration 2); the warehouse format stays 3. The build changed some decisions, recorded as D76–D85: croft serve holds the file in a worker process that it kills to release it, holds in a scheduled run are warnings, a phase has a completion flag, the scheduler caches what it knows of each asset by file hash, interval crons fire at both passes of a repeated hour, `GET /status` is the status envelope without asset code, the registry takes an OS lock and keeps missing projects for 30 days, the job's Bun is never older than croft needs, a generated serve token is new on every start, and a scheduled transform's failure backs off. Phase 3 ships the `CLAUDE.md` block of §9 word for word, and SKILL.md with its phase-3 lines restored and only phase 4–5 lines left out, plus a Schedule recipe; the docs topics `scheduling`, `serve` and `read-copy`; and pages for five more codes (§9). The e2e suite gains `j20`–`j23`, and the concurrency suite and the read client under Node now run against real processes (§10). Not yet: `--rebuild`, `rename`, `delete` and `restore` (phase 4), and `croft new` (phase 5).

**Phase 4 is complete** (2026-09-24), with about 3,310 tests. It ships the full trash (§6): versions of a whole table or of the rows a `delete --where` removed, kept 30 days and 5 versions per asset, pruned after each trash and by `doctor`; `croft restore` (the list, and a version picked with `--at`) and `croft delete` (a whole table, or rows by `--where`), which ask first, spend their tokens under the asset's lease and are recorded as runs. It ships `run --rebuild` (§6): an ingest refetched with its old table kept until the refetch commits, an incremental TS transform redone with one token for the rebuild and its cost guard, and SQL recomputed as always, with the `--rebuild` texts of §8's backfill table and of `EDITED_SINCE_LAST_RUN`. It ships `croft rename` with its crash-safe journal, and `ASSET_RENAMED` in `validate`, `status`, `describe` and `context`, whose asset `run` and `preview` never refetch; `INGEST_CONFIG_CHANGED` with the key conversion `croft run` asks for, and `PIN_CHANGES_DATA` with lossless retypes applied directly, both reported ahead of the run from the catalog mirror; monotone partial commits for cursor ingests (§8) and `EMPTY_EXTRACT` (§3a); `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE` at every write lease and in `doctor`, and the drift warnings in `status`, `context` and `doctor` (§5, §7); and backups before a DuckDB upgrade (§6). A scheduled run no longer imports TS code a human has not run (§6). The warehouse format stays 3, and `runs.sqlite` gains the setting `duckdb`. The build changed some decisions, recorded as D86–D95: the trash keeps a version while either retention limit holds, and `doctor` prunes it; a lossy pin trashes the whole table; `croft run` itself asks for a key conversion or a pin change; an ingest `--rebuild` swaps its table at commit; the partial-commit order is checked per value, and the cursor goes back when it breaks after a commit; `EMPTY_EXTRACT` needs a configured lookback; a rename keeps a journal, and runs refuse a renamed asset; the pre-upgrade backup is made before the open, not under the write lease; `doctor` compares tables read-only within a time budget; and delete and restore run as a run's step. Phase 4 ships the `CLAUDE.md` block of §9 word for word, and SKILL.md with its phase-4 lines restored and only phase 5's `croft new` lines left out; the docs topics `rename` and `trash`; and pages for five more codes (§9). The e2e suite gains `j24`–`j27` (§10). Not yet: `croft new`, `validate --hook` and `init --with-hook` (phase 5).

**Phase 5 is complete** (2026-09-24), with about 3,610 tests, so **all five phases are complete**. It ships `croft new` with every template (§3, §4.2, D98): `api` in all four pagination styles (keyset, cursor as the default, link and page), `file`, `sql` and `transform`, each commented, saying when it applies and passing `croft validate` as written; `new --list`; and refusals that never overwrite a file. It ships a docs page for every one of the 105 registered codes (§9), and JSON Schemas of every command's `--json` output, generated from the TypeScript types, shipped in `schemas/` and golden-tested against real output (§4.3, D99), with `schemaVersion: 1` on every envelope. It ships generated input types (§3e, D96): `.croft/types` after every run and preview, `rows("x")`, `newRows("x")` and `query<"x">` typed by name, the `tsconfig.json` of `croft init` including `.croft/types/**/*.d.ts`, and `croft validate --types` reporting a column renamed upstream as `UNKNOWN_INPUT_COLUMN` before anything runs. It ships the opt-in Claude Code hook (§9 item 7, D97): `croft init --with-hook` merges it into `.claude/settings.json`, the only way init writes that file, and `croft validate --hook` checks each edit in `assets/` and `lib/`, silent unless there is an error, which goes to stderr with exit 2, a behavior checked against Claude Code's hook documentation [V]. The `CLAUDE.md` block and SKILL.md ship as §9 word for word, with no cut list and no "This version" section. The six agent evals pass 6 of 6 in the `p5-full` run (§10 item 9), with no `croft confirm` without asking, no attempt to read `.env`, and $1.49 for all six; the CI workflow has the tier-1 matrix and the smoke jobs (§10 item 8). The warehouse format stays 3, and `runs.sqlite` gains no migration. The build changed some decisions, recorded as D96–D99: the input types reach code by augmenting an empty `CroftAssets` interface, and the row types have no index signature; the hook runs the project's pinned bin from `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, also checks `lib/` edits and SQL readers, and stays silent on warnings; `croft new` picks the input of an `sql` or `transform` template from the project and defaults to cursor paging; and the schemas are generated rather than written. The e2e suite gains `j28`–`j30`, and `tests/golden` its `g01`–`g05` (§10). Not done as planned:
- the agent evals run by hand, not in CI;
- GitHub Actions has never run the workflow (billing), so the gates ran locally on macOS arm64 and in a Linux arm64 container;
- the Windows smoke job prints no "unsupported" message, since croft has none;
- the hook has not run inside a live Claude Code session [U];
- `croft delete`, `restore` and `rename` do not regenerate `.croft/types`;
- the `croft new transform` template's explicit row type keeps `validate --types` from checking the transform (§3e); fixed before the release (R51-01), the template now reads `newRows("x")` untyped.

Also since 0.1.0: `croft query` groups thousands only in integer columns, `croft wait` returns once the run's process has exited, the hook's outside-the-project case uses a temp folder of its own, and `BUN_TESTED` is 1.4.3. **The 0.2.1 release (2026-10-18).** Package metadata only: the npm README follows the repository README's message (packages/site/test/readmes.test.ts keeps the two in step), and `package.json` gains `homepage`, `repository`, `bugs` and `keywords`. No code changed.

**The 0.3.0 release (2026-10-18).** What two croft projects had to build themselves (mined with the consumer-mining skill), built in: CSVs whose lines mix CRLF and LF load, file ingests read YAML, and files outside the project are documented (D101); hints that say only what DuckDB's message proves, including the `->>` precedence trap (D102); `okStatus`, `http.head()` and a public `getBytes()` in ctx.http (D103); per-host request budgets in croft.json (`http.budgets`, `HTTP_BUDGET_SPENT`), counted in runs.sqlite, whose schema goes to version 3, so an older croft refuses a project this one has opened (D104); a run and the scheduler hold an asset inside a known wait (`HTTP_WAIT`, D105); `incremental: { once: "key" }` for paid work once per output key (D106); a blocking `not_null` the last run passed narrows the generated types, and two holes in when checks run again are closed (D107); `secretsFrom`, a command that prints secrets (`SECRETS_COMMAND_FAILED`, D108); and `croft backup`, the 21st command (D109). The full suite passed on macOS arm64 (3,760 tests). The `npm pack` tarball was inspected (335 files: 0.2.1's 328 and the seven new ones, `bin/croft.mjs` at mode 755) and `npm publish --dry-run` corrected nothing; installed in a temporary folder it made a project, ran the example, answered a query, took a backup and loaded a YAML file. It is the first release published by `.github/workflows/publish-npm.yml` (§10 item 8) from its `croft-v0.3.0` tag.

**The 0.4.0 release (2026-10-28).** croft moves to DuckDB 2.0.0 (`@duckdb/node-api` 2.0.0-r.1), and only 2.0 (D111). An agent-lab experiment (`experiments/2026-10-28-croft-duckdb2-release`) ran the suite on the bare bump (309 of 3,756 tests failed) and found that 2.0 runs `WITH x AS (DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE … RETURNING *)` and `WITH x AS (COPY … TO …)` as one SELECT, through the gate: the gate and check vetting now refuse every query node that is not a read (D112), and `tests/e2e/j31` sends that battery through every way croft runs user SQL. The AST walk reads 2.0's shapes and byte positions; an arrow lambda is `LAMBDA_ARROW` with the edit that rewrites it (D113); a PIVOT without IN is found by 2.0's refusal to serialize it; `->`'s hint and the docs follow 2.0's precedence; a partly read stream is closed before its connection runs anything else, and a write whose body went on after DuckDB refused a statement no longer commits (on 2.0 that COMMIT silently wrote nothing). An SQL asset's code hash is DuckDB's tree, so the upgrade rebuilds each SQL transform once, "DuckDB upgraded (1.5.5 → 2.0.0)", with no `EDITED_SINCE_LAST_RUN` and no `SCHEDULE_HELD` when its source is unchanged (D114); `runs.sqlite` goes to schema 4 for that (`code_sources`), so croft 0.3 refuses a project croft 0.4 has opened, and `doctor` names the pre-upgrade backup, the way back. Parquet `TIMESTAMP_NS` now rounds (D115). The full suite passed on macOS arm64 (3,807 tests, 0 failing; the flaky serve memory test aside, below). A manual journey upgraded a croft 0.3.0 project in place: `doctor` announced the backup; `status` and `run --dry-run` said "DuckDB upgraded" for the unedited transforms, "SQL changed" and held for the edited one, and `LAMBDA_ARROW` with its edit for the arrow lambda; the first `run --due` made `…-1.5.5-to-2.0.0.duckdb`, rebuilt and re-approved the unedited transforms and held the edited ones, and the next tick ran nothing; `show t` worked over croft serve and the DELETE CTE did not; a delete and a restore worked; croft 0.3.0 then refused `runs.sqlite` with `DB_NEWER_FORMAT`, and opened the backup. Not done: `serve/instance.test.ts`'s worker-memory test stays flaky on macOS, as on 1.5.5 (`peakRss()` can take a byte `maxRSS` for kilobytes); the Bun range and glibc floor of the 2.0 bindings were not measured.

**The 0.4.1 release (2026-10-30).** A SQL transform's new or recreated table is created with its rows (D116). On DuckDB 2.0.0 the empty `CREATE … AS SELECT … LIMIT 0` then `INSERT` of 0.4.0 left a table over one row group (122,880 rows) reading as empty to aggregates and joins in the process that wrote it (duckdb/duckdb#28158): its recorded row count was 0, its blocking checks passed on no rows, the SQL downstream in the same run read it as empty, and the next write reported `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE`. Upgrading does not repair a table 0.4.0 built that way: a SQL transform over about 122,880 rows first built or reshaped on 0.4.0, and what reads it, keep their contents until they are rebuilt. The full suite passed on macOS arm64 (3,813 tests, 0 failing) and on CI's macOS, Ubuntu x64 and Ubuntu arm64 jobs at Bun 1.3.14 and latest. The `npm pack` tarball was inspected (340 files, as 0.4.0; `bin/croft.mjs` at mode 755, `dist/read.js` and `read.d.ts` present, no tests or fixtures) and installed in a temporary folder: `croft init` made a project, the example ran (120 rows) and a query answered; a 200,000-row SQL transform and the SQL over it built right on its first run, where 0.4.0 gave `0, NULL` [V].

**The 0.5.0 release (2026-11-04).** croft gets two optional modes, each off until a project turns it on; a project that turns neither on keeps its file warehouse format, stays offline and gets no new files (its writes are now counted by classifying the batch first, D133, to the same numbers, and D158 below applies to it). Server mode (`serverMode.enabled` in `croft.json`; D119 to D131, D136) puts the readers in a process of their own over a read copy of the warehouse, so `croft serve` never holds the live file or waits for a run; a person gets a read-only key (`croft serve key add <name>`, D122), which reaches only the tables the project names in `serve.sharedTables`, works only in server mode (D128), and is checked on every request and by one synchronous gate that every query passes (D123). Those people can also connect with their own DuckDB 2.0 through Quack (D125), which listens on loopback unless the project accepts plaintext on the network (D131) and caps its queries (D130, D136). Lake mode (a `lake` block in `croft.json`; D132, D137 to D154) makes the warehouse a DuckLake: the catalog is a Postgres, the data is Parquet in an S3-compatible bucket such as Cloudflare R2, and croft's own bookkeeping is an append-only log in the lake (D132). One machine writes and any number read (D144). A pass of maintenance runs daily, or on `croft maintain`, and keeps what the trash promises (D149, D150, D152); a backup is a dump of the catalog and a mirror of the bucket's folder (D151); the catalog connection and the store are checked over TLS and a failure says which (D159 to D161); credentials live only in named secrets (D141). `croft move-to-lake` moves a project that keeps a file into a lake that has been described in `croft.json` with `"enabled": false`: it backs up, copies in one transaction, proves the copy equal from the read-only login and then switches, as one confirmation (D167 to D172), and the way back is the setting (D170). Server mode works over a lake as well, answering from the lake's newest snapshot with no copy (D183 to D186). The extension files these modes load come from DuckDB's own servers on first use, are checked against the checksums croft pins, and are kept on the machine (D195): a download of about 21 MB for server mode and 34 MB for lake mode, which take about 66 MB and 109 MB on disk once unpacked (macOS arm64; the Linux files are larger), once per machine and DuckDB version; `croft fetch-extensions` fetches ahead of time for a machine that will have no network, and `CROFT_NO_FETCH=1` turns the first-use fetch off; croft publishes nothing but itself, and `croft validate`, `doctor` and `status` never fetch. What an upgrader must know: a `croft serve` or a long run that is still the older croft across the upgrade must be restarted after it, because this release stamps leases, write intents and run records with macOS's boot session UUID and a croft older than this release reads a stamp of that kind as another boot's, and so as dead (D158; a run in progress can finish first). No file project changes format: the file warehouse stays at format 3 and `runs.sqlite` at schema 4, so nothing is migrated or rebuilt.
