It checks `.ts` and `.sql` files in `assets/` and any file in `lib/`, with what they can break (an SQL asset's readers; a `lib/` file's importers). Errors go to stderr with exit 2; warnings and a clean check are silent with exit 0. init merges the entry into the settings file, keeps everything else, never adds it twice, and leaves a file it cannot read untouched with a `USAGE_ERROR` that carries the snippet.
- Reason: `bunx` fetches from the registry when nothing is installed, and the npm name `croft` is another package. A bare `croft` makes the launcher plan from Claude's current folder, which follows its `cd`: outside a project that is `PROJECT_NOT_FOUND` with exit 2, which would block Claude on every edit, and inside another croft project it would run that project's copy. `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is the folder whose settings hold the hook [V: Claude Code's documentation]. A `lib/` edit breaks assets as surely as an asset edit, and an SQL edit breaks its readers' bind. PostToolUse exit 2 shows stderr to Claude after the tool ran [V], which is the point; a warning such as `SECRET_MISSING` would otherwise follow every edit, so success stays silent, as §9 asks. The handler avoids newer fields (`if`, `args`) so older Claude Code versions read it; croft answers an edit outside its folders in about 0.1 s without them.

**D98. What `croft new` writes, and what it reads. (new, 2026-09-24; refines §3a–§3e, §4.1 and §4.2)**
- Options: templates that name a placeholder input, or read one from the project; `--pagination` required for `api`, or a default; overwrite an existing file, or refuse.
- Choice: `agent/new.ts` renders every template in code (`templateFor(kind, name, {pagination, input})`, pure), and `cli/commands/new.ts` checks the name, picks the input, creates the file exclusively and says what to do next. `api` defaults to `cursor`. An `sql` template reads the asset whose file changed most recently, and a `transform` the most recent one with a key; with nothing suitable to read, the command refuses. Each API template reads one secret named after the asset, with a placeholder URL on `api.example.com`, so `validate` passes with only `SECRET_MISSING`, and `next` is `croft secrets` while that secret is missing. A name taken by a file anywhere in `assets/**`, or by a table whose file is gone, is `NAME_CONFLICT` with the first free `<name>_N`.
- Reason: the skill says "start from a template, don't invent APIs", so every template must pass `validate` in the actual project, which a placeholder input would not; the asset just made is almost always the one to read next. Cursor paging over a newest-first list is both the common API shape and the safe one, whereas keyset over a newest-first API skips records (§3a); the output says the default was used. A template written over a file, or into a table that still holds data, would destroy work, so croft new never does either. The transform template makes no request as written, so it neither needs a secret nor counts as paid work until the user adds the call.

**D99. JSON Schemas generated from the TypeScript types. (new, 2026-09-24; refines §4.3)**
- Options: hand-written schemas beside the types; schemas generated from the types by a script whose output is committed; runtime validation of every envelope.
- Choice: generated. `scripts/build-schemas.ts` reads `core/types.ts` `Envelope` and each command module's `CommandImpl<T>` with the TypeScript compiler, and writes `schemas/` (draft 2020-12, closed objects, `$defs`). The files are committed and shipped; `cli/schemas.ts` imports only types and `schemaFor()` reads the files. A test fails while they differ from the generator's output, and the golden tests validate real envelopes with a small test-only validator. croft never validates its own output at run time.
- Reason: a hand-written schema drifts from the code the first time a field is added, and the golden tests would then check the wrong thing. The generator needs the `typescript` devDependency, which must not load at run time, so it is a script and its output is data. A test-only validator of the subset the generator writes adds no dependency, and it throws on any other keyword, so no schema relies on a rule it would skip.

**D100. Apps read typed rows by table name. (new, 2026-10-18; extends D96 to @zabaca/croft/read)**
- Options: augment a `CroftAssets` interface of the `@zabaca/croft/read` module, as D96 does for transforms; a global interface; the app imports the generated row types by path.
- Choice: global. `src/read-types.ts` declares an empty global `CroftTables` and `TableRow<N>` (the table's row type when croft wrote one, plain rows otherwise), and `query()` gains a second overload, `query<N extends string>`, returning `TableRow<N>[]`; an explicit row type still selects the first. `.croft/types/<asset>.d.ts` adds `<Asset>ReadRow`, the same columns typed as json mode renders them (BIGINT `number | string`, HUGEINT and every DECIMAL `string`; a DOUBLE stays `number` although NaN and Infinity arrive as text), and `index.d.ts` adds each to `CroftTables` in a `declare global` block beside the `CroftAssets` augmentation.
- Reason: an app with its project in `data/` has its own copy of croft, and a module augmentation from `data/.croft/types` reaches only the copy it resolves, never the app's [V: tsc 5.9, two installed copies of the same version]; a global merges whichever copy declares it [V]. The transform types cannot be reused: `ts` and `json` mode hand over different values. `query<"x">` for a table with no type yet is plain rows rather than an error, so an app typechecks on a machine that has not run the project [V]. The rows are as typed as the app's `tsconfig.json` lets them be: it must include the project's `.croft/types`. For an app with the project in `data/`, `croft init` proposes it (D42): `exclude` names `data/assets` and `data/lib` rather than `data`, since `exclude` filters whatever `include` matches and would drop `data/.croft/types` [V: tsc 5.9], and `include` gains `data/.croft/types/**/*.d.ts`, which matches nothing before the first run and is then no error [V]. Without an `include`, TypeScript's default `**/*` is written out with it; under `extends` the base may set its own, so that half is left to the user, and so is an app that already excludes all of `data/`.

**D101. File ingests read CSVs with mixed line endings, and YAML. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §3b)**
- Options for a CSV whose lines end in both CRLF and LF: let DuckDB's error stand under a better hint; refuse it with `FILE_UNREADABLE` naming the line endings; rewrite the user's file; read a rewritten copy. To find the mix: a scan that ignores quotes, or one that tracks `"`. For YAML: leave it to a rows() ingest; a YAML package; `Bun.YAML`. A top-level mapping as one row or one row per key; empty documents skipped or `ROW_NOT_OBJECT`; integers beyond ±2^53 refused or warned.
- Choice: read a copy. A native `indexOf` pass looks for a CRLF and a bare LF anywhere; only a file with both gets a second, quote-aware pass that writes `<snapshot>-lf.csv` with every CR of a CRLF outside quotes dropped, and the copy is kept only when both kinds occur outside quotes. The recorded sha256 and size stay the snapshot's; the step's log says how many lines ended in each. UTF-16 files are not checked. `format: "yaml"` (`.yaml`, `.yml`, the YAML content types) parses with `Bun.YAML.parse` and stages rows like JSON: a list is rows, a mapping is one row, a document stream is one row per document, and null items and empty documents are skipped. Big integers keep the existing `UNSAFE_INTEGER` warning, with a hint to quote them in the file.
- Reason: a project's CSV gained one row ending in LF among 106 ending in CRLF; the sniffer failed for every dialect, and so did a declared one [V], so there is nothing to declare and refusing would leave the user to fix a file that holds no wrong value. Outside quotes a line ending only separates rows, so the copy changes no value, and keeping the user's file and its hash untouched keeps change tracking (§3b "Tracking files") exactly as it was. Tracking `"` keeps an Excel export, whose cells break lines with a bare LF inside CRLF rows, from counting as mixed [V]; a file quoted with another character is rare enough to fall back to DuckDB's error. YAML specs beside a project were read through hand-written `fs` code; Bun parses YAML with no dependency, and mapping it as JSON maps keeps one rule for both. `Bun.YAML` cannot return big integers losslessly and a stream of documents arrives as a list, so the warning and the skipped empty documents are the honest limits rather than new rules; YAML's own typing (`007` is 7) is what any YAML reader does, and the docs say to quote.

**D102. Hints say what the message proves, and name what it hides. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §2, §3b and §5 "Errors from user queries")**
- Options: DuckDB's message as the only guidance ("DuckDB's message says what went wrong"); a regex on broad words choosing one cause (the old `FILE_UNREADABLE` hint matched "line", "column", "quote" or "dialect" and said the rows do not all have the same columns); hints keyed on the exact shape of a message, each saying only what that shape proves. For a project inside a package-manager workspace: refuse, edit the workspace's `package.json`, skip `bun install`, or say so.
- Choice: shapes. `FILE_UNREADABLE` names a ragged line only after a strict read's "Expected Number of Columns", tries such a read when the sniffer finds no dialect, and otherwise lists the usual causes. `QUERY_FAILED` from a Conversion Error that quotes a whole JSON value, or a `json_extract(…BOOLEAN…)` Binder Error, says that `->>` and `->` take everything to their left and to parenthesise; the same hint reaches `ctx.query`'s errors. `croft init` reports a workspace that takes the new project in (`data.workspace`, with the `!` pattern to add) and changes nothing.
- Reason: the old CSV hint was wrong for a mixed-line-ending file, and the project it misled wrote "never append to a CSV" into its README and skill; almost every DuckDB CSV message contains "line", so the regex proved nothing. `a AND j->>'k' = 'v'` failed three SQL assets of one project six times, and DuckDB's message ("Failed to cast value to numerical: {…}") points at the data, not the precedence [V]. Both are facts croft can recognise in the message, so the hint can be exact where it speaks and modest where it cannot. The workspace's `package.json` is the user's file and `bun install` there works, only not as a project pinned on its own, so a printed exclusion is enough: with `"!packages/data"` added, `bun install` in the project wrote its own `bun.lock` and `node_modules` [V: Bun 1.3.14].

**D103. Expected statuses, HEAD and bytes in ctx.http. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §3a "ctx.http" and §10 public types)**
- Options for an expected non-2xx: leave it to `.catch()`; a `throwOn` list of statuses that throw; an `okStatus` list of statuses (400 and above) returned as a response. For bytes: keep `getBytes` croft's own; type it in the public `Http`; read every body as bytes and add `res.bytes` to every response. For conditional requests: `ifNoneMatch`/`ifModifiedSince` options, or the `headers` code already passes.
- Choice: `okStatus`. A listed status is returned at once and never retried, a 5xx or 429 included, since the code asked to see it; an unlisted 429 or 5xx is retried and thrown as before. `head()` joins `get()` and `post()`. `getBytes()` and `HttpBytesResponse` (`res.bytes`, `text` decoded only when read) become public in ingests and transforms. Conditional requests stay plain headers, and a 304 is a response, as it always was; the docs now say so.
- Reason: the `.catch(() => null)` that a "does this exist" probe needed also swallowed 429s, 5xx and timeouts, so an outage of one API silently spent another's quota; a list of what the code handles keeps every other failure loud. `throwOn` would turn the default around and make every caller list the errors. `getBytes` was internal only because file ingests were its one user; it already had the retry, `Retry-After`, timeout and redaction rules, and code that read a PDF as text measured characters of a decoded binary. Bytes on every response would hold each JSON page twice. Header options would add names for what `headers` already says.

**D104. Per-host request budgets. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §3a "ctx.http", §5 "Where state lives" and §8 "Retries")**
- Options for where: on the asset; in `croft.json` by host. For counting: logical requests or attempts; fixed windows (the clock hour, the calendar day) or rolling ones; in memory per run, or in `runs.sqlite` across runs. When spent: fail with `HTTP_ERROR` as if the server had said 429; a code of its own. For previews: exempt, or counted. For the dry run: a request estimate from a declared `requestsPerRow` times the pending rows it counts.
- Choice: `croft.json` `http.budgets`, keyed by host (`URL.host`, or the hostname), with `perMinute`, `perHour` and `perDay`, rolling. Every attempt is counted, before it is sent, in `runs.sqlite` `http_requests` (migration 3), read and recorded in one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, and kept a day. A spent budget is waited out within `maxRetryAfterMs`, like a `Retry-After`; past it the request is not sent and fails with `HTTP_BUDGET_SPENT` (retryable, `details.retryAfterMs` and `freeAt`), which the runner's `retryAfterOf` treats as a long `Retry-After`: `nextRetryAt`, partial commits and the scheduler's backoff work as they do for one. Previews count, in the live `runs.sqlite`. The dry run shows no request estimate.
- Reason: a quota belongs to the API account, which every asset that calls the host shares, so a per-asset budget would let two assets spend it twice; the host is what `ctx.http` sees. The API counts retries, so croft does. A rolling window never sends more in a span than a fixed-window API allows either, so croft need not know which kind the API is. A run learns nothing from a previous run in memory, and every rerun spent requests learning the limit from a 429 again; `runs.sqlite` is local, already shared by every process of the project, and keeps the design's one machine. A code of its own says "croft did not send this", so it cost nothing and the fix is the budget, not the API. A preview's requests are real. The dry run cannot know how many requests code makes: a `requestsPerRow` hint would be a guess multiplied by a count that excludes rows not yet fetched, and the cost guard already shows the rows it would pay for (`estimatedRequests`), so a number of requests would claim more than croft knows. `fetch` and SDKs bypass the budget; only `ctx.http` can count.

**D105. A run holds an asset inside a known wait. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §8 "Retries" and "What counts as due")**
- Options: print `nextRetryAt` and leave it there (as built before); refuse `croft run <asset>` with an error; hold the step with a warning; hold it with a `--force`-style override. For the scheduler: an ingest waits for its next fire whatever failed (as built); a fire inside the wait waits for the wait.
- Choice: hold, with the warning `HTTP_WAIT` (exit 0), in every run by hand and its dry run: an asset whose latest step failed with a `Retry-After` not over yet (from when the step ended), or with `HTTP_BUDGET_SPENT` while the budget is still spent (asked again, so a raised budget or one freed since ends it). The held step is skipped and not recorded, and what reads it still runs. No override flag. The scheduler holds such an ingest as `backoff`, still due, and its `--due` plan as `retry_after`. A preview is not held.
- Reason: an agent loop made a run every 20 minutes inside a wait the server had already stated, each spending one request on the same 429; nextRetryAt in the output did not stop the next command. An error would fail the run and make a bare `croft run` fail for one asset that is only waiting; a warning, like `SCHEDULE_HELD` (D77), is what a hold is. Readers go ahead because the held table is unchanged, which is what they would read anyway. A flag would hand the loop that caused this a way past the hold, and the hold costs only the wait the server asked for; the budget's wait is re-asked each time, so the user's fix (a raised budget) applies at once. The preview stays the way to try now on purpose.

**D106. Paid work once per key: incremental: { once: "key" }. (new, 2026-10-18; refines §3e, §5 "Cost guard" and §8 "Incrementality by asset type")**
- Options: (a) `incremental: { once: "key" }` over the input's key: `newRows()` hands an input row over only if its input key was never handed over before, which needs a new record of every key handed over, kept in step with chunks, `--rebuild`, the trash and restores; (b) leave out the input rows whose output key the transform's own table already holds, the output key read from the input row (by name, or through a `from` mapping); (c) give the code read-only access to its own table (`has(key)`, `existing()`), keeping `UNDECLARED_INPUT` for every other table. Separately: which spelling (`once: "key"`, `skipExisting`), and whether the template defaults to it.
- Choice: (b), spelled `incremental: { once: "key", from? }` beside `true`, which keeps its meaning. croft decides in the `new.parquet` snapshot, under its lease: `NOT EXISTS` against the table, and one row per output key in position order. The cost guard and `croft describe` count the same rows. `paidReadersOf` leaves such a transform out of an ingest rebuild's paid readers. A `from` column the input lacks is `UNKNOWN_INPUT_COLUMN` before any of its rows. `croft new transform` keeps `incremental: true` and names the option in its comments; the paid example of `croft docs transforms` uses it, and the skill says when to.
- Reason: the unit of paid work is the output key, and the input key is not always it: an input keyed `(a, b)` feeding a transform keyed `b` would still pay again under (a) whenever a new `a` finds an old `b`. The table already records which keys are done, durably and in step with every commit, so (b) adds no state: `--rebuild` (the table trashed) and `croft restore` (the table back) need no new rules. Under (c) each project writes the check itself, and the cost guard, which counts before any code runs, cannot know which rows the code will skip, so it would ask for work the code never does. Deciding in the snapshot keeps the code's view, the guard's count and the preview's cap the same rows. `true` stays the default, and the template's, because re-processing a changed row is right for work on the row's content, such as a summary of edited text.
- Open: `croft run --dry-run` reads only `runs.sqlite`, so for a once-per-key transform its estimate is an upper bound and may show a confirmation the run would not ask for.

**D107. Blocking `not_null` checks narrow the generated row types. (new, 2026-10-18; refines D96, D100 and §3f)**
- Options: keep every non-key column `T | null`, so code that relies on a check writes `String(row.x)` or `row.x!`; narrow from the asset's code (its blocking `not_null` checks, from the SQL header or the TS `checks`); narrow from the record of the step that last built the table. For the record: tell blocking checks from warnings in `StepResult.checks`, or keep a separate list in the catalog mirror. Narrow in every write mode, or only where each save rewrites every row (a full-refresh SQL asset).
- Choice: the record. `StepResult.checks[]` gains `blocking` (false for a warning). types-gen reads the asset's last ok step (`RunsDb.lastStepChecks`) and drops `| null` from the columns of its passing blocking `not_null` results, in `<Asset>Row` and `<Asset>ReadRow` (`vouchedNotNull`), in every write mode. `validate --types` narrows an SQL asset's code columns only where its code and the record agree. Two gaps in "a new or edited check covers the whole table once" close with it: a blocking check counts only blocking ones as run before (a warning made blocking is new), and the last ok step's record does not count while a later run that did not end ok has written the table (the mirror's `lastRunId`), unless that run is the one asking. `validate --types`' NULL hint suggests the check.
- Reason: the code says what the next build must pass, not what the table holds; a check added since the last run has not looked at it, and a transform run on its own reads that table. The record says what every row passed: a check covers each write's rows and, when new, the whole table (§3f), so rows an append or merge kept were checked when written, and narrowing only full refreshes would leave out the ingests and incremental transforms where the check matters most. Its two gaps were real for the checks themselves and would have made the types lie: a warning's failing rows commit, and a failed chunked transform commits rows under checks its last ok step never ran. A separate list in the mirror would have to be kept right by every path that writes the mirror (restore, delete, reconcile, rename, pin changes); the results are written once, by the checks, and a restore or delete records a step with none. Results an older croft recorded do not say which were blocking, so they narrow nothing until the asset's next run. `blocking` is optional in the type for those records; everything croft writes now has it.

**D108. Secrets from a command named in croft.json. (new, 2026-10-18; extends D26, refines §6 "The scheduler only runs code a human has run")**
- Options: an OS keychain or a SOPS integration built into croft; one command per secret (`{"STRIPE_KEY": ["sops", "-d", "--extract", …]}`); one command whose output is `.env` text, `secretsFrom: {command: [...]}`. For its place in the order: shell, command, `.env`; shell, `.env`, command. For when it runs: on every command, as a wrapper script does; whenever a `ProjectEnv` loads; only when a secret the shell and `.env` lack is asked for.
- Choice: one command, an argv run without a shell, whose stdout is parsed as `.env`; the shell, then `.env`, then the command; run only by `ctx.secret()` and `croft secrets` for a name the other two lack, at most once per process, with no input, croft's environment minus its own credentials, and 60 s. Its values stay in memory and join the `.env` redaction set; a failure is `SECRETS_COMMAND_FAILED` with its redacted stderr, remembered and raised for every name it would supply; `validate` and `doctor` call such names `unchecked` and never run it, and `doctor` checks only that its program is on `PATH`, and on the scheduler's. A human-initiated run or preview of an asset that declares secrets approves the command (its hash in `runs.sqlite`), and an unapproved command holds the assets that read secrets with `SCHEDULE_HELD`.
- Reason: one command covers every store that can print dotenv (`sops -d --output-type dotenv`, `op inject`, a script) and runs once, where a command per secret runs one decryption per key and says nothing a single one cannot. Most local wins: a shell variable is the most specific override, `.env` is this checkout's, the store is shared, so `.env` beats the store; that also keeps `croft secrets set` and every "add NAME=… to .env" hint working, and lets a project whose secrets are all set elsewhere never run the command. Running it only on demand is what the wrapper got wrong: read-only commands (status, query) and the hook after every edit pay a decryption and possibly a prompt for nothing. The scheduler runs without the user's shell, so the command must not depend on it (absolute paths, variables set in the command, no prompt), and the program check in `doctor` says so before the first scheduled run fails. The command is code that a scheduled run would execute on the first `ctx.secret()`; holding the assets that read secrets until a person has run one under it keeps §6's rule without putting the command in any code hash, which would make transforms stale and re-bill them. croft.json is the user's own file, as asset code is, and D3 is unaffected: the launcher and the tick read it and never run the command. Not covered: a value only the command holds is unknown to processes that did not run it, so `croft query` cannot redact it from table data, which `.env` values are.

**D109. A consistent backup of the project's data. (new, 2026-10-18; extends D93 to backups a person asks for)**
- Options: tell users to copy `warehouse.duckdb` by hand; `EXPORT DATABASE` or `ATTACH … COPY FROM DATABASE` on croft's own connection; `CHECKPOINT` plus a child-process clone under a write lease, as the read copy does. For where: a folder the user must name; `.croft/backups/` by default; a folder outside the project by default. For putting it back: a `croft restore` of backups; a separate command; manual steps.
- Choice: `croft backup [<dir>]`, a new folder per backup in `<dir>` or `.croft/backups/`, with the warehouse checkpointed and cloned, `runs.sqlite` through `VACUUM INTO` and the trash cloned, all under one write lease behind a write intent, and `backup.json` written last; staged in `.croft/backups/` and copied across after the lease when `<dir>` is on another filesystem; never overwritten, never deleted. Putting one back is manual, documented in `croft docs backup`.
- Reason: a hand copy while a writer or croft serve holds the file, or with commits in the WAL, is torn or short: a clone without `CHECKPOINT` missed 1,500 committed rows [V]. The lease is the one protocol every croft process already obeys, so croft serve steps aside and runs wait without new code, and the clone keeps it to milliseconds (172 MB: checkpoint 1.8 ms, clone 1.3 ms) where a plain copy took 61 ms, `EXPORT DATABASE` 156 ms and `COPY FROM DATABASE` 197 ms [V]; the last two rewrite every row and write only inside the sandbox's `allowed_directories`, so they could not reach another disk ("file system operations are disabled by configuration") [V]. `.croft/backups/` as the default works with no argument and clones for free, at the price of sharing the disk, which the output says; it is relocated with the state folder off synced folders. Restoring by hand keeps `croft restore` the trash's alone, and replacing a whole warehouse is rare and needs the user anyway; a command for it would need its own confirmation and checks against a running croft serve. The cost: a project with no cloning filesystem holds the file for a full copy, as the read copy does.

**D110. A croft subagent next to the skill. (new, 2026-10-19; extends §9)**
- Options: leave delegation to the user, who writes their own subagent around the skill; ship an agent only in the Claude Code plugin; have `croft init` write one into the project, beside the skill. For how it gets the skill: tell it in its text to load the skill; preload it through the `skills` field.
- Choice: `croft init` writes `.claude/agents/croft.md` (§9 item 2a) wherever it writes the skill (the project, and the app root for a project in `data/`), stamped with the croft version; `init --claude` rewrites it and `doctor`'s `CLAUDE_FILES_OUTDATED` covers it. It preloads the skill with `skills: [croft]` and also says to load the skill when it is not in its context, which is the case in a session started as the agent. It names no `tools`, so it has what the session gives subagents, under the session's permission rules, with `model: inherit`. The plugin ships one too (`croft:croft`), whose text sends it to the project's skill inside a project and to the plugin's getting-started skill before there is one.
- Reason: every project, however small, benefits from a warehouse and the reports on it, and the person who wants one most often asks their coding agent for it; a subagent that owns that work keeps the main conversation's context for the app, and a team gets one by name instead of writing it. The project copy is versioned with the skill it preloads, as the skill is with the CLI, so they never disagree; the plugin's copy cannot be, and only routes. Preloading is documented ("the full skill content is injected") [V: code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents, read 2026-10-19], and a session on a new project found the project skill by its bare name: the agent, with every tool denied, quoted the skill's Orient line and version stamp [V: Claude Code 2.1.304, 2026-10-19]. A session started as the agent (`claude -p --agent croft`) does not preload it and had no `AskUserQuestion`, and the agent's text was its system prompt [V: Claude Code 2.1.304, 2026-10-19]; the sentence in its text covers that case, and the person in that session can answer in the conversation. The one rule that depends on how it runs is asking. In a session of its own the user is there, and the skill's rule holds as written. As a subagent it has no `AskUserQuestion` [V, same page], and a yes it read in its task was given before the impact existed, so its text turns each ask-first step into a stop that returns the impact and the command, and runs it only when the main conversation answers with the user's yes. A subagent cannot check that answer, and does not need to: the main conversation could run `croft confirm` itself, so the gate is the person, through the `ask` rule below, not which agent types the command. In a session told up front that "the user already said yes", the subagent ran `croft delete`, stopped at the confirmation and returned; the main conversation then sent it the approval and it confirmed [V: Claude Code 2.1.304, haiku, 2026-10-19]. Both start by stopping with the impact and the command, so an agent that cannot tell which it is loses nothing by acting as a subagent. Permission prompts still reach the user from a subagent [V, same page], so the `ask` rule on `croft confirm` (item 7) gates it as well.

**D111. DuckDB 2.0, and only 2.0. (new, 2026-10-28; refines §5 "Owning the DuckDB file", §6 "Before an engine upgrade", §10 "Runtime")**
- Options: support 1.5.5 and 2.0 side by side (two AST shapes, two gates) or move to 2.0 alone. For storage: write new files in 1.5's format (`storage_compatibility_version`), or in 2.0's own; convert existing files, or leave them. For going back: an export croft 0.3 can read, or the pre-upgrade backup.
- Choice: `@duckdb/node-api` 2.0.0-r.1, pinned exactly, and nothing for 1.5.5. Files DuckDB 2.0 creates use its own storage format; a file 1.5.5 made stays in its format (2.0 opens it, replays its WAL and checkpoints into it, and 1.5.5 still opens it afterwards) [V]. Going back to croft 0.3 is through the pre-upgrade backup (§6), which `doctor` names; runs.sqlite goes to schema 4 (D114), which 0.3 refuses, as 0.3.0 set the precedent for (D104). A file a newer DuckDB made is `DB_NEWER_FORMAT` with `details.kind: "storage"` and the newest backup, wherever croft opens or attaches one.
- Reason: the AST croft walks (the gate, dependencies, code hashes) changed shape in 2.0 (function arguments, literals, casts, SHOW, positions in bytes), and two walkers would double the surface the gate's safety rests on. A compatibility storage version would keep 2.0's newer encodings off every file for the sake of an older croft that cannot open the project anyway (runs.sqlite). The backup is already made before the first 2.0 write, so the way back costs nothing new.

**D112. A read is a query node croft knows. (new, 2026-10-28; refines §5 "Sandboxing every DuckDB instance")**
- Options: deny the write statements by name; allow the read query nodes by type.
- Choice: the gate and check vetting refuse any query node (an object whose `type` ends in `_NODE`) other than SELECT_NODE, SET_OPERATION_NODE and RECURSIVE_CTE_NODE, anywhere in the tree (`QUERY_NOT_SELECT`, `SQL_NOT_SELECT`, `CHECK_INVALID`), with a hint that names a CTE that writes or exports.
- Reason: DuckDB 2.0 parses `WITH x AS (DELETE … RETURNING *) SELECT …` and `WITH x AS (COPY … TO …) SELECT …` as one SELECT that json_serialize_sql accepts, and runs them; COPY wrote files even on a READ_ONLY connection [V: agent-lab 2026-10-28-croft-duckdb2-release]. An allowlist of three types fails closed on whatever node a later DuckDB adds.

**D113. Arrow lambdas are an error with the edit that fixes them. (new, 2026-10-28; refines §3c)**
- Options: set DuckDB's hidden `lambda_syntax` setting so `x -> …` keeps working; refuse arrow lambdas with a fix.
- Choice: `LAMBDA_ARROW`: an SQL asset with an arrow lambda (a SINGLE_ARROW LAMBDA that is an argument of one of the twelve functions DuckDB gives a LAMBDA parameter, or the expression of `COLUMNS(...)`) does not load, a check with one is `CHECK_INVALID`, and `croft query`, croft serve and `ctx.query` map DuckDB's binder error to it. The fix is an edit, `(a, b) -> a + b` to `lambda a, b: a + b`, cut from the lambda's byte span; a manual fix when the span cannot be split.
- Reason: the setting is hidden, DuckDB says the arrow goes away in its next release, and the sandbox locks the configuration anyway. JSON's `j->'k'` parses as a SINGLE_ARROW lambda too; only a lambda function's argument is one, so JSON is never matched.

**D114. An engine upgrade rebuilds once, unedited and unheld. (new, 2026-10-28; refines §8 "What a code change does", §6 "The scheduler only runs code a human has run")**
- Options: treat the new code hashes as edits (EDITED_SINCE_LAST_RUN, and SCHEDULE_HELD until a person runs each SQL asset); keep the 1.5.5 hash; prove the source unchanged and carry the approval.
- Choice: every SQL transform rebuilds once with the reason "DuckDB upgraded (1.5.5 → 2.0.0)", with no `EDITED_SINCE_LAST_RUN` and no `SCHEDULE_HELD` when its source is unchanged; the run that rebuilds it approves the new hash, a scheduled run included. runs.sqlite schema 4 records, per SQL code hash, the source hash (header and body as written, with the time zone) and the engine (`code_sources`). A hash with no row (croft 0.3) counts when it is the asset's build, that build predates the engine switch, and the file is not newer than the build. A real edit is still an edit.
- Reason: the hash is DuckDB's parse tree, so the upgrade changes it without anyone editing anything, and a hold on every SQL asset would stop every schedule until a person ran each by hand, for a change the person made by upgrading. The rebuild stays: the new engine may compute some values differently (D115), and a rebuild is safe where a missed one is not. A git checkout bumps mtimes, so a 0.3 project checked out again falls to the safe side, an edit.

**D115. Parquet TIMESTAMP_NS rounds as DuckDB 2.0 does. (new, 2026-10-28; refines §7)**
- Options: read nanosecond Parquet timestamps through croft's own truncation; accept DuckDB 2.0's rounding to microseconds.
- Choice: accept it. DuckDB 1.5.5 truncated (`.0000005` read as `.000000`); 2.0 rounds (`.000001`, and `2024-12-31 23:59:59.9999995` reads as `2025-01-01 00:00:00`) [V: 2.0.0, `load/files.test.ts`]. A file ingest that re-reads a Parquet file with nanosecond timestamps may update its rows once after the upgrade.
- Reason: croft stores microseconds either way; rounding is DuckDB's reading of the file, and a one-time update is what a changed reading of the source should be.

**D116. A SQL transform's table is created with its rows. (new, 2026-10-30; refines §5 "Transforms", D71)**
- Options: keep the empty `CREATE OR REPLACE … AS SELECT … LIMIT 0` and `CHECKPOINT` after the write; create the table from column definitions spelled as text, then `INSERT`; create it with its rows in one `CREATE OR REPLACE … AS SELECT`.
- Choice: the last. A first build or a recreate is `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t AS SELECT <columns>, <stamp>::TIMESTAMPTZ AS _loaded_at FROM <source> ORDER BY _croft_seq`; it counts every row as added and every earlier row as deleted, as before. The same shape is still a diff into the table. The source of a keyed file reload with fallback rows (§3b, `load/write.ts` "Overlapping files") is one `CREATE` as well, never an empty one and then an `INSERT`.
- Reason: on DuckDB 2.0.0, a table an empty `CREATE … AS SELECT` (`LIMIT 0`, `WHERE false`, or a filter nothing passes) made in a transaction, and then given more than one row group (122,880 rows) by an `INSERT` from a TEMP table, reads as empty to ungrouped aggregates (`sum` and `max` NULL, `count(*)` beside them 0) and to joins, a `MERGE` included, until a `CHECKPOINT` or a reopen; a bare `count(*)`, filtered counts and `GROUP BY` are right, and 1.4.3 is right [V: 2.0.0, duckdb/duckdb#28158]. So the first build of a 200,000-row SQL transform recorded a row count of 0, its blocking checks passed on no rows, the SQL downstream in the same run read it as empty, and the next run reported `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE` [V: 2.0.0, `run/sql.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/j16-sql-transforms.test.ts`]. A `CHECKPOINT` would fix the table only after the checks and the row count had already seen it empty, and spelled types are what D71 avoids. The fallback source's empty `CREATE` deduplicated with a window function, which kept it clear of the bug on 2.0.0 [V: 2.0.0]; it follows the same rule so that no write depends on which plans the bug spares.

**D117. Pinned extensions, loaded by path. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §2 "No extension downloads", §5 "Sandboxing every DuckDB instance"; option 06 slice 1, shared with 07)**
- Options: let DuckDB `INSTALL` an extension from its repository the first time a mode needs it; bundle the files in croft's npm package; load files from a folder by absolute path after checking each against a checksum croft pins.
- Choice: the last. `db/extension-pins.ts` holds, for DuckDB 2.0.0 and each tier-1 platform (osx_arm64, osx_amd64, linux_amd64, linux_arm64), the sha256 and size of the unpacked quack, httpfs, ducklake, postgres and sqlite (test lakes only) files, generated from DuckDB's official repository over HTTPS by `scripts/pin-extensions.ts`. A mode checks every file before it loads the first, then `LOAD`s each by absolute path in a fixed order. A missing file or an unpinned platform is `EXTENSION_MISSING`, a different file `EXTENSION_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH`, one whose footer names another DuckDB version or platform `EXTENSION_WRONG_BUILD`, and DuckDB refusing a checked file `EXTENSION_LOAD_FAILED`; each has a hint and a fix: a manual one for a file in a folder, and, since D195, the fetch command. The file errors are found before anything loads, so they leave the instance clean; `EXTENSION_LOAD_FAILED` comes after earlier files may have loaded, so the instance is marked failed and not reused (D118). No code path issues `INSTALL`, and a test reads croft's source to prove it. In slice 1 the files came from a folder the caller names, filled by `scripts/fetch-extensions.ts` for tests, builders and CI (a CI step fetches and verifies them, and the tests fail in CI rather than skip). How a user gets them (add-on packages, a first-use download, or bundled) was decision a of the option: add-on packages (D134), replaced by a fetch from DuckDB's servers (D195); nothing in `croft.json` turned a mode on in slice 1 (`serverMode`, D119, turns the readers' mode on).
- Reason: croft's promise is that it never installs anything and works offline; a run-time `INSTALL` would break both, and would let the extension repository (or whatever answers for it) put native code in croft's process. The files are over 100 MB per platform, so bundling them would multiply a default install by an order of magnitude for projects that never turn a mode on. Pinning the checksum of the unpacked file, the thing that is loaded, keeps the guarantee whatever way the files arrive later. The footer read gives the common mistake (a file copied from another DuckDB or machine) its own code, instead of a bare mismatch.

**D118. A lockdown per mode, and its order. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Sandboxing every DuckDB instance"; option 06 slice 1, shared with 07)**
- Options: one lockdown for every instance, widened to what the widest mode needs; a lockdown per mode, built from the instance's local-folder profile plus what the mode attaches and allows; locking first and attaching through a side door.
- Choice: the second. A `SandboxSpec` keeps its profile (which local folders) and gains an optional `mode`: `readers` (quack, httpfs; the read copy attached read-only; afterwards the copy's path allowed through `allowed_paths` and no folder), `lake` (httpfs, postgres, ducklake; the one Postgres catalog attached through a named secret, writer or read-only; the bucket folder the only remote path), `lake-readers` (the lake read-only plus quack) and `lake-test` (a SQLite catalog and a local data folder; croft's own suite). The order is fixed: check the files, load them, point DuckDB's secret folder into the state folder, create the lake's two in-memory named secrets and attach, run the caller's hooks and start the listener, then lock. Credentials are only in those secrets, never in an attach text, a fingerprint or an error: a failed lake attach is `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED`, with every credential scrubbed from DuckDB's text, and `scrubError` is the same for a caller's query errors, but wiring it into the query paths that run on a lake is option 07's slice 2 and is not done in this slice. A mode runs only under the local-folder profile it fits (`readers`, `lake-readers` and `lake-test` under `serve`, with no folder), the sandbox fingerprint holds the mode's access, catalog and bucket so a read-only request cannot be handed a writer's instance, and a mode that fails after it started marks its instance failed. The mode adds no setting the lock does not already refuse, and `lock_configuration` stays on every instance.
- Reason: DuckDB refuses `LOAD`, a remote attach and Quack's `quack_serve` once outside access is off, so everything a mode needs has to happen first, and Quack's server reads DuckDB's default secret folder in the user's home unless it is pointed elsewhere before it starts [V: 2.0.0]. The profiles differ in what they must reach afterwards: the readers' process reaches one file and nothing else (not the live warehouse, `files/` or the state folder), a lake reaches its bucket folder and, for a writer, the project's own folders. Keeping the local-folder profile separate from the mode lets a lake behind croft serve be `serve` plus `lake-readers` without a fifth copy of the rules. Reading the lock honestly mattered: it does not refuse a local attach inside the allowed folders or paths (the trash and the readers' swap need that), so the gate has to refuse attaches in user SQL, as it already does.

**D119. Server mode reads only the read copy. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs", "Owning the DuckDB file" and "Processes", D53 and D76; option 06 slice 2)**
- Options: one long-running croft process that owns the warehouse file and takes every read and write (the first spec); croft serve keeps holding the live file read-only and stepping aside (D53, D76); croft serve holds only the read copy, in a readers' process, and croft's writes stay exactly as they are.
- Choice: the last, behind `serverMode.enabled` in `croft.json` (off by default; turning it on turns the read copy on). croft serve then never opens the live file, holds no lock on it and creates no write intent; `serve/readers.ts` is a second engine behind the same HTTP layer (`serve/open.ts` picks it), and the readers' process is `serve/worker.ts` started with `readers`: an in-memory instance with quack and httpfs loaded by path, the copy attached `READ_ONLY` as `wh`, and the lockdown of D118's `readers` mode, with every connection on `USE wh` so the serve gate and the app token see the copy as they see the live file. The engine polls the copy's identity every 250 ms and swaps a refreshed copy in (detach, attach); the refresh marks its temporary file read-only before the rename and removes `<copy>.wal`; a query past its deadline ends with the process and a new one starts at once; a process that cannot start its mode ends itself and is started again after a backoff, and one whose swap fails is killed and replaced at once (its replacement's start then backs off if it fails too); every answer carries `asOf` and none is `stale`. D1 (no write daemon), D53's token, Host and Origin checks and D76's kill-to-release hold as written, and croft's writes still run in short-lived processes.
- Reason: the first spec's owner process needed a writer password any program on the machine could read, exposed a database that writes to remote queries, could not stop a runaway query without killing croft's writes in flight (croft ends such queries by killing their process, D76), and left open how croft's own commands would send their writes. Reading from a copy keeps all of that out: nothing remote can reach a database that writes, a kill touches no write, and a refresh was already croft's code. It costs freshness (an answer is as of the end of the last run that changed data, and says so) and, where the filesystem cannot clone, disk and write time (D121). It gives readers a process with no lock on the live file, so nobody waits for anybody, at the price of tools that opened the copy read-write now having to open it read-only.
- Naming: DESIGN.md called apps reading through croft serve "server mode" (D53, §5). From here that is **reading through croft serve**, and "server mode" is this setting; the sections and D53 are reworded, and §5's heading keeps its name so the cross-references to it stand.
- Build: the readers' process keeps its instance referenced for its whole life (Quack's listener, once slice 4 starts one, stops when its instance is collected [V: 2.0.0]). `DuckDBInstance.fromCache(":memory:")` returned two different instances with separate catalogs in two calls [V: 2.0.0, `@duckdb/node-api` 2.0.0-r.1], so reuse is not the hazard it was feared to be; what is marked failed is the instance object (D118), and the process exits anyway. A read-only attach replays a valid WAL in memory, where the option's text said it ignores it [V: 2.0.0], and SQL can create `<copy>.wal` (the sandbox lets a database's own WAL path through), so the readers' process removes it before every attach and the refresh removes it before and after its rename. `ATTACH OR REPLACE` on the same path does not read the new file, so a swap is a detach then an attach; a connection's `USE wh` follows by name, a query that starts during a swap waits for it, and one that straddled it is run again once. This slice starts no Quack listener, registers no hooks and creates no views: the shared tables, keys and Quack are slices 3 and 4, so "the app token is refused on Quack" has nothing to refuse yet. The extension files come from `$CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR` or `~/.cache/croft/test-extensions` (`resolveExtensionDir`), filled by `scripts/fetch-extensions.ts`, until slice 5 decided how users get them (the cache is `~/.cache/croft/extensions` since D195, which fetches them from DuckDB's servers). New codes: `SERVER_MODE_COPY_COSTLY` and `READ_COPY_NOT_CLONED` (D121). The first copy: a project that turns server mode on with nothing left for a run to change would have no copy (a run makes none when every asset skips), so croft serve makes a missing, behind or failed copy itself in a child process (§5), which keeps its own promise never to open the live file.

**D120. One read-copy refresh per run. (new, 2026-11-01; confirms §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs"; option 06 slice 2)**
- Options: refresh after every write step; refresh once, at the end of every run that changed data (what croft already did).
- Choice: the second, and in server mode it is the only refresh: a checkpoint, a child `cp -c` (reflink, plain `cp` as fallback), the checkpoint's time as the copy's mtime, then the rename, once per run, under the write lease, as `db/readcopy.ts` does for `readCopy`.
- Reason: a run's downstream transforms rebuild in the same run, so a copy taken at its end shows every table at one consistent point; a copy taken after each step could show an ingest's new rows beside a revenue table not yet rebuilt from them. It also makes one copy per run rather than one per step, which matters where the filesystem cannot clone, and it is the code croft already has. The cost: during a long run, readers see the state before it. A run that failed partway still refreshes the copy when a step committed, so readers see the partial state the live file holds (a run is not one transaction, §5). A refresh per step later is a decision for when a team asks.

**D121. The copy policy where the filesystem cannot clone. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs"; option 06 slice 2)**
- Options: say nothing; warn; refuse server mode above a size unless the project accepts the cost.
- Choice: warn, refuse at turn-on, and report loudly after. `db/copy-policy.ts` tries to clone a 64 KiB file in the warehouse's folder strictly (`copyFileSync` with `COPYFILE_FICLONE_FORCE` on macOS, since `cp -c` copies silently on a volume that cannot clone and exited 0 on FAT; `cp` with reflink always on Linux), only for a warehouse of 100 MB or more, once per folder per process. `croft doctor` and `croft status` warn (`READ_COPY_NOT_CLONED`) when the read copy is on, the clone fails and the warehouse is at least 100 MB, naming the disk and the seconds each refresh costs (a range). Server mode refuses to start (`SERVER_MODE_COPY_COSTLY`, an error with the setting named in its hint) when the clone fails and the warehouse is over 1 GB (1,000,000,000 bytes), unless `serverMode.acceptFullCopyCost` is true. The refresh never refuses: a warehouse that grows past 1 GB under a running server keeps being refreshed, because a refresh that stopped would leave the server answering older and older data. The cost is reported in four places instead: a warning in each run's output, an error in `croft status` and `croft doctor`, `serverMode.copyCost` in `GET /status`, and `degraded` in `GET /health`. The setting is the user's to accept: the skill lists it as ask-first.
- Reason: the cost of a plain copy is the warehouse's size in disk and in write-lease time at every run. Measured on an Apple SSD (APFS): checkpoint 5 to 12 ms and a clone 3.3 to 10.5 ms at 1 to 5 GB with about no extra disk, against a plain copy of 0.44 s and 1.07 GB at 1 GB and 1.96 s and 5.35 GB at 5 GB. On Linux without reflink (ext4, the usual filesystem) a full copy costs as much disk again as the warehouse, and the run holds its write lease for the whole copy, roughly 2 to 40 s at 5 GB (inferred, not measured). So the warning is the normal case on most Linux servers, and the refusal applies there to any warehouse over 1 GB. The threshold is the plan's choice: 1 GB is where a plain copy already took 0.44 s and 1.07 GB of disk; Linux measurements can move it. The 100 MB floor for the warning is this build's: below it a copy costs well under a second and next to no disk, and a warning on every small project would be noise.

**D122. A key per person, and the tables a key may read. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs" (Security) and D84; option 06 slice 3)**
- Options: one token for every reader; a token per person with the app token's reach; a key per person that reads only the tables the project names; database logins in a server.
- Choice: the third, over croft serve's HTTP API, in server mode only (amended 2026-11-01 by the maintainer's decision, D128; as built it worked with or without server mode). `croft serve key add <name>` makes 32 random bytes behind `croftkey_`, prints them once and keeps only their SHA-256 in `<state>/serve-keys.json` (0600, never in `croft.json`, git, the warehouse or a backup); `key list` shows names, creation and last use; `key remove <name>` ends one. The tables are `serve.sharedTables` in `croft.json` (asset names, validated like every setting, reviewed like code); with none named, every key query is refused (`SERVE_NO_SHARED_TABLES`, 403) before its body is read, and each engine refuses it too. A key is checked on every request (`verify()` compares the keys file's identity and reads it again when it changed), so a key removed or added while croft serve runs is honoured on the very next request, and a keys file it cannot read means no key is valid. A key is valid on `POST /query` only. Any table that is not shared is refused in the words for one that does not exist, the same words whether or not it does (no suggestion, no list of what else exists); `SHOW TABLES` lists the shared tables that exist; a CTE may take any name but DuckDB's own built-in ones, a hidden table's included, because refusing it would tell a key which names are tables (D122, Build). `serve.sharedTables` is read when croft serve starts, so a change to it needs a restart; the keys file needs none. In server mode the readers' process makes a view of each shared table the copy has in its in-memory database and a key's connection works there (`USE memory`), rebuilt at every swap; without server mode the query used to run on today's query worker, which steps aside for writes as for the app token, behind the gate alone; from D128 a key is refused there. One log line per key query on stderr: name, time, tables read, rows, duration, a refusal's code. `key add` is on the skill's ask-first list; `remove` and `list` are not.
- Reason: a shared token cannot be taken from one person without changing it for everyone, and says nothing about who read what; the app token's reach is every table, which is right for an app the project owns and wrong for a person it does not. A hash makes a copy of the project folder, or a backup, harmless; SHA-256 rather than a slow password hash because a key is 256 random bits, not something a person chose. Checking on every request is what makes "removing someone takes effect at once" true, and Quack's sessions in slice 4, which outlive a request, need the same check. Failing closed on both a missing table list and an unreadable keys file (`SERVE_KEYS_UNREADABLE`: croft serve accepts no key, and the key commands never overwrite the file) means turning keys on never exposes anything by accident. `serve.sharedTables` is read at start, so a change to it needs a restart of croft serve. Whether a key may ever write is the option's decision b, recommended never and not yet made: this slice builds read-only, which is safe either way (a key reaches only the one SELECT the gate allows).
- Build: the gate had a hole that the key's attack list found: `SHOW TABLES FROM _croft` (SHOW_REF, show type SHOW_FROM) was allowed over HTTP for the app token and listed croft's own tables; it is refused for every serve connection now (`collect()` reports it as the show use `__show_from`). `getenv` is refused by name for the serve profile although DuckDB 2.0.0 has no such function (it errors at bind), since the attack list names it and a build that has it would read the server's environment. A key's `SHOW TABLES` is rewritten into a SELECT of the shared names (the core returns the SQL to run), and refused inside a larger query. The readers' process caches a catalog snapshot per way of reading the copy (the app token's `wh`, a key's views) and drops it at a swap; a key's connection is a pooled connection told `USE memory` on use. A CTE named after a hidden table was first refused (as a name a CTE may not take), while one named after a name that no table has was allowed, which let a key list the project's table names one guess at a time; the review found it. A CTE's name is now judged the same whatever tables exist: only DuckDB's built-in names are refused, and `serve/key-queries.test.ts` and `sql/gate-core.test.ts` send 13 CTE shapes (nested, recursive, read by earlier and later CTEs, in subqueries, with the case changed, quoted) twice, once with a hidden name and once with an absent one of the same length, and require the same status, words, position and rows. What keeps such a CTE from reaching the hidden table is the walk's reading of CTE scopes (`sql/ast.ts`, held to DuckDB's plans by `ast.test.ts`), and, in server mode only, the views database, where a hidden table has no name; a file-mode key's connection is the live file, and an in-memory database cannot be attached to a read-only instance (`Cannot launch in-memory database in read-only mode`) [V: 2.0.0], nor can `USE temp` be used. The key commands' `--json` data has `key` in `add` and nowhere else. Slice 4 built what was left: passing key changes to the readers' process (D126; the HTTP path checks in croft serve itself and needs no push), the Quack hooks and the as-of view (D125).

**D123. One synchronous gate. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D112 and §5 "Sandboxing every DuckDB instance"; option 06 slice 3)**
- Options: keep the async gate and let Quack's authorization hook wait on DuckDB; a second, hand-written check for the hook; one synchronous decision with its inputs computed beforehand.
- Choice: the third. `sql/gate-core.ts` `decide()` takes the query's text, the statement count and `json_serialize_sql`'s text, the profile's options, a catalog snapshot (serve profile) and, for a query that names a path, a path policy with the glob matches, and returns the AST, the SQL to run and the tables read, or throws the same `CroftError`s as before. `sql/gate.ts` is the async shell that fetches the inputs (`gateSelect`, `assertOneSelect`, `loadCatalog`) and takes a precomputed catalog snapshot from a caller that runs many queries on one attached file (croft serve's workers); the path policy is read per gated query that names a path. The importers of `lineColumn`, `TABLE_FUNCTIONS` and `SelectAst` were repointed at `gate-core.ts` and nothing re-exports them. Checks (`checks/parse.ts` `vetCheck`) keep their own narrower rules and then decide with a policy that lets a check read no file, in place of their own copies of the write-node, `write_log` and `setval` refusals. Glob expansion stays an async step before the decision, and only for profiles that allow paths.
- Reason: Quack's authorization hook must decide at once, and the gate waited on DuckDB four times (statement count, serialization, catalog, globs). Two copies of the rules would drift; one function cannot, and the test that sends the existing gate cases through every path (`serve/gate-paths.test.ts`) and the one that sends the same query through the shell and the core (`sql/gate-core.test.ts`) keep it so. The catalog snapshot is one read per attached file because the file cannot change under a worker until the swap that replaces it.
- Build: the serve profile now reads its catalog before it decides, where it read it lazily when a table appeared; croft serve's workers keep it, `croft query` and the other paths read it per query only for the serve profile. The catalog holds views as well as tables, so a key's connection in the readers' process (whose shared names are views in its own database) and the file engine's (tables) are the same rule. For a key the names a CTE may not take are DuckDB's built-in ones only (D122).

**D124. Ending a refresh child. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D119; option 06 slice 2's review)**
- Options: SIGKILL, as before; SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period; and, for a child whose croft serve was itself killed, nothing, or a bound it sets itself.
- Choice: SIGTERM first (stopping, and the 12-minute bound), SIGKILL after `stopGraceMs` (5 s); the child catches SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP, finishes the refresh in hand and exits. It watches its parent every 500 ms and, once the parent has changed, gives the refresh in hand `orphanGraceMs` (a minute) and then kills itself.
- Reason: the refresh checkpoints the live warehouse, and a SIGKILL there leaves DuckDB a crash to recover from; a refresh is milliseconds to seconds, so asking costs little. A SIGKILLed croft serve cannot tell its child anything, and a refresh waiting for the write lease (up to 30 s) or copying a large warehouse must not outlive its server by long. A refresh that is waiting for the lease cannot be aborted from outside, so a stop can wait out the grace.
- Build: tested with a real refresh (the read-copy code against a real project, held by a hook between the checkpoint and the clone): asked to stop it finishes and the copy is whole; with a short grace it is killed and the live warehouse still opens with all its rows; with its parent SIGKILLed it ends itself within its grace. Replacing SIGTERM with SIGKILL in `CopyMaker.end()` fails the first two.

**D125. Quack for people's DuckDB, from the read copy. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs", D118, D119, D122 and D123; option 06 slice 4)**
- Options: HTTP only for people; Quack from a process that owns the live file (the first spec); Quack from the readers' process on the read copy, with croft's own hooks deciding every sign-in and query.
- Choice: the third. The readers' process registers two JavaScript hooks and a macro in its in-memory database and starts Quack's listener in `prepare`, before the lock (D118's order), on `serverMode.quackHost` and `quackPort` (127.0.0.1 and 9494, 0 for a free port). Authentication maps a key (its SHA-256, compared with every listed digest in constant time) to a person and the session to that person; the app token is refused. Authorization checks on every query that the session's key is still listed, lets the client's transaction control and two catalog queries through by their exact bytes (the catalog ones swapped for queries that list only the main schema and the views), and sends everything else through `decide()` (D123) narrowed to the shared tables and the as-of view `_croft_as_of`, on the parsed query the macro passes in. A refusal is a thrown error carrying the CroftError's message, hint and code. The shared tables are views in the in-memory database (D122), which a Quack session always starts in; the as-of view is one row, rebuilt at every swap. Any address but loopback sets Quack's `allow_other_hostname` and turns its TLS off and says an HTTPS reverse proxy belongs in front. The key command and `croft serve --json` carry how to attach (`data.quack`), so an agent gets what a person does.
- Reason: Quack's hooks must answer at once, which the synchronous core (D123) was built for; the catalog queries are what makes an attach list the right things, and recognising them by exact bytes is the only rule the reviewer's bypasses (a catalog function's name in a comment, a string or after `--`, the exact text with a trailing space or `; DROP` appended) could not get past. Views in the in-memory database are the allow-list a Quack session needs, since it starts there and no setting changes that. A listener past localhost serves TLS with a certificate of its own, which a client cannot use without pinning it; croft's design is a proxy that holds the real certificate, as for the HTTP API, so the listener speaks plain HTTP to it. The log line has no rows and no time because the hook runs before the query does (the spec's "the same log line" is the same line without those two numbers, and it says `over Quack`).
- Build: a hook that throws shows the client `Authorization callback failed: <message>`; a null return shows only `Authorization failed` [V: 2.0.0]. The scalar functions croft registers take the session as its 32-character upper-case hex id, the same one `quack_active_connections()` lists. The serve gate refuses any scalar named `croft_*` or `quack_*`, and the attack list gained the hooks and Quack's helpers. A `SHOW TABLES` over Quack is the SELECT of the shared names; a `json_serialize_sql` error that is not a parse error counts as one statement that is not a SELECT. The catalog texts are tied to quack build `f96420ed46`; a test fails when that build or a text changes, and until the texts are captured again an attach fails closed. The as-of view is listed with the shared tables and a key's `SHOW TABLES` over Quack includes it; over HTTP a key cannot name it (the answer carries `asOf`). Views are replaced in place at a swap.

**D126. A key change reaches the readers' process within a poll. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D122; option 06 slice 4)**
- Options: the process reads the keys file on every query, as HTTP's `verify()` does; croft serve hands the process the list when the file changes; the key commands tell the server.
- Choice: the second. croft serve polls the keys file's identity (device, inode, time, size) in the same 250 ms tick that watches the copy, reads it again when it changed (`KeyStore.changes()`, which fails closed: a missing or unreadable file is no keys) and sends the names and digests to the process; a process that opens starts with the list. The hook compares the session's key with that list on every query.
- Reason: a Quack session outlives a request, so a key checked only at sign-in would let a removed person read until they disconnect (the reviewer found this in the follow-up's readers' process); the file read on every query would put file I/O in a hook that must answer at once and in a process locked away from the state folder's other files. A poll that already exists is the cheapest honest bound: removal within a second (250 ms plus a message), addition within a quarter of a second more.
- Build: the process forgets a session `quack_active_connections()` no longer lists after 30 s, so attach and detach in a loop cannot grow its table. The command notes a key's use from the process's reports (sign-ins and queries), so `key list` shows Quack use.

**D127. Quack's time limit ends the process, and what a kill drops. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D76 and D119; option 06 slice 4)**
- Options: no limit on Quack; a LIMIT added to every query; the process looks at the queries running and croft serve ends it past the deadline, as it ends a stuck HTTP query.
- Choice: the third, with `serve.queryTimeoutMs` (30 s) as the deadline and `quack_active_connections()` as the way to see how long a query has run. The process asks every 250 ms on a connection of its own; the first query still `active` past the deadline makes it tell croft serve, which kills it and starts another at once.
- Reason: Quack has no server-side cancel, and a hook sees a query begin and never end; a LIMIT would cut a client's join short with no sign, and croft never truncates silently. Killing the process bounds every query, at the price the docs state: every session on it drops, and each client attaches again (12 to 40 ms; 14 ms measured, locally; the replacement is serving about 0.4 s after the kill, and until then the client gets "Could not connect to server", then "Invalid connection id").
- Build: Quack queries are capped separately (D130), and the deadline and the process's `memory_limit` bound each one. A fixed port comes back at the same address after a kill; a port of 0 does not.

**D128. A person's key works only in server mode. (new, 2026-11-01, the maintainer's decision; amends D122; option 06 slice 4)**
- Options: keys with or without server mode, as D122 built them (on the file engine a key's query ran on the live file's worker, behind the gate alone); keys in server mode only.
- Choice: the second, the maintainer's, on 2026-11-01: every key query has two walls, the gate and the readers' views database, and keys get no single-wall path in file mode. A valid key on `POST /query` without server mode is refused in `serve/server.ts` after it authenticates and before the body is read, with a `403` and the code `SERVE_KEY_NEEDS_SERVER_MODE` (a docs page; the fix asks the user), and the usual key log line. It is not done by leaving keys out of `startServer`, which would turn a valid key into a `401` that says the key is wrong. The file engine refuses any query that carries a key's scope (`serve/instance.ts`), as a second guard. `key add` and `key list` warn and do not refuse: `data.serverMode` in the `--json` and a warning problem `SERVER_MODE_OFF_FOR_KEYS` in the envelope that names `serverMode.enabled` (exit 0, and the text prints it once), so a person can be set up before the mode is turned on; croft serve's banner says it for keys that exist (`keys.needsServerMode`). The gate's key rules, the worker's handling of a key's `shared` list and the views stay: server mode needs them.
- Reason: with a key in file mode the gate was the only wall, and a bug in it would have been a hole in the data with the live file one query away; in server mode a hidden table has no name in the key's database, so a gate bug still cannot reach it (D122, Build). A 403 with a code says what to turn on, where a 401 would say the key is wrong.
- Build: the key suite that ran on both engines now runs in server mode, and the file engine has the refusal test (`serve/key-queries.test.ts`: the 403 and its words, before the body is read, the whole attack list answered the same way with nothing written, a removed or made-up key still a 401, the app token unaffected, the engine's own guard, and a key refused at once while a writer holds the file, where the app token waits); the hidden-table and CTE pair lists and the attack list keep running through the core (`sql/gate-core.test.ts`) and in server mode; the paths test sends a key through the readers' process; the keys journey (`j33`) is the refusal and the server-mode run. The key path of the live file's worker is now unreachable and left in place, since nothing else changes.

**D129. The read copy is swapped in without a gap. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D119 and D125; option 06 slice 4's review)**
- Options: detach the old copy and attach the new one under the same name (D119); a lock or a pause that makes Quack queries wait out the swap; attach the new copy under a second name beside the old, move the views to it in one transaction, then detach the old.
- Choice: the third. The copy is attached as `wh` or `wh2`, whichever the current one is not. The format check runs on the new one before anything reads it, the views of the shared tables and the as-of view are replaced in one transaction, the app token's connections switch to the new name as they are taken, and the old one is detached last.
- Reason: Quack's hook decides at once and cannot wait, so a query that landed between the detach and the attach failed with a catalog error, about once in three swaps in the reviewer's probe. The HTTP path waited the swap out; Quack's cannot. Two names for one path work because the new file is a different inode after the rename and DuckDB 2.0 attaches it beside the old [V: 2.0.0].
- Build: `serve/quack.test.ts` requires no failed query across 20 swaps under steady load from two DuckDB clients and the HTTP API (the app token and a key), where it required only whole answers across three before. A query that straddles the switch on the app token's side is run again once, as before.

**D130. Quack queries are capped. (new, 2026-11-01; refines D125 and D127; option 06 slice 4's review)**
- Options: no cap beyond the deadline (D127 as built); the HTTP API's admission slots shared with Quack; a separate cap on running Quack queries, from the look croft already takes every 250 ms.
- Choice: the third. `serverMode.quackMaxConcurrent` (1 to 64, default 4, the same as `serve.maxConcurrent`) is the most Quack queries running at once over all sessions; the authorization hook refuses one past it, after the gate has accepted it, with a retryable `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE` (reason "busy") that names the setting. The count is what `quack_active_connections()` showed running at the last look.
- Reason: the option asks for a deadline, a concurrency limit and a queue for every remote read; many people's queries would otherwise crowd the apps' HTTP readers out of the process's threads. The hook sees a query begin and never end, so the only honest count of what runs is the server's own list. Counting the queries the hook let through since the last look (the first build) refused a client that sent a query after another within a quarter of a second, and `quack_query` opens a session per call, so only what the look saw running counts. The cap is therefore soft by one look: a burst inside it is seen at the next. No queue: a refused query is retried by its client.
- Amended by D136: each session admitted a query counts at once, until the next look.
- Build: unit tests (`quack-access.test.ts`) with a set count; `quack.test.ts` holds the only slot with a slow query, sees a second refused with the setting named while the HTTP API answers at once, and sees the cap lift when the first ends. The client's transaction control and catalog queries are never counted.

**D131. Quack listens on loopback only unless the project accepts plaintext on the network. (new, 2026-11-01; stricter than option 06 slice 4's text; refines D125)**
- Options: any address, with a banner warning (D125 as built); loopback only, always; loopback by default and any other address only with an explicit opt-in whose name says plaintext.
- Choice: the third. `serverMode.quackHost` other than loopback makes croft serve refuse to start (`QUACK_PLAINTEXT_NOT_ACCEPTED`, with the setting named in the hint and a fix that asks the user) unless `serverMode.quackPlaintextOnNetwork` is true. With it, croft keeps D125's behaviour: `allow_other_hostname` and `disable_ssl` on, the banner and `data.quack.loopback` warn that an HTTPS reverse proxy belongs in front. The setting is on the skill's ask-first list.
- Reason: past localhost Quack serves TLS with a certificate of its own, which a plain client cannot use, so croft turns it off for the proxy; that sends keys in the clear if no proxy is there. A reverse proxy on the same machine connects to 127.0.0.1 and needs nothing else, so an address beyond the machine is the case that needs a name that says what it costs. A decision that exposes data should not be one setting a typo away.
- Build: `quack.test.ts` refuses 0.0.0.0, `::`, an IPv4 address and a name without the opt-in and starts with it; loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost`) needs nothing.

**D132. croft's bookkeeping behind one interface, with two adapters; in a lake an append-only log ordered by croft's own number. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "Where state lives" and "One ingest step, end to end" and §6 "Trash, restore and delete"; option 07, slice 1)**
- Options: keep the `_croft` tables and ask the lake to hold them (it refuses primary keys, unique and check constraints, indexes, sequences, `INSERT OR REPLACE`, and `RETURNING` on `MERGE`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`); change the tables to logs for every project; two adapters behind one interface, the file's tables exactly as they are and a log for a lake. For the log's order: a write-time column, the row id, or a number croft assigns.
- Choice: the third, and croft's own number. `db/bookkeeping.ts` has the table specs, the two adapters and `bookkeepingOf(sql)`; every write to `_croft` in `load/`, `run/`, `safety/` and `project/rename.ts` goes through `upsert`, `insert`, `update`, `remove`, `rekey` or `insertSelect`, and every read stays SQL over `_croft.<table>`, which is a view in the log adapter. `seq` is one more than the highest in the log, read inside the writing transaction; a closing row (`closed`) ends a key; a rename is a new row and a closing row per key; the meta table is upserted by a `MERGE` that returns nothing; the primary key is a query (`insert()` asks before it writes). See §5 "Where state lives" for the layout.
- Reason: a file must not change for any existing project (no migration, golden outputs unchanged), and a lake cannot hold the file's tables. Of the orders, a write-time column returned the older of two rows written to one key (`now()` is fixed for a transaction), and a row id does not survive the trash copying rows out and a restore copying them back, while croft's own number does: a restore writes the rows again with numbers above the rest. Append-only bookkeeping gave zero commit conflicts for two writers on different tables in the lake spike, where delete-then-insert gave 19 per writer.
- Build: the adapter is found from what is in the database (`assets_log` makes it a log), so a project keeps its adapter however croft is started. A log warehouse is format 4 (`LOG_FORMAT_VERSION`) so that a croft before this refuses it with `DB_NEWER_FORMAT`: a reviewer built a log project, ran croft at bb492ce on it, and got `INTERNAL_ERROR` "assets is not an table" at its first write, because the log had recorded format 3. `CROFT_BOOKKEEPING=log` is internal and for the test suite alone: it makes a new warehouse a log only together with `CROFT_TEST_HARNESS=1` (set by `tests/preload.ts` and given to every child by `bookkeepingEnv()`), so nobody makes a log warehouse by accident before slice 2 gives a lake its own path (setting both undocumented variables still makes one, which is harmless, since format 4 is refused cleanly); it exists so the whole suite runs on the log with no lake and no Postgres (ci.yml runs it on one job). A test that seeds `_croft` with SQL goes through `seedState()`. Two things the build found: `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO t (some columns)` sets only the columns it names in DuckDB, so every upsert names every column (the log's new row would have NULL in the others); and a log column called `deleted` clashes with `_croft.writes.deleted`, hence `closed`. In a local lake (SQLite catalog, local folder) the same sequence of writes reads the same through the file adapter, the log on a plain file and the log in the lake after every step (`db/bookkeeping.test.ts`).
- Cost of the number: each log write asks for the highest `seq` in a subquery of its own. Measured in a local lake, that is flat in the log's size: a bookkeeping INSERT takes 2.3 to 2.8 ms with the subquery and 0.4 ms when the number is given, whether the log has 1,000 or 100,000 rows, and `max(seq)` alone took 3.2 to 3.6 ms from 100 to 300,000 rows; grown the way a log grows in use (many small commits, which a lake keeps inlined in its catalog) it took 3.4 ms behind 100 writes of three rows and 5.2 ms behind 3,000. In a file the same INSERT takes 0.5 ms against 0.3 ms. A write with 14 bookkeeping statements spends about 34 ms of 62 in a lake on it. It is not cached, because a counter that outlives one transaction can go stale when another command writes the same key between two of this command's transactions (slice 2 keeps one instance for a command's life), and one kept per `Sql` object would split in two where a step wraps its `Sql` (`abortable`). Slice 2 measured it against Postgres, where it is a round trip, and found it slow at any distance (five round trips an INSERT); D145 keeps the number per transaction on the connection in a lake.

**D133. Counting a write by classifying it first, in a file too. (new, 2026-11-01; refines §5 "One ingest step, end to end" (item i) and §7 "Merge semantics"; option 07, slice 1)**
- Options: keep counting the actions a `MERGE ... RETURNING` gives back (a lake refuses `RETURNING` on `MERGE`); classify in a lake and keep the MERGE in a file (two paths that must be held to the same numbers); classify everywhere, if it costs a file no more than 15% on the whole write step.
- Choice: the third. `load/write.ts` `mergeByKey` classifies the deduplicated batch against the table in one LEFT JOIN into a temp table of each row's sequence number and verdict (`added`, `updated`, `unchanged`, or `skipped` for a fallback row that matches nothing); if the join returns more rows than the batch has (a key in the table twice, changed outside croft) it classifies again one EXISTS at a time, which is slower and exact. It then INSERTs the added rows (no probe of the table), MERGEs only the updated ones, and DELETEs the table rows no batch row has the key of (a replace, or the rows of a reloaded file). `unchanged` is the batch less added and updated, as before.
