A MERGE has one UPDATE action, which is all DuckLake takes, so a fallback row (replaced in full) and an ordinary changed row (the batch's columns) are two statements. The old statement stays as `counting: "returning"`, used by the benchmark and by the tests that hold the two to the same numbers; nothing else selects it.
- Reason: measured on the merge benchmark (`scripts/bench-merge.ts`, results in `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-01-keyed-write.md`; macOS arm64, load average 5 to 7, medians of 11 interleaved runs, `main` measured by running the script in a clean checkout of bb492ce), classifying first costs the whole write step between -9.5% and +9.6% in the five scenarios of 100k to 1M rows, and the worst figures over every run made while building were +14.5% once on a busy machine (a re-run that finds nothing new on 100k rows, with the first classification table, which copied every column; +9.6% and +3.2% with the narrow one) and +9.7% in the reviewer's rerun at load 4 to 5, against the 15% ceiling. The merge statement alone is 15% to 71% faster where rows changed, because it merges only those (15% to 19% for 10k rows against a 1M-row table, where the MERGE was 4 ms to begin with). The old MERGE with `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` was the slow statement of a replace, so a replace is 9% to 10% faster. One path means a run reports the same numbers in both modes without a test to hold two paths together, and that a lake is exercised by every file test. In a local lake, at 100k rows, croft's statements take 14 ms to classify, 8 ms to insert and 36 ms to merge, 58 ms against 22 ms for one plain MERGE that counts nothing; a re-run that finds nothing new costs 13 ms against 13 ms.
- Build: the one disagreement is a table that has a key twice: the MERGE counts an update per table row it changed, the classification one per batch row (a test pins both). The changed rows are merged with `WHEN MATCHED AND <row differs>`, so a copy that already equals the batch's row keeps its stamp, as it did (a first version merged every matched row unconditionally and restamped it, waking downstream work). Added rows are inserted in the batch's order (`ORDER BY _croft_seq`, as a first load does); the MERGE put them in no order. The correlated names inside the classification are `__s` and `__t`, not `s` and `t`: with a STRUCT column named `s`, `s.id` in a subquery read as the field `id` of that column. The `MERGE` source is the changed rows only, so a re-run that finds nothing new runs no MERGE at all.

**D134. How the extension files reach users: add-on packages. (SUPERSEDED 2026-11-04 by D195 in how files reach users: the add-on packages were never published and were deleted; kept as the record of the decision and its sizes. new, 2026-11-01, the maintainer's decision a; refines §2 "No extension downloads", §5 "Pinned extensions" and D117; option 06 slice 5)**
- Superseded (2026-11-04, D195): the maintainer, shown the 18 packages this meant publishing: "i don't think we should be publishing something that is already published". croft now fetches DuckDB's files from DuckDB's own servers. Everything below that says how a file reaches a user (the packages, `ModeSpec.projectRoot`, `details.kind: "addon"`, `bun add`, `addonsNeeded`, `MODE_ADDONS`) is gone from the code.
- Options: files croft downloads on first use, checked against the pins (which would end "croft never downloads" for the modes); the files bundled in every croft install (about 155 MB bigger for everyone); optional add-on packages, one per mode, that a project installs when it turns a mode on.
- Choice: the third, the maintainer's, on 2026-11-01. `@zabaca/croft-addon-server` carries quack and httpfs, `@zabaca/croft-addon-lake` ducklake, httpfs and postgres. croft finds the file in the project's `node_modules`, hashes it against the pin and loads it by path; a folder named by the caller or `$CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR` still wins, for croft's own tests, and the builders' cache is the last resort. A missing add-on is `EXTENSION_MISSING` with `details.kind: "addon"` and the install command as its fix, in `croft validate` (an error), `croft doctor`, `croft status` and `--json`. `ModeSpec.extensionDir` became optional and `ModeSpec.projectRoot` was added; the readers' process is told the project's root and no longer a folder.
- Reason: plain croft stays offline and unchanged, so its promise never to download code stays literally true: it depends on neither add-on, reaches no registry at run time, and the package is the size it was (1,146,265 bytes packed at 0.4.1 and 1,159,740 with this change, which is the small source files that find the add-ons and their docs pages; no dependency was added). A user who never turns a mode on pays nothing; one who does pays 22 to 28 MB of download (server) or 35 to 45 MB (lake), for their platform only, and the checksum check means a file from npm is held to the same pin as one from DuckDB's repository, so the registry is not trusted any more than the folder was. The cost, which the decision accepted: Zabaca publishes 18 packages with each DuckDB version, each publish on the maintainer's word.
- Build: lake mode has no setting in croft yet (option 07), so `croft validate` checks the lake add-on's files only once that setting exists; the lake add-on is built, packed and resolved like the server one, and `addonsNeeded` (`db/addon-status.ts`) is the one line that setting adds. `lake-readers` needs both add-ons, `lake-test` none (its sqlite and ducklake come from a folder). A package manager finds a package in the add-on's own place too (`createRequire` from the add-on's folder), because with Bun's isolated linker the add-on's dependencies are not at the top of `node_modules` [V: Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64, both layouts]. The fix is a `command` and not `requiresHuman`: the user turned the mode on, which is the ask-first step, and the skill says so.

**D135. The packages' layout, npm's limits, and what can publish. (SUPERSEDED 2026-11-04 by D195 and deleted: the packages, `publish-addons.yml`, `scripts/build-addons.ts`, `scripts/addon-packages.ts` and the licence-notice machinery (`scripts/notices.ts`, `scripts/check-notices.ts`, `scripts/notices/`, `scripts/build-source-owners.ts`, `scripts/elf-files.ts`), because croft redistributes no extension file; kept as the record of the sizes and limits found. new, 2026-11-01; option 06 slice 5)**
- Superseded (2026-11-04, D195): only `publish-npm.yml` can publish now, and `tests/workflows.test.ts` pins that. What stays true from this decision: `publish-npm.yml` publishes `@zabaca/croft` only from a `croft-v*` tag's ref (a manual run from a branch publishes nothing).
- Options: one package per mode holding every platform (up to about 141 MB of files per platform, four platforms in one tarball); one package per mode per platform (up to 45 MB packed, with httpfs duplicated between modes); one package per extension per platform plus a no-code add-on per mode.
- Choice: the third. 16 extension packages (quack, httpfs, ducklake, postgres on osx_arm64, osx_amd64, linux_amd64, linux_arm64) and 2 add-ons. The largest tarball is 19.2 MB (quack on linux_amd64), the whole of the server add-on on one platform 21.6 to 28.0 MB packed and the lake add-on 34.6 to 45.3 MB, and `scripts/build-addons.ts` refuses any single tarball over 50 MB. httpfs is one package a project with both modes installs once.
- npm's limits: npm's documentation states none for a package's size (its open-source terms, the one page read for this, name only a request-volume limit and the rule against using the registry as a general database), and the CLI sets none ("The cli itself does not limit payload sizes, it works with many different registries", an npm maintainer, 2022, npm/cli #4794). The registry rejects large uploads with E413 Payload Too Large. Reported ceilings are all outside our sizes: tarballs of 113.9 MB and 117.9 MB were accepted in the same publish run that a tarball of about 198 MB failed (Brokk's mjolnir, 2026-10, BrokkAi/mjolnir #1269), and a 229.9 MB tarball (297.7 MB unpacked) failed in 2022 (npm/cli #4794). The guard of 50 MB is under half of the largest tarball seen accepted, and our largest is a sixth of it. Packages this large have never been uploaded by croft: whether the registry takes these exact files is unverified until the first publish.
- What can publish: before this slice, `publish-npm.yml` on a pushed `croft-v*` tag and on its own manual run, which published `@zabaca/croft` at `packages/croft/package.json`'s version from whatever ref it was run on when that version was not yet on npm, a branch included (the check that a tag names the version ran only for tags; the review confirmed it). Now `publish-npm.yml` has both its jobs behind `github.ref_type == 'tag'`: the tag release is as it was, a manual run is for running a release again from the tag's ref (`gh workflow run publish-npm.yml --ref croft-v<version>`), and from a branch it publishes nothing. Also `publish-addons.yml`, whose only trigger is a manual run: it builds and measures by default, and publishes only when the run says `publish`, types `publish croft add-ons <version>`, names the version `ADDON_VERSION` holds, runs on main, and passes the `npm-addons` environment. The `croft-v*` tag does not match any add-on trigger and a croft release does not publish add-ons. No workflow has an npm token, and only these two can mint an OIDC token. `tests/workflows.test.ts` pins all of this, and reads the scripts the workflows run as well as the workflows (npm, Bun, pnpm, Yarn, release tools, publishing actions and scripts that spawn a publish all count).
- Reason: a package per extension and platform is how esbuild and DuckDB's own Node package ship native files, and it keeps every upload small enough that no limit npm has been seen to enforce is in reach, with the platform filter in package.json doing the choosing. A manual, typed, version-checked trigger cannot fire from a tag push, a merge or a stray run.
- Build: trusted publishing cannot do a package's first publish and cannot be set up for a package that does not exist (`npm trust`'s documentation: "The package you're configuring must already exist on the npm registry", and npm 11.15.0 or above), so the first version of each of the 18 packages must be published once by hand, then `npm trust github` names this repository and `publish-addons.yml` for each; until then the publish job fails at the first package. The tarballs the build job uploads are the files to publish. `os`, `cpu` or `libc` to dependencies that are `file:` tarballs (all eight server extension packages installed), so the filter is unproven here and rests on how Bun treats registry packages [U].
- Release checklist (the `main` and `npm-addons` checks in `publish-addons.yml` are advisory: anyone who can push a branch can edit the file there and dispatch it, and a run that names an environment that does not exist creates it with no protection, so these hold only with settings no file in the repository can make): (1) create the `npm-addons` environment on GitHub before the first run, with a deployment-branch rule that allows `main` only and the maintainer as required reviewer; (2) publish the first version of each of the 18 packages by hand; (3) on npmjs.com, set each package's trusted publisher to this repository, `publish-addons.yml` and the environment `npm-addons` (`npm trust github`), so that npm itself refuses a publish from any other workflow, branch or environment; (4) run the workflow with `publish` at `build-only` and read the sizes, then publish. The same list is in `croft docs addons`.
- Licenses: the extension files are DuckDB's builds under MIT, and they link other projects statically: the files need only the system's libc and C++ runtime (`otool -L` on macOS; the ELF NEEDED entries, read with `objdump -p`, on Linux), so their licenses must travel with them. What is in them was read from the 16 files themselves (4 extensions on osx_arm64, osx_amd64, linux_amd64 and linux_arm64), with `strings`, `nm -a -C` (which reads the ELF files too) and a scan of each file's raw bytes for the markers in `scripts/notices.ts`, not from DuckDB's manifests. The two kinds of file differ and the notices follow the difference: the macOS builds are stripped of source file names and most local symbols, so a library shows there by its C++ namespace (`duckdb_mbedtls`, `duckdb_re2`, ...), an exported function (`PQconnectdb`, `roaring_bitmap_`, `curl_easy_`) or a banner; the Linux builds also keep the names of the source files they were compiled from, and they compile in parts of DuckDB itself that the macOS builds do not, which the first version of this decision missed because it was read from the macOS files: jemalloc (65 of its 66 source files by name), FSST (`libfsst.cpp`), nanoarrow (`ub_duckdb_adbc_nanoarrow.cpp`), SkipList (`SkipList.cpp`), fastpforlib (`bitpacking.cpp`), hyperloglog and miniz (the latter two also by namespace elsewhere), and Zstandard, in all four Linux files. A component is listed for an extension if any of the four platforms' files shows it (the union), so each package's `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` covers the file of every platform it is installed on. Found: OpenSSL 3.6.0 (Apache-2.0) in httpfs, quack and postgres; libcurl 8.21.0 (curl license) and zlib 1.3.2 (Zlib; the inflate banner on Linux, its error messages on macOS) in httpfs only; libpq 18 (PostgreSQL license) in postgres; CRoaring (Apache-2.0 OR MIT, taken under Apache-2.0) in ducklake; and from DuckDB's third_party tree at v2.0.0, in all four: Mbed TLS (Apache-2.0 of its Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-or-later), RE2, {fmt}, yyjson, jaro_winkler, moodycamel's queue, fast_float, utf8proc (MIT and the Unicode data terms), Zstandard, hyperloglog, miniz, jemalloc (BSD-2-Clause, which asks for its copyright notice in binary copies), FSST (MIT), SkipList (MIT), fastpforlib (Apache-2.0) and nanoarrow (Apache-2.0, with the NOTICE file Apache asks to be kept); cpp-httplib in httpfs and quack; pdqsort, vergesort and ska_sort in quack, ducklake and postgres. Each extension package ships DuckDB's MIT `LICENSE`, a `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` with the full text of each license its file needs (the projects' own files, from the tags named in it, kept in `scripts/notices/`) and a `license` field that is the SPDX expression of them (`scripts/notices.ts`). The notices stay complete by a check, not by a reading: `scripts/check-notices.ts` fails the build when a file shows a component its package does not list, in three ways. (1) Source files, on the Linux files, which keep the names of what they were compiled from: the ELF symbol table's file entries are read (`scripts/elf-files.ts`) and every name must have an owner in `scripts/notices/source-owners.json`, built by `scripts/build-source-owners.ts` from the git trees the files were built from (DuckDB v2.0.0, with each third_party directory and the nanoarrow copy as its own component, the data generators and linenoise as libraries with no notice, and the rest as DuckDB's; each extension's repository at the commit DuckDB v2.0.0's `.github/config/extensions/*.cmake` pins, and postgres's compiled-in submodule; OpenSSL 3.6.0, libcurl 8.21.0, zlib 1.3.2, PostgreSQL 18's libpq with the src/common and src/port code it compiles, and the names of CRoaring's latest release, v5.4.0, since the version in the files is not known). A name nobody owns, or one owned only by a library that extension's package does not list, is a finding; the unity-build files DuckDB generates (`ub_duckdb_*.cpp`) are DuckDB's, except nanoarrow's, and `crtstuff.c` is the toolchain's. This is what finds a library with no namespace and no marker, which the markers alone could not (jemalloc's `duckdb_je_` is C; FSST, nanoarrow, SkipList, fastpforlib and zlib have none). (2) Markers: each component has a marker (a namespace, banner, function or file name), and one that shows in a file whose package does not list the component is a finding; this is the only look at a macOS file. (3) Namespaces: DuckDB wraps each C++ library it vendors in a `duckdb_<name>` namespace, and one no component covers is a finding. `scripts/build-addons.ts` runs it on the files it packs, so the publish workflow's build job does, and it refuses to build unless all 16 files are there. On the 16 real files it passes with nothing unseen but what only the Linux builds compile in. What it cannot do: the macOS files are stripped of source names and most symbols, so a library there with no namespace and no marker is not found, but the Linux files of the same extension, built from the same sources, are checked by name; a name that two projects share is accepted when either owner is allowed (bitpacking.cpp is DuckDB's and fastpforlib's, so fastpforlib is held by its marker and not by that name); code that leaves no name is not found; and the owner map has to be rebuilt when DUCKDB_VERSION or the libraries change (a test fails when its DuckDB version is not this one). Not settled: quack's `vcpkg.json` lists curl but no quack file shows it, so curl is not listed for quack; the nanoarrow text is the upstream project's (DuckDB's tree keeps no license file for its copy) and its version is not known; the Unicode data terms in utf8proc's file (1991-2007) match no SPDX identifier, so they are `LicenseRef-Unicode-1991-2007` in the expression and the text is in the notices; the OpenSSL, curl, zlib and libpq texts are those of the versions read from a banner or a path, not of a build manifest; t-digest, which DuckDB's tree has and the review of a8a789c first reported, was withdrawn after a search of all 16 files (namespace, symbol and file name) found none of it, and its license is not shipped. None of this was reviewed by a lawyer.

**D136. Quack's cap counts the sessions it admits a query. (new, 2026-11-01; amends D130 and §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs", "Running queries are capped"; option 06 slice 4's review)**
- Options: only what the last look saw running (D130 as built); every admitted query counted at once, the next look setting the count back to what the server shows (the review's wording); each session counted once when it is admitted a query, the next look setting the count back.
- Choice: the third. `QuackAccess` keeps the server's own number from the last look and, for each session admitted a query, the time of its latest admission. A session passes the cap check when the number plus the sessions counted is under the cap, or when it is already counted; it is not counted twice and not turned away by the count it is part of. `setActive` (every 250 ms) takes the look's number and the time the look began, and forgets the sessions admitted before then, since the look has seen them (running, or finished); a session admitted while the look's query was in flight stays counted until the next look, so a look cannot erase an admission it never saw (the review's second finding: the cap could briefly admit about twice its limit). A look that fails changes nothing: the count only grows and new sessions are refused until one succeeds, which fails closed.
- Reason: with D130 as built a burst inside one look's 250 ms all passed the cap, since none was counted until the next look. The second option closes that, and it was built first: journey 34 then failed, because a client that polls with one query after another inside 250 ms was refused with `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE` for queries that had finished, which is the first build D130 rejected for the same reason. A session sends one query at a time, so its next query means its last is over; counting sessions closes the burst (the most that can be running past the look is one query per session, and each new session counts) and leaves a client that sends queries one after another alone.
- Cost: a client that opens a session per query (`quack_query` does) and sends more than `serverMode.quackMaxConcurrent` (4) of them inside 250 ms is refused the later ones with the retryable `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE` until the next look, though the earlier ones have finished; retried, it passes within a look. A session counted at one look and still running at the next is counted twice for up to 250 ms, which errs toward refusing.
- Build: `quack-access.test.ts` sends five sessions' queries inside one look (two pass, three are refused), shows the next look replacing the count in both directions, sends a hundred queries one after another on one session (never refused, with a second session counted beside it and a third refused), a hundred sessions with one query per look, a look that began before an admission leaving it counted (and one that began after clearing it), and a look that never succeeds leaving the count to grow.

**D137. A lake is created at DuckLake format 1.0 and attached with it, and `lake-test` becomes `lake-local`. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Pinned extensions, and a lockdown per mode" and D118; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: leave the format to DuckDB 2.0's default (it creates 1.1 now); pin `DUCKLAKE_VERSION` at 1.0 on every attach; let the project choose it in croft.json; allow `AUTOMATIC_MIGRATION`.
- Choice: the second. Both attaches (writer and reader) carry `DUCKLAKE_VERSION '1.0'` (`DUCKLAKE_FORMAT` in `db/modes.ts`); `AUTOMATIC_MIGRATION` is never given. A read-only attach of a 1.0 lake from DuckDB 2.0 needs no version option. The mode that served the suite as `lake-test` is `lake-local` (every importer repointed in the same change, no alias), because it is now also what a project with a SQLite catalog and a local folder runs in, under all four profiles.
- Reason: a lake outlives the machine and the people reading it are not all on the DuckDB croft pins; one made at 1.1 cannot be read by DuckDB 1.5.x, and 1.0 can be read by both [V: 2.0.0 and 1.5.5, the lake spike]. A catalog at a format other than the one asked for is refused with DuckDB's own words instead of being rewritten under a reader who has not upgraded. What it costs: the features of 1.1, none of which croft uses. Acceptance 11 is a test: a lake croft wrote in Postgres and a bucket is read by DuckDB 1.5.5 through the docs' recipe (`db/lake-reader-recipe.test.ts`, run on 2026-11-02 against `@duckdb/node-api` 1.5.5-r.5 and the 1.5.5 extension files).
- Build: the DuckDB-file catalog is out for shared use (a file cannot be read by two versions at once); Postgres is the shared catalog. A SQLite catalog with a local folder stays, for croft's own suite alone and not as a user setting: option 07's open question 2 kept it for the tests in its smallest version, its gate is the only wall (no key stands between SQL and the folder) and its extension is in no mode's list of files for users (D195), so croft.json refuses `kind: "sqlite"` unless `CROFT_TEST_HARNESS=1` is set, as the log switch needs it (`project/lake-config.ts`); it may be opened to users later as a decision of its own. The pin: `db/modes.test.ts` attaches a 1.1 catalog (made by DuckDB 2.0's default) with the pin, for the writer and for a reader, and gets DuckDB's "Cannot downgrade a DuckLake catalog" as `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED`, the catalog still 1.1; a lake croft makes is 1.0.

**D138. A `lake` block in croft.json makes the warehouse a DuckLake, and a command holds one instance of it. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "A warehouse in a lake"; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: lake as a second kind of file path in `database`; a project-level flag with the rest in environment variables; a validated `lake` block that names secrets, not values; opening and attaching per lease.
- Choice: the third and, for opening, one instance for the command. `project/lake-config.ts` validates the block like every setting (key, expected, found, a fix), `Project.config.lake` carries it, and `DuckWarehouse` gets a `LakeConnection` (`db/lake.ts` `lakeConnection`, which turns the settings and the project's secrets into the `ModeSpec` an access needs, resolving the writer's login and key only for a process that writes). The lake attaches before `lock_configuration`, so one instance is opened for the command, `USE lake` is run, and every lease takes a connection of it; it is never re-attached. A connection that dies takes its instance with it, and the next lease opens a new one. Everything that only reads (`query`, `status`, `describe`, `context`, `doctor`, `preview`, `croft serve`) attaches `READ_ONLY` with the read-only login and key.
- Reason: the file and the lake must behave the same to every command, so the lake is the warehouse's database, not a thing a command asks for (`main`, `_croft` and each asset's table resolve in it). Credentials by name keep croft.json committable, and a reader that never holds the writer's login cannot be talked into using it. DuckDB cannot attach after the lock, and an attach costs a round trip to the catalog (about 52 ms to a local Postgres), so it is paid once.
- Build: `warehouseExists(project)` replaces the file test everywhere (a lake nobody has written is `DB_NOT_FOUND` with `details.notCreated`, which every read command treats as it treats a missing file); `Project.databaseLabel` shows where the lake is, with no credential; `serverMode.enabled` and `readCopy` are refused with a lake (a later part, and nothing to copy); `croft backup` was `LAKE_UNSUPPORTED` in slice 2 and is built in slice 3 (D151); a lake has no write intent and no file lock (D144).

**D139. A lake's connection comes and goes: reads are tried again, a write is tried again as a whole, and a commit is found by its tag. (new, 2026-11-02; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: surface every connection error; retry statements; retry the transaction and tell whether it landed by the bookkeeping's run id; or by a tag on the commit itself.
- Choice: reads that fail with a connection error are tried again on a new instance, twice, with a backoff. A write commits with `set_commit_message('croft', 'croft:<pid>:<uuid>')` and, when a commit fails in a way that may have landed, a new connection looks in `ducklake_snapshots` for the tags of all the step's attempts that reached their commit, before every retry (also one after a conflict): found, the step is done and is not run again (its result is the landed attempt's); not found, the whole step runs again in a new transaction (once for a connection error, up to three times for a transaction conflict). A tag that cannot be looked up is `LAKE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN`, and a lake that stays down is `LAKE_CONNECTION_LOST`. A write that runs its own transactions (delete, restore) is tagged and recorded by hooks on its BEGIN and COMMIT, and is retried the same way; one whose commit landed without its answer cannot return its result, so it is `LAKE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN` with `details.landed: true` and is not run again. A write that touches only a trash file has no lake commit and is neither tagged nor retried (`touchesLake: false`).
- Reason: the brief offered the run id in `_croft.writes` to tell a landed commit from a lost one. A tag is better because it is in the lake's own snapshot list, written by the same commit, and does not depend on the step writing a run's bookkeeping row (a delete, a restore and a rename write no run of their own). This differs from the brief's suggestion on purpose. A refused login or key is not a connection error and is not retried (waiting does not change it): a first build retried a wrong password three times. Same-table writers conflict and retrying the whole transaction is safe (the lake spike); two writers on different tables conflict only with replace-style bookkeeping, which the log avoids (D132).
- Build: `isConnectionError`, `isCommitFailure` and `isConflict` classify DuckDB's, DuckLake's and libpq's words as they really came back (`db/lake.test.ts` holds the real messages; `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` ends connections with `pg_terminate_backend`, restarts Postgres, and drops the answer of a commit that landed). Tested: a read whose connection drops inside it succeeds on the second try; a write whose connection dropped before its commit leaves one row, not two; a commit that landed and lost its answer is found by its tag and is not run again; one whose outcome cannot be found is `LAKE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN`; an attempt's commit that lands after a later attempt began (the connection died at its commit, and it lands while the next attempt is about to commit, from another connection with its tag) is found before the retry, so the step lands once (`db/lake-warehouse.test.ts`; with only the last attempt's tag looked up it landed twice); a body that runs its own transactions is tagged and recorded, and one whose answer was lost is said to have landed; `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` restarts Postgres under a real run that waits on a slow API, and kills a run, a rebuild, a delete, a restore and a rename (all five of its points) with `kill -9` on a local and a Postgres lake.

**D140. The gate in a lake project refuses everything that reaches past the tables. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "The gate also walks the AST", D123; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: leave it to the lake's read-only login and key; a second list beside the gate; one flag on the one gate (`GateOptions.lake`), with the shared attack list.
- Choice: the third. In a lake project `decide()` refuses `postgres_query`, `postgres_execute` and every other `postgres_*`, `sqlite_*` and `ducklake_*` table function and scalar function (`postgres_pin_connection()` ran against the catalog database of a lake until the review found it; croft serve's allowlist refuses those scalars too), `duckdb_secrets()`, `which_secret()`, `duckdb_databases()`, any relation or catalog named `__ducklake_metadata_*`, every non-local path (the bucket's `s3://` files) and, for a local lake, the data files and the SQLite catalog. `gateSelect()` finds the lake from the connection (`duckdb_databases()`), so a caller cannot forget it; a SQL asset is gated again at execution time, and the resolver's dependency pass, check vetting, `delete --where`, `ctx.query` and `croft query` pass the same flag.
- Reason: these still run after the lock on an instance that attached first [V: 2.0.0, the lake spike], and `postgres_execute` as the writer would let SQL rewrite the catalog; the read-only login is the second wall, not the first. A glob whose base lies inside a protected folder had been allowed by its base (the data folder is in `allowed_directories` for a local lake): the check is now on the glob's base too (a bug the first attack list found).
- Build: `sql/attack-testkit.ts` `lakeAttacks()` holds each of these over every path to user SQL (croft query, SQL assets, checks, `ctx.query`, `delete --where`, croft serve's HTTP API for the app token, and a key's query); `sql/lake-gate.test.ts` runs the list against a Postgres lake and a local one. For a local lake the gate is the only wall (no key stands between SQL and the folder); the docs say so. A `COPY ... TO` into a Postgres lake's bucket is refused by the bucket (the reader's key), not only by the gate.

**D141. A lake's credentials live only in named secrets, and nothing croft prints can carry one. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Errors carry no credential", D118; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: credentials in the ATTACH text; environment variables DuckDB reads; temporary named secrets created before the lock.
- Choice: the third, the one D118 built. The writer and the reader have separate Postgres logins and separate bucket keys, and the writer's are resolved only by a process that writes. `ProjectEnv.secret()` finds each one by its name; the key ids, the passwords and the secret keys (and a session token) are in the project's redaction set, so the existing log, `--json` and error scrubbing covers them; `scrubError` is wired into every path out of a lake instance (reads, writes, a rollback, the retry's own errors), which D118 had left for this slice. `duckdb_secrets()` and `duckdb_databases()` are the gate's refusals (D140). The `secret_directory` is a folder in the state folder (`lake-secrets/`), which nothing writes, and a command that only reads leaves none behind.
- Reason: a refused bucket key (HTTP 403) echoes the key id, DuckDB's catalog errors can quote a connection string, and `duckdb_secrets()` shows the key id to any SQL; any one of these in an agent's context is a credential in a transcript. Separate credentials make the wall real: a reader that got past every check cannot write, because its login is `SELECT` only and its key can only read.
- Build: `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` and `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` run a wrong password, a refused key (with a write big enough to make a file; a few rows stay in the catalog), a host nobody listens on and a killed run, and search the text and `--json` output of `run`, `status`, `doctor` and `query`, and every text file in the state folder with `runs.sqlite`, for the password, the key ids and the secret keys; the secret folder is empty.

**D142. A lake cannot store an ENUM, a UNION or a VARINT; a type change a lake cannot ALTER is a rewrite. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §7 "Evolution of an existing column"; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: let DuckLake fail in the middle of the write; refuse before writing, with croft's code and the cast; convert the column silently.
- Choice: the second. `load/write.ts` calls `refuseUnfitLakeColumns` on the batch's columns in a lake: `LAKE_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED` (run error, "nothing was written") names every column, its type and the cast that fixes it (`CAST(x AS VARCHAR)`; `HUGEINT` for a VARINT, which DuckDB 2.0 names BIGNUM), also inside a STRUCT, LIST or MAP. A silent conversion would change a column's meaning without anyone asking.
- Reason: DuckLake 1.0 stores none of the three; its own message ("Failed to convert DuckDB type to DuckLake - unsupported type BIGNUM") is from the middle of a write and names no fix. Found by the end-to-end test: the first version matched `VARINT` only and let `BIGNUM` through to that internal error.
- Type changes: a lake takes only widening promotions as `ALTER ... TYPE` (INTEGER to BIGINT, HUGEINT or DOUBLE; BIGINT to HUGEINT or DOUBLE; HUGEINT to DOUBLE; DATE to TIMESTAMP or TIMESTAMPTZ; TIMESTAMP to TIMESTAMPTZ) [V: 2.0.0]. Every other change croft makes (a pin that retypes a stored column, a placeholder that received values) is `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT` of the same columns in the same order, in the write's own transaction (`load/evolve.ts` `retypeColumns`). That works only as the first change to the table in its transaction and only once: DuckLake 2.0.0 cannot read a table back in a transaction that changed it ("Table 0 does not exist" after an ALTER or an ADD COLUMN, a missing data file after a rewrite; probed with 2 and with 50 rows), so `evolveTable` and the pin changes make all their rewrites together and first, and what is left to ALTER comes after it (which a lake takes). A second rewrite, or one after another change to the table, is `LAKE_UNSUPPORTED` ("nothing was written", split the change over two runs) instead of that internal error. croft counts this itself and does not wait for DuckLake's error: `retypeColumns` keeps a connection variable per table with the name of the write transaction (`croft_tx`, set as a lake write begins) that last changed it by an ALTER or a rewrite, and refuses a rewrite that finds its own transaction's name there before it runs. The first build relied on DuckLake's error, and a CI run on a slow runner found a second rewrite succeeding where every local run failed (for a small table DuckLake does read the rewrite back, which `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` now tests with three rows); what DuckLake reads back in a transaction varies, and one that works by luck must not be allowed. A key conversion confirmed in the same write as a pin that retypes (the DELETE reads the rewritten table) is the one combination that reaches it; not built around.

**D143. croft serve reads a lake with an engine of its own, and a reader never waits for a run. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs"; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: the file engine on the lake (hold the warehouse, step aside for every writer); the readers' engine on a copy (there is no file to copy); an engine that holds no lock and reads the lake's last snapshot.
- Choice: the third. `serve/lake-engine.ts` opens one child process (`serve/worker.ts` with `lake`): an in-memory DuckDB that loads the lake's extensions by path, attaches the lake `READ_ONLY` with the read-only login and key and runs `USE lake`, with the serve profile's gate, row and byte limits, and the queue, kill and restart logic of the other engines. The credentials reach the process over IPC, never the environment or a command line. There is no write intent and no stepping aside, so a query is never `SERVE_BUSY` or delayed by a run, and it reads the snapshot that was last committed while a writer works on the next. A lake nobody has written is `DB_NOT_FOUND` until a run creates it; the engine looks again every second. A key query is refused (`SERVE_KEY_NEEDS_SERVER_MODE`) until slice 5.
- Reason: a lake is built for many readers; stepping aside would give away the thing it is for. `@zabaca/croft/read` in direct mode opens the warehouse file, which a lake project does not have: `LAKE_DIRECT_READ`, with the fix "use croft serve".
- Build: `serve/lake-engine.test.ts` holds a write open for 10 s and reads throughout (a hundred queries answer from the last commit, with no step-aside and no 503), kills the lake process (running queries fail with a retryable `SERVE_UNAVAILABLE`, a new process starts), and refuses a key. Acceptance 4.
- Refinement (D183): a key is refused only while the project has no `serverMode`; with it, this engine is server mode over the lake.

**D144. A lake has one writing machine, and croft's own lock keeps this machine's writers in turn. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Owning the DuckDB file"; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: the lake's own commit conflicts alone; a lock row in the catalog; a lock folder in the state folder; and a record of who wrote (the last writer only, or each machine's last write).
- Choice: the third, and a record for each machine. `LakeWriteLock` (`db/lake.ts`): `.croft/lake-write.lock/`, made with `mkdir` (atomic on every file system), holding `holder.json` (pid with its start identity, the run, the asset); a second writer on this machine waits as the file's second writer does, with the same budgets and the same `DB_BUSY` naming the holder, and gives it up at once to a signal; a holder whose process is gone is reclaimed by the next taker (one that took the reclaim lock and found the holder it judged still there and still dead), and a folder with no `holder.json` after 10 s. Every write records inside its transaction the machine's own row of `_croft.meta`, `writer.<machine>`: a hash of the platform's machine id (or `$CROFT_MACHINE_ID`), the host name, run, time, croft's version, a counter `n` (one more than the largest any record holds, read and written in the write's transaction, so it follows the lake's commit order and not any clock), and `crossed`, the newest record of another machine whose counter was larger than this machine's previous write's (or this machine had none), kept by this machine's later writes for 7 days from the other machine's write or from the write that found it. `croft doctor` warns with `LAKE_OTHER_WRITER` when any other machine's counter is larger than this machine's or this machine's `crossed` is within its 7 days. The warning staying 7 days after the other machine's write, whatever this machine writes meanwhile, is a policy of the maintainer's, made on the review of this slice.
- Reason: commit conflicts keep two machines from corrupting a lake, but not from running the same schedule twice, fetching the same API twice and billing it twice, and each would think the other's runs were not there. A lock in the catalog would need the writer's login for a lock that the machine's own writers never contest. The lock is for the writers on one machine, the record is what makes the mistake of a second machine visible, and the docs say a lake has one writing machine. Ordering by the records' times (the second build) let a machine whose clock ran behind write without the other ever marking a crossing, so the counter orders them and the time is for display and for how long a warning stays. A single `last_writer` row (the first build) lost the history: after B wrote and then A wrote, A's doctor said nothing, and a test pinned the silence; a row for each machine and the `crossed` mark keep what a machine found at its last write until its next write finds nothing. A machine that has never written is not a competing writer (a reader's `croft doctor` is told who wrote and nothing more). Two copies of one project folder on one machine share the machine id, so neither the lock nor the warning tells them apart: documented in `croft docs lake` (the alternative, the project's path in the identity, would make every move of a folder a new machine).
- Build: `db/lake.test.ts` takes the lock, shows the holder, queues eight writers (never two inside), gives it up to a signal, reclaims it from a writer killed with `kill -9`, and has a late waiter act on a holder it judged dead after the first reclaimer let a new taker make the lock (the new lock stays; with the first build's reclaim it was removed); `cli/commands/lake-doctor.test.ts` runs two machines (`CROFT_MACHINE_ID`) writing in turn, the other with a clock three days behind: a warning for the one that was written over, still there after it writes over the other and after a clean write of its own, gone only past the 7 days, and nothing for a machine that never wrote; the counters are one more than the largest with clocks ahead, behind and going backwards. A dead holder that a reclaim cannot remove (another reclaimer's lock is fresh) is waited on, not spun on (`acquire` pauses when a reclaim removed nothing). `croft doctor` also says the lake's folder must hold nothing but the lake (DuckLake's cleanup deletes what it does not recognise), and so does `croft docs lake`.

**D145. The log's order number is read once per transaction in a lake, not once per INSERT. (new, 2026-11-02; amends D132 "Cost of the number"; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: keep `(SELECT coalesce(max(seq), 0) FROM log) + 1` in every INSERT (D132 as built); read the highest once per transaction and number the rows from it, which D132 said to do if the subquery is slow against Postgres.
- Choice: the second, in a lake only. `db/bookkeeping.ts` `LogBookkeeping` keeps the highest number of each log table in a variable of the connection (`croft_seq_<table>`, `SET VARIABLE`/`getvariable()`, which are local to the connection and need no round trip): the first write to a table in a transaction reads it from the log, every INSERT numbers from `getvariable(...)` and moves it on by the rows it wrote (an INSERT's own `Count`), and the lake write path runs `RESET VARIABLE` for each table as it begins a transaction (`seqResetSql()`, a rolled-back transaction and another process's writes since the last one are forgotten). A file keeps the subquery, which costs it nothing. A variable belongs to the connection, so every wrapper around a transaction's `Sql` (a step's `abortable`) goes on from the same number, which a counter kept in the adapter object would not (D132's reason for not caching). `inLake()` moved from `db/state.ts` to `db/bookkeeping.ts` for it (every importer repointed).
- Measured (`scripts/bench-lake-seq.ts`, `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-02-lake-seq.md`; macOS arm64, 25 log rows per step, medians of 7): on this machine the subquery is 2.4 to 3.0 ms an INSERT in SQLite and in Postgres, flat from 0 to 20,000 rows of log, and the new way 1.4 to 1.6 ms. Behind a TCP proxy that simulates distance it is 104 ms an INSERT at a 20 ms round trip and 275 ms at 60 ms, against 10 and 25 ms: five round trips an INSERT. A write that makes a dozen bookkeeping INSERTs spent over a second (20 ms) or over three (60 ms) on the number. The simulation holds bytes back and nothing else; no real network, no R2 and no remote Postgres was measured.
- Reason: D132 kept the subquery because a local lake took 2.3 to 2.8 ms for it and said to measure against Postgres. Locally Postgres is no slower than SQLite, which is why the first look said keep it; the cost is the distance, and a lake exists to be reached across one.
- Build: the lake path of the adapter is tested in a local lake (`db/bookkeeping.test.ts`: every kind of write numbered from one variable, through a wrapper of the transaction's `Sql`, and on after a rolled-back transaction), and `db/bookkeeping.test.ts`, `load/write.test.ts` and the lake journeys compare the log in a lake with the file adapter after every step. Found on the way: an empty write transaction costs a remote lake about 38 round trips (BEGIN and COMMIT against DuckLake's catalog; 770 ms at 20 ms), which nothing of croft's can remove; a remote lake wants a nearby catalog.

**D146. The format number stays 4, a full refresh is already in place, and the whole suite runs on a lake of each kind in CI. (new, 2026-11-02; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: a number of its own for a lake warehouse, or format 4 with the log adapter; for a full refresh, leave a SQL transform's `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` to make a new lake table each run and let maintenance (slice 3) drop the old, or replace the rows in the write path; for the suite, a manual run on a local lake, or CI jobs that run the journeys on a lake of each kind.
- Choice: format 4; nothing to build for the full refresh; two CI jobs.
- Reason: a croft before slice 1 refuses a log warehouse with `DB_NEWER_FORMAT` (D132), and a lake is reachable only through a `lake` block, which a croft before this slice refuses as an unknown key; no croft can open a lake as if it were a file. What a lake adds is not in the tables (a `writer.<machine>` row is one more `_croft.meta` key, ignored by a croft that does not know it). Its own number would also make a file with the log adapter (the test suite's) and a lake two formats of one set of tables. A SQL transform whose SELECT keeps its shape is already written in place (`load/write.ts` `sqlShape`: the same shape keeps the table, diff-replaces its rows and counts them; only a first load or a changed shape is a `CREATE OR REPLACE`), so a full refresh in a lake is one table across runs; a shape change makes a new lake table, and the old stays readable as of the earlier snapshots until slice 3's expiry. A lake that runs only its own tests would leave the rest of croft (every journey) untried on it.
- Build: the next change that gives the lake tables of its own (maintenance state, slice 3) bumps the format. `tests/e2e/j36-lake.test.ts` step h reads the SQLite catalog: one `ducklake_table` row, never ended, after a run that changed 25 rows and deleted 5. `CROFT_E2E_LAKE=local|postgres bun test tests/e2e` runs the CLI journeys with every project's warehouse in a lake (`tests/e2e/harness.ts`: a SQLite lake for the children by `CROFT_TEST_LAKE`, or a Postgres database and a store folder per project, written into its croft.json and `.env` by `initProject`, the Postgres and the store started once per test file and stopped with it). A journey about the warehouse file (a direct read, a deleted file, a held file, its mtime, a seeded one, its name in an envelope), or about server mode, the read copy and keys (refused with a lake until slice 5), says so with `fileOnly(reason)` and is skipped on a lake with that reason in its name; `j01`, `j12`, `j18`, `j19`, `j21` and the rest assert the lake's own label, doctor line, banner and untouched-ness. Two jobs of `ci.yml`, `test-lake-local` and `test-lake-postgres`, run them, each its own parallel job with its own timeout (45 and 60 minutes), and the second also runs the DuckDB 1.5.5 read (D147). Run on 2026-11-02 on macOS arm64 with `CROFT_CI=1`: 186 journeys pass and 13 are skipped for those reasons on a local lake (10 minutes) and on a Postgres lake (12 minutes), none fails; the first runs found `croft serve`'s banner saying it steps aside on a lake, a `postgres_*` scalar the gate let through, and journeys that wrote `.env` whole over a lake's secrets.

**D147. The lake add-on is listed, the recipe for outside readers is a test, and croft never migrates or writes into a lake in a format older tools still read. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D134, D135; option 07, slice 2 and acceptances 1, 10, 11. The distribution part, the lake add-on and `addonsNeeded`, is SUPERSEDED 2026-11-04 by D195: the lake's extension files are fetched from DuckDB, `modesNeeded` lists the lake and `details.kind` is `file`, not `addon`. The recipe and the format refusal stand.)**
- Options: for the add-on, leave `croft validate` silent about a lake until a run fails, or list the lake add-on in `addonsNeeded` as server mode's is; for outside readers, a recipe in the docs, or a recipe the suite runs; for the format, let DuckLake migrate a catalog it finds older or newer, or refuse.
- Choice: list it; run the recipe; refuse.
- Reason: a project with a `lake` and no add-on should get the code and the install command at once, and a published recipe that nobody ran is a guess. A catalog at a format other than the pin (D137) is refused with DuckDB's own words, never migrated, and a reader on DuckDB 1.5 can read the lake as long as it stays at 1.0.
- Build: `addonsNeeded` (`db/addon-status.ts`) lists `lake` for a project with a `lake` block. A fresh lake project with no add-on gets `EXTENSION_MISSING` with `details.kind: "addon"` and the `bun add` command from `croft validate` (exit 2), `croft doctor` and `croft status`, in text and `--json`; after the install it starts with the network off (acceptance 1's lake half, moved here from option 06's slice 5; since D195 `cli/commands/extension-status.test.ts`, with the fetch command in place of the install). A file that is not the pinned one is refused like any other. `croft docs lake` gives a person a recipe for reading the lake from their own DuckDB 2.0: a Postgres login with `SELECT` on the catalog, a bucket key that can only read the folder, `ATTACH ... READ_ONLY`. `db/lake-reader-recipe.test.ts` runs the page's own fenced blocks (`postgres-admin` and `duckdb-reader`, with placeholders filled in; `INSTALL` becomes a `LOAD` of the pinned file), reads a table croft wrote, and shows an INSERT, a CREATE TABLE, a COPY into the bucket and a `postgres_execute` DROP on the catalog all refused (acceptance 10). It was published only once that passed. Such a person sees every table of the lake; limiting them to chosen tables is what server mode over a lake (slice 5) adds, and the docs say so. The same recipe is run in an older DuckDB (1.5.5, its `@duckdb/node-api` and extension files, fetched by `scripts/fetch-old-duckdb.ts`) when `CROFT_TEST_OLD_DUCKDB` and `CROFT_TEST_OLD_EXTENSIONS` name them (acceptance 11): run on 2026-11-02 locally, and by the `test-lake-postgres` job of `ci.yml`, which fetches them (that job has not run on GitHub's runners). The 1.5.5 files are checked against sha256 pins taken from DuckDB's repository for the four platforms (`db/old-extension-pins.ts`, `scripts/fetch-old-duckdb.ts`). This slice used no real R2 and no remote Postgres, only a local Postgres and an S3-compatible store started as children of the test.

**D148. Two departures from option 07's text. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D138, D139; option 07, slice 2)**
- Options: for a lake that has to be attached again, re-attach on the instance, or open a new instance and attach it before its own lock (option 07 said "one instance per command, never re-attach"); for telling whether an ambiguous commit landed, the run id in `_croft.writes` (option 07's text), or a tag on the commit.
- Choice: a new instance; the tag.
- Reason: option 07's rule exists because DuckDB cannot attach after `lock_configuration`, and a connection that dies leaves an instance whose catalog connection is gone; `db/connect.ts` marks an instance whose start failed as unusable for good. So croft never attaches on a locked instance: a command opens one instance and attaches the lake before its lock, and only when that instance's connection was lost (or its attach failed) it opens another instance, with its own attach before its own lock, at the cost of about 52 ms to a local Postgres; the credentials are re-created in the new instance and in no other. A run id tells a landed write from a lost one only for a step that writes a run's bookkeeping; a delete, a restore and a rename write none, and D139 was written for exactly these.
- Build: `db/warehouse.ts` `openLake`/`dropInstance` (one instance at a time, a failed or lost one dropped with its connections), `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` (a Postgres restarted between leases is reached again by the next one; a connection ended between leases reconnects by itself) and D139's tests.

**D149. croft runs a lake's maintenance one named step at a time, under its lock, and never calls CHECKPOINT or sets an option on a lake. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "A warehouse in a lake", "Owning the DuckDB file" and §6; option 07, slice 3)**
- Options: `CHECKPOINT` (it runs all of DuckLake's maintenance from the lake's stored options); `CHECKPOINT` with the options cleared first; each step by name, in croft's order.
- Choice: the third: prune croft's bookkeeping log (D154); flush the rows held in the catalog (`ducklake_flush_inlined_data`); expire by an explicit list of snapshot ids (`ducklake_expire_snapshots(versions => [...])`, in chunks of 2,000); merge (`ducklake_merge_adjacent_files`); rewrite (`ducklake_rewrite_data_files`); clean up at once (`ducklake_cleanup_old_files(cleanup_all => true)`, since by default the freed files wait 2 days). The whole pass is one `warehouse.write` of `transaction: false, touchesLake: false` under `LakeWriteLock` with the label `lake maintenance`, so the lock's holder is told as `maintenance` and a write that waits for it says "croft is running the lake's maintenance". Each step is tried again up to 4 times (750 ms doubling, jittered) when the store or the catalog fails in a way waiting can mend: an HTTP 5xx or 429, `SlowDown`, a timeout, a dropped connection; a refused login or key and every other error is not retried. A step that still fails ends the pass: the steps after it are `skipped`, the report is not an exception, and every step is safe to run again from where it stopped (files a failed cleanup did not delete stay in `ducklake_files_scheduled_for_deletion`). Credentials are taken out of a step's error text before it is kept or shown (`DuckWarehouse.redact`).
- Reason: the follow-up of 2026-11-01 (option 07's Further Notes, "What the follow-ups settled", item 1): `CHECKPOINT` with `expire_older_than` set expired an 8-day-old snapshot the trash had pinned, and it deletes any file in the folder that is not the lake's own; the explicit steps in this order kept the pin. Another tool's option cannot be trusted away, so croft's pass does not read it, and closing croft's instance on the lake runs nothing of DuckLake's [V: 2.0.0, `db/lake-steps.test.ts`: an option set by another tool, a pass, and a closed and reopened instance expired nothing the promise keeps, on a local and a Postgres lake; `DETACH` of a lake does not expire either].
- Build: `LeaseSql` of a lake warehouse refuses `CHECKPOINT`, any `set_option` call and any `ducklake_expire_snapshots` without `versions =>` with `INTERNAL_ERROR` (`refuseOnLake`, `db/warehouse.ts`), and a test reads every string of croft's source for them (the file warehouse's own `CHECKPOINT`, in `db/backup.ts` and `db/readcopy.ts`, is the only one, and a lake project reaches neither). `S3` faults are a test rig feature (`db/s3-store-testkit.ts`: the next N deletes answer HTTP `status`, listings page at the size asked): a store that refuses a bulk delete twice and then works finishes in the cleanup's third try; one that refuses all of them ends the pass at the cleanup after 4 tries, `pendingDeletion > 0`, the lake reads and writes, and the next pass, with the store back, deletes the files (`db/lake-steps.test.ts`, `cli/commands/lake-maintain-faults.test.ts`: no credential in any output). DuckDB's httpfs does not retry a bulk delete that answers 500 itself: one request per call [V: 2.0.0], and its message is `HTTP Error: Request returned HTTP 500 for HTTP POST to '<url>'`. A pass takes the lock for its whole body: a run's step that waits for it has the usual 90 s off a terminal, and the passes measured took 0.2 to 0.9 s.

**D150. What a pass keeps is the trash's promise, computed from the catalog; the trash pins its snapshots; and a pass is due once a day. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §6 "Trash, restore and delete" and §8; option 07, slice 3)**
- Options for what to keep: every snapshot of the last 30 days and the newest 5 snapshots of the lake; the same but with the newest 5 versions of each asset (a version being a snapshot in which a table of `main` changed); that and the snapshots the trash names. For when: every run; once an interval; a number of runs. For where croft remembers it: a row of `_croft.meta` in the lake; `runs.sqlite`.
- Choice: the third promise; once an interval, 24 hours (`lake.maintenance.everyHours`, 1 to 720), an hour after a failed pass, switched off by `lake.maintenance.enabled: false`; `runs.sqlite`. A snapshot stays when it is in the last 30 days and an hour (`WINDOW_SKEW_MS`: croft's clock and the catalog's, a Postgres on another machine, may differ, and the edge must not move with them), is the newest before them (the state when the window began, so `AT (TIMESTAMP => 30 days ago)` lands on a snapshot), is among the 5 newest versions of any asset, is pinned by the trash, or is the newest. The versions are read from `ducklake_snapshots()` (id, time, `changes`), the tables from the catalog's `ducklake_table` and `ducklake_schema`: a change that creates, writes, deletes from or alters a table of `main` is a version of the table with that NAME (a `CREATE OR REPLACE` makes a new table id; a renamed table has a row of `ducklake_table` for each name under one id and goes by the one that begins last, `tablesByLatestName`), a drop and croft's own `_croft` tables are not, and a change kind croft does not know counts as a version, so a new DuckLake never keeps less. The trash records the lake's current snapshot in the sidecar of each version it takes (`lakeSnapshot`, read under the lock the trash's write holds); a pass prunes the trash first (the same retention) and then keeps the snapshots of the versions that remain, so the lake and the trash let a version go together. A dropped table keeps its last 5 versions, as its trash versions stay until 5 newer ones exist. A pass runs after a run (`run/runner.ts` `afterRun`, last of the hooks, in the run's process, never failing the run), from the scheduler (`schedule/tick.ts`: when `runs.sqlite` says one is due, the tick notes `spawnedAt` and starts a detached `croft maintain --due`, never inline, since a tick only plans and spawns; the notice holds the next ticks off for 10 minutes, and the child's own claim in `runs.sqlite` keeps two passes from running at once) and on demand. A lake croft has not seen is stamped on the first look and not maintained for `everyHours`, so a new lake, and every short-lived project in croft's own suite, runs no pass. The state (`baselineAt`, `lastAttemptAt`, `lastOkAt`, the last pass's counts, `lastError`, a running claim) is the setting `lake.maintenance` in `runs.sqlite`, read by `status` without DuckDB (`status --json` `data.lake.maintenance`) and by `doctor`, which adds the lake's own counts (`ducklake` catalog tables through the read-only login): snapshots, files and how many are read now, the tables that keep small inserts in the catalog, files waiting for deletion. A pass that fails is `LAKE_MAINTENANCE_FAILED`, a warning in both; `healthy` in `status` is about the assets and does not change. A write that finds the lake locked for the whole wait is not an attempt (`busy`). The format number stays 4: croft makes no table in the lake for this (D146 said the next change that does would bump it).
- Reason: the promise is the trash's (30 days or 5 versions per asset, §6) and the spec said not to let the lake expire what it keeps; counting by name is what makes a table rebuilt by `CREATE OR REPLACE` one asset; the pins are what keeps a version the trash holds beyond 30 days readable in the lake (its 5-newest rule applies to the trash's versions, not to the lake's snapshots, which differ). Daily because one pass over a week of hourly runs took under 1 s and each pass adds 2 to 3 snapshots of its own, which the window removes in time. `runs.sqlite` because a pass is this machine's housekeeping and the scheduler must decide without opening the lake.
- Measured (`scripts/simulate-lake-maintenance.ts` over the spike's five assets, hourly runs, `db/lake-simulation-testkit.ts`; macOS arm64, a local lake and a Postgres 17 with a local S3-compatible store; `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-02-lake-maintenance.md`): a week as the spike wrote it (a full refresh by `CREATE OR REPLACE`): 842 snapshots, 839 files (339 read now), 181 inlined-data tables and a 13.1 MB catalog (1.9 MB in SQLite), against the spike's 849, 841, 176 and 12 MB. Pass at the end of that week, all of it inside 30 days: 0 expired, flush 4,205 rows of 5 tables, 336 files merged into 2, 336 files deleted, 0.32 to 0.35 s, 839 files tracked → 511 and 339 read now → 10. The same week with the pass made 40 days later: 817 snapshots expired, 842 → 28 snapshots, 839 → 26 files (10 read now), 181 → 18 inlined tables, data 2.2 → 0.3 MB, pass 0.66 s (local) and 0.90 s (Postgres); the catalog's row counts fall and its size on disk is Postgres's to give back (13.1 → 11.9 MB). With croft's own full refresh (rows changed in place, D146) 13 inlined tables stay 13 and the pass takes 0.46 and 0.49 s. A month of hourly runs with a pass every 24 hours (30 passes): the pass costs 0.22 to 0.42 s (median 0.34 s local, 0.31 s Postgres) while all 3,693 snapshots are within the window; over 45 days (5,400 commits) the lake settles at 3,699 snapshots from day 31, when each pass expires the oldest day (116 to 124 snapshots) and costs 0.45 to 0.68 s (median 0.49 s local, 0.46 s Postgres). Readers: 100 reads of the last snapshot through a read-only handle during 3 passes on each kind of lake failed none (a probe, not a test).
- Build: `db/lake-maintenance.ts` (`planExpiry` is a pure function of the lake's snapshots and tables, the trash's pins and the time: `db/lake-maintenance.test.ts` pins the window, its start, the 5 newest by name across table ids, a drop not being a version, the pins, the edge of the window), `db/lake-steps.test.ts` (acceptance 2 on a local and a Postgres lake: orders' 5 newest versions read back exactly, the 3 older ones are gone, a pin keeps a 59-day-old one, the plan expires nothing on a second pass; the lock both ways, acceptance 8), `db/lake-maintenance-state.test.ts` (when a pass is due), `cli/commands/maintain.test.ts` (the command, `--due`, the run's hook, the tick's spawn, the pins, an age-based expiry set by another tool, acceptance 3), `tests/e2e/j38-lake-maintenance.test.ts` (the lake jobs only, `CROFT_E2E_LAKE`: the promise end to end with the project's clock moved day to day, below; the week of acceptance 1 on that job's lake). End to end in j38, on both kinds of lake: `orders` rewritten on 8 days, 60 to 53 days before T: its 5 newest versions read back by `croft query ... AT (VERSION => n)` with exactly their rows and the 3 older answer "No snapshot found"; 7 rows deleted from `rowsdel` on 7 days (7 trash versions): after one pass at T the 5 newest versions and the one snapshot only the trash pins read back, the creation and the first delete are gone, the trash holds 5 of its 7, and the table `gone`, deleted 29 days before T, is restored from the trash with all its rows.

**D151. A backup of a lake is a pg_dump of the catalog and a mirror of the folder, and the mirror reads the bucket with a client of croft's own. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §6 "Backups of the project's data", D109; option 07, slice 3)**
- Options for the catalog: `pg_dump`; a dump of croft's own through DuckDB over the catalog's tables; a base backup. For the folder: DuckDB's httpfs; Bun's `S3Client`; a signed `fetch` of croft's own; leaving it to the user. For consistency: hold the lake's lock for the whole copy; hold it for the dump and mark a backup in progress.
- Choice: `pg_dump -Fc -O -x` as the read-only login (found on `PATH`, `$CROFT_PG_DUMP`, Homebrew, Postgres.app or `/usr/lib/postgresql`, the newest; missing is `LAKE_BACKUP_TOOL_MISSING` before anything is written; a server newer than the tool, a login that cannot read, or a failed copy is `LAKE_BACKUP_FAILED`, the message and hint saying which); a signed ListObjectsV2 and GET over `fetch` (`db/s3-mirror.ts`, AWS signature 4, path or virtual-hosted style, paged listings, streamed to disk through a temporary name and checked against the listed size), with the read-only bucket key; the lock for the dump, `runs.sqlite` and the trash only, and `markBackupRunning` (a marker file of its own for each backup, with the process's identity, in `lake-backups/` of the state folder, taken under the lock with the dump and removed by that backup alone when the folder is whole) which `maintainProject` and `deleteOrphansOf` read before they wait for the lock and again with it held, since a backup that dumped while they waited is copying files they would delete. A file of a lake is immutable under its name (DuckLake names each by a new id), so a backup links, as a hard link, the same-named file of the newest earlier backup of the same folder (`backup.json` `lake.folder`) when the size is the same, and downloads the rest; across filesystems the link fails and the file is downloaded. A local lake (croft's own tests) is `VACUUM INTO` of the SQLite catalog and a clone of the data folder.
- Reason: a dump is complete and restorable with the standard tool, by whoever runs the Postgres, whatever DuckLake adds in a later format; the read-only pair is all a copy needs, so a backup can never write the lake; the copy of a large folder must not hold up runs, and a write only adds files, so what the dump names is all there, and the one thing that deletes files, the pass, is kept off. Bun's `S3Client` was tried first and sent a request for a store on `127.0.0.1` to the environment's HTTP proxy, ignoring `NO_PROXY` where `fetch` honours it [V: Bun 1.3.14, in one environment with a proxy set], so the client is `fetch` and 90 lines of signing, held to AWS's own worked example (the IAM `ListUsers` request of 2015-08-30, signature `5d672d79…`).
- Build: `db/lake-backup.ts`, `db/s3-mirror.ts`, `db/lake-backup.test.ts` (acceptance 7, a local lake and a Postgres lake with the store: the manifest carries no credential; the mirror is the store's folder file for file; a second backup links the first's files; the dump restored with `pg_restore -O` as the writer into a fresh database, the files copied into a fresh bucket folder, `ducklake_metadata`'s `data_path` changed with one `UPDATE`, a project pointed at them, and every table of `main` and `_croft` read back row for row equal, with a run on it changing nothing; the same with a SQLite catalog), `db/s3-mirror.test.ts`. The read-only login can `pg_dump` the catalog (SELECT on its tables is all that needs) [V: Postgres 17]. DuckLake refuses a catalog whose stored data path differs from the attach's, so a restore into a new bucket must change the stored path; croft does not pass `OVERRIDE_DATA_PATH` (it would let a wrong folder attach silently). `croft backup` of a lake is not behind `croft confirm` (it copies, as a file's does).

**D152. `croft maintain`, and the files that are not the lake's own behind `croft confirm`. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §4.1, §6 "Destructive operations need confirmation"; option 07, slice 3)**
- Options for the name: `croft maintain`; `croft lake maintain` (the placeholder in option 07). For the pass itself: behind `croft confirm` like a delete, or not. For the files the lake does not own (`ducklake_delete_orphaned_files`, which has a dry run): in every pass; a flag; a command of its own behind `croft confirm`.
- Choice: `croft maintain [--dry-run] [--orphans]` (and the scheduler's hidden `--due`), flat like `backup`, since croft's commands are verbs and a `lake` group would hold one; `MAINTAIN_NEEDS_LAKE` (exit 2) in a project that keeps a file. A pass needs no confirmation: it removes nothing the promise keeps, croft runs one by itself every day, and an agent can ask what it would do (`--dry-run`, from the read-only login: no lock, no write). `--orphans` is the destructive one: it lists the files in the lake's folder that the catalog does not name and that are at least a day old (so a write in flight on another machine is not caught), by the function's dry run, and deletes them only through `croft confirm`, whose token is tied to the list (`Impact.files` and `Impact.asOf`, with `rows` 0; the generation is a hash of the cutoff and the paths: a different list is `CONFIRMATION_STALE`, and the deletion itself deletes only if the files found under the lock with the same cutoff are exactly the list it was given). The age a file must be older than is a cutoff fixed when the list is made, to the second, and the confirmation carries it (`asOf`): `croft confirm` lists and deletes with the cutoff the person was shown, not `now() - 1 day` of a later moment, so a file whose age has crossed the line since is not deleted unseen. Neither this nor a pass runs while a backup is copying the folder, looked for again with the lock held. On a terminal it asks `Proceed? [y/N]`. A pass never does it. `--json` (schemas/maintain.schema.json): `status` (ran, failed, planned, not_due, no_lake, busy, backup_running, running, orphans, needs_confirmation, declined, orphans_deleted), `report` (each step's status, time, tries and what it did; the lake's counts before and after; what the promise kept and why), `plan` (the same without doing it, with the pins and the expiry options found), `orphans` (the files, how many were deleted, the cutoff `olderThan`), `auto` (whether croft runs it, the last pass, the next due). The skill lists `lake.maintenance.enabled: false` and `--orphans` as ask-first, and says a pass, `--dry-run` and a lake's backup are not.
- Reason: option 07 said "optionally delete files that are not the lake's own, after a dry run that lists them", and croft's way to make a person see a list first is a token. The pass is not a delete of anything the user has not already been promised away (the promise is the retention), which is the same standing as the trash's own pruning in `croft doctor`. Whether a pass should ask is the one call here the maintainer may want the other way: it is a one-line change to put `maintain` behind a confirmation too, at the cost of every agent asking before housekeeping croft already does daily.
- Build: `cli/commands/maintain.ts`, `cli/commands/maintain.test.ts` (a file project is told so; a never-written lake is not made by `--dry-run`, a pass or `--orphans`; `--dry-run` changes nothing; the orphans through `croft confirm`, stale after a new file, spent after use; the human words), `tests/golden/g03-safety.test.ts` and `tests/e2e/j38-lake-maintenance.test.ts` (the envelopes against `schemas/maintain.schema.json`). The agent-contract scan found `--due` in a docs page and `--no-owner`, `--format` and the like in the source: the hidden flag is not named in the docs, and `pg_dump` is run with its short flags.

**D153. What differs from option 07's text, slice 3. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D149 to D152; option 07, slice 3)**
- Options: build the text as written (a command `croft lake maintain`, the files that are not the lake's own as an optional step of a pass, a record of maintenance in the lake, the window as 30 days exactly, a restore of a backup by a croft command); or build what the findings of the build and its review called for.
- Choice: the second, in these places. The command is `croft maintain` (D152). Deleting files that are not the lake's own is `croft maintain --orphans` behind `croft confirm`, not a part of a pass (D152). Maintenance is shown by `status` from `runs.sqlite` and by `doctor` with the lake's own counts, so "when maintenance last ran" is this machine's record (a machine that never ran a pass says "no pass yet"), not a row of the lake. The window has an hour's margin and keeps the state when it began (D150). A table that was dropped keeps its last 5 versions, as the trash does (D150). A pass has a first step, the bookkeeping log's prune, that the spec of slice 1 promised and slice 3's text did not list (D154). `LAKE_MAINTENANCE_FAILED` is a warning everywhere, `croft maintain` exiting 1 for it by hand. A backup restores into a new database and bucket with the standard tools and one `UPDATE` by hand (documented and run as written by a test), not with a croft command: moving a project into a lake is slice 4.
- Reason: each is the smaller or the safer of two readings that the findings of the build made apart: a command group for one command; a deletion croft cannot vouch for inside housekeeping that runs by itself; a record in the lake that a scheduler could not read without opening it; an edge that moved with a clock. D146 expected the next change to make a table in the lake and bump the format number; nothing here makes one, so the format stays 4.
- Build: the places are D149 to D152 and D154; the tests are theirs.

**D154. The pass prunes croft's bookkeeping log, and keeps its order. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Where state lives", D132; option 07, slices 1 and 3)**
- Options: leave the log (slice 1's spec says superseded rows are removed by maintenance, slice 3); delete in each write that supersedes a row (a concurrent writer's job, which slice 1 ruled out: the lake spike found delete-then-insert conflicted 19 times per writer where append-only never did); remove them in the pass, under the lock; and for what to remove: every row that is not its key's newest, with or without the rows of a key whose newest is a closing row.
- Choice: the third, with both: the pass's first step, `pruneBookkeeping`, runs for each of the five logs `DELETE FROM _croft.<t>_log WHERE rowid IN (rows that are not the newest of their key, or whose key's newest row is a closing row)`, "newest" being the view's own order, `seq` descending with NULL last, and the row id descending to break a tie (the view of a log made before that was added breaks it as DuckDB happens to; the prune keeps every row that ties for newest, whichever the view shows, and removes a key whole only when all of them are closing rows; croft never writes two rows of a key with one number, but a row inserted by hand can tie, and `db/lake-steps.test.ts` pins it). A key whose newest row is a closing row (a renamed table's old name, a deleted table's) is removed whole, closing row and all. One DELETE per log, each atomic; the views `_croft.<t>` read the same before and after (a test compares every row of all six), and each log is then one row for each key the view shows. `croft maintain --dry-run` says how many rows the step would remove (`plan.supersededLogRows`); a lake whose bookkeeping is not a log has none to prune.
- Reason: every read of a view and every numbering of a write scans the whole log (D145 reads the highest `seq` once per transaction, which is a scan of it), and it only grows. The order survives: a surviving row of a key is its newest, so a row written next, numbered above the highest left, is newer than it; a log emptied by the prune numbers from 1 with no older row of any key left to outrank; a closed key has no row left to come back. The trash holds copies of the view's rows and a restore numbers the rows it puts back above the rest (D132), so neither depends on the numbers pruned; the lake's snapshots inside the window still hold the old rows for time travel (the rows are deleted, in a new snapshot, as any delete is). The pass holds croft's lock, so no croft write runs meanwhile. The step comes first, so that the flush, merge and rewrite after it deal with the smaller log, and the rewrite takes the delete files the prune made.
- Build: `db/lake-maintenance.ts` `pruneBookkeeping`, `countSuperseded`; `cli/commands/lake-prune.test.ts`, on a local lake and a Postgres lake: three runs that change the table, a delete and its restore from the trash, a rename; the views equal before and after; each log is one row per live key; a second pass removes nothing; then a run, a delete and a restore, a rename back and the status go on right, and a pass prunes what they added. `rowid` works in a DELETE on a DuckLake table [V: 2.0.0]. The step is one of six (`prune` is in `StepName`, the report, `status`'s last pass, `schemas/maintain.schema.json`).

**D155. The full suite runs in two shards per platform, and a test file that leaves a process behind fails by name. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §10 "Test strategy"; the flake sweep)**
- Options for the length of a job: leave the whole suite in one job per platform and raise its limit; split the files by hand; Bun's `--shard=K/N`. For a leaked process: leave it to the next run's tripwire; a `process.on("exit")` that kills the children; a check per file.
- Choice: `bun test --shard=K/2` (Bun 1.3.14 has it, and so does the newest; it deals the sorted test files out in turn) in a matrix of two for the platforms and Bun versions, in two jobs for the bookkeeping-as-a-log run and in two for each of the lake journey jobs; the typecheck and the run against DuckDB 1.5 in shard 1. A leak guard of a last `afterAll` per file that fails the file when a process it started outlives it, and `bun test --no-orphans` in package.json's script.
- Reason: the jobs of the last pull request took 40 m 22 s, 40 m 8 s, 36 m and 31 to 32 m against 45; a next slice would have crossed. In two shards the matrix jobs took 14 to 21 minutes and the log run 15 to 21 (CI run 41600188818), and the lake journeys 8 to 14 minutes in place of 23 and 29. Measured on the baseline (233 files), dealing the files out in turn gives 639 and 665 s of test time to the two shards (1.02 of an even split), three shards would be 1.22. The files that start the processes are the ones that flake when a process outlives its test (a port held, a lock held, a Postgres still shutting down for the next file's); only a check made as each file ends can name the file.
- Build: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `tests/workflows.test.ts`, `tests/shards.test.ts`, `tests/preload.ts` (a Bun plugin that appends an import of `tests/file-guard.ts` to each test file as it loads: a hook registered by a preload belongs to the run and not to a file [V: Bun 1.3.14, a preload `afterAll` ran once, after the last file]), `tests/file-guard.ts`, `tests/leak-guard.ts`, `tests/leak-guard.test.ts` (real runs over throwaway files: a leaked child, a kill that is not awaited, an orphaned grandchild, a leak failing its own file only, on Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.4).

**D156. No test asserts how long something took, and no test file gets a new fixed sleep. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §10 "Test strategy"; the flake sweep)**
- Options: widen the bounds on CI; retry a failed test; assert on events and states and give a hang its own timeout.
- Choice: the third.
