An upper bound on a measured time is replaced by holding the thing the code must not wait for until the test lets go and an explicit timeout on the test, by an order of events, or, for a latency the design promises, by `TIMING_GAP` over the promise; a lower bound is kept. `tests/timing-assertions.test.ts` fails on a new upper bound and on a new fixed sleep.
- Reason: a widened bound moves the failure to a slower machine, and a retry hides the next one. The flakes found were all a test deciding by time what an event or a state would have decided.
- Build: see §10; `tests/timing-assertions.test.ts` and `tests/timing-scan.ts` (an `expect(` split over lines, a clock read held in a variable, a comparison passed on to `toBe(true)` or into an object, a bare `timing-gap:` tag, `sleep(CONSTANT)` and `node:timers/promises`' `setTimeout` are all seen; the e2e harness and the golden kit are scanned too). The flakes it fixed are named in the messages of the commits that fixed them (`git log` of `tests/` and `src/`, "croft tests: three flakes fixed by waiting for the state" and the commits after it).

**D157. The eval tasks that date their story by the clock run on a clock the test sets, and the days of a story are counted on the calendar. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §10 item 9; the flake sweep)**
- Options: skip the task between 23:00 and midnight; leave the clock the machine's; give the fixture a clock.
- Choice: the third: `Fixture.now()` and `setupFixture(task, { now })`, the clock croft's commands get as `CROFT_NOW`, which runs on from the instant it is given. `failed-last-night` and `api-type-change` run at a fixed mid-day; `failed-last-night` also runs at the hours below. "Last night" is the calendar day before today in the fixture's zone (`shiftDay`), not now less 24 hours.
- Reason: a day of the zone is 23 or 25 hours long twice a year, and "now less 24 hours" and "now less 48 hours" land on the wrong day in the hour after midnight and the hour before it. Measured with the old arithmetic (every half hour of each day): on 2026-11-02 from 23:00 to midnight the night before last and last night were both 2026-11-01 (the story's two runs at one instant), which is the evening the report of a failure between 23:00 and midnight came from; on 2026-11-01, the 25-hour day itself, from 23:00 to midnight last night was today; on 2026-03-09 and 2026-03-10, the first two days after the clocks went forward, from midnight to 01:00 a night was skipped. A real clock passed the self-test in every run from 23:03 to 23:59 on 2026-11-02 [V: 17 runs, at least five of them before the arithmetic was changed], so these collisions alone did not fail it; they are the only defect found in that window.
- Build: `evals/harness.ts`, `evals/tasks/failed-last-night.ts`, `evals/tasks/api-type-change.ts`, `evals/tasks/tasks.test.ts` (the hours; `lastNight` for every hour of the days around both clock changes).


**D158. On macOS the boot id is the boot session UUID, not `kern.boottime`. (new, 2026-11-03; amends §5 "Asset leases" and "Write intents"; the flake sweep)**
- Options: `kern.boottime`'s seconds as before; the same with a tolerance for a step of the clock; `kern.bootsessionuuid`; the uptime subtracted from the time now.
- Choice: `kern.bootsessionuuid`, with `kern.boottime`'s seconds as the fallback for a macOS without it; `sameBoot` takes a record of the old kind (seconds) against a UUID as no evidence of a reboot, and two readings of the seconds within an hour as one boot; a lease compares its holder's boot id with `sameBoot` as well, where it compared the strings.
- Reason: the system moves `kern.boottime` when it steps the clock (time sync, waking from sleep). Two full runs of the suite at once on one Mac saw it go from 1790105420 to 1790105421, and from then on every process that read it was on another boot than the one that had written a lease, a write intent or a run record: 11 tests failed in both runs at the same moment, and live runs were marked crashed and their leases taken. The same had failed `tests/concurrency/runs.test.ts` ("a second run waits for the lease") in an earlier run under load, with the feed asked twice. A user's Mac steps its clock after every sleep, so this was croft's to fix and not the suite's [V: macOS 15: `kern.boottime` moved by a second during a run, as the two failing readings above show; `sysctl -n kern.bootsessionuuid` prints a UUID, which is the boot session's by its name and was read the same by every process of the later runs].
- Release note: The release that carries this stamps leases, write intents and run records with the UUID. A `croft serve` or a long run that is still running the older croft across the upgrade reads those as another boot's, and so as dead: restart it after upgrading (`croft serve` stops and starts; a run in progress can finish first).
- Build: `core/proc.ts` (`readBootId`, `macBootId`, which picks the UUID or the seconds from what `sysctl` prints, and `sameBoot`), `history/leases.ts` (`sameProcess`), `core/proc.test.ts` (the UUID on macOS; `kern.boottime` moved by a second with and without the UUID, which `macBootId` is fed to simulate; the old kind against the new; a step of two hours is a restart) and `history/leases.test.ts` (a live holder, ours and another process's, recorded with the seconds keeps its lease).

**D159. The catalog connection verifies the server's certificate, unless the catalog is on this machine. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D138, D141, D147; option 07)**
- Options: for the default, keep libpq's `prefer` (encrypts when offered, verifies nothing) everywhere and document `verify-full` for remote hosts, or make `verify-full` the default for every host, or make it the default for every host that is not on this machine; for the CA, `sslrootcert=system`, a path croft finds, or only a path the project names; for passing it to DuckDB, secret options, the connection string, or libpq's `PG*` environment variables.
- Choice: `lake.catalog.sslMode` is `verify-full`, `require`, `prefer` or `disable`; left out, it is `verify-full` for any host but `localhost` and `127.x.x.x` (four octets, each 0 to 255), and `prefer` for those. `lake.catalog.sslRootCert` is the PEM file `verify-full` checks against; left out, croft uses `$SSL_CERT_FILE` or the first CA bundle it finds at the usual places of macOS, Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and RHEL, openSUSE and FreeBSD, and refuses (CONFIG_INVALID, naming the setting) when there is none. The setting reaches DuckDB as `SSLMODE` and `SSLROOTCERT` options of the catalog's temporary secret, always, so a stray `PGSSLMODE` in the shell changes nothing.
- Reason: the password and every catalog row of a hosted catalog (Neon, Supabase) cross the internet, and `prefer` lets anyone in the path read both without a warning, so the unsafe choice must not be the silent one. A catalog on this machine crosses no network and usually has no certificate, and a default that refused it would break croft's own suite and every local development setup for nothing; the exception is `localhost` and `127.x.x.x` as written, not any other name that happens to resolve to this machine. A catalog reached over a private network (a tailnet, a LAN) is another machine too, so it needs `sslMode` written once, even where nobody could listen in. A catalog on another machine that has no TLS is refused at the first attach with the setting named, and the person (not the agent: the hint and `croft docs LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` say so) decides to write `require`, `prefer` or `disable`; `croft doctor` then warns on that line for as long as the host is not this machine. `sslrootcert=system` is not used: DuckDB 1.4.3's libpq refused it ("root certificate file \"system\" does not exist", measured against Neon, 2026-11-03), and 2.0.0's accepts it but a self-signed test server cannot show it trusts the system store, so a real file is the one form that works on both and the one a message can name. A connection string in the ATTACH text would split the catalog's settings between two places, and environment variables are ambient state that any shell can change under a project.
- Build: `project/lake-config.ts` (`sslMode` with its default, `sslRootCert` only with `verify-full`, neither on a local lake; the file is not opened there), `db/ca-bundle.ts` (the search, `$SSL_CERT_FILE` then the usual places, and the CONFIG_INVALID refusal in the caller's words, shared with any other client that verifies with a CA file) and `db/catalog-tls.ts` (the catalog's CA file: the one `sslRootCert` names, else the bundle; `$SSL_CERT_FILE` read through the project's environment), `db/modes.ts` (the two secret options, both in the sandbox fingerprint; `TLS_REFUSED`: a failed check is `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` with `details.tls`, not retryable, its message the line about the TLS check, since libpq lists a failure per address and DuckDB's first line can be the one about `::1`; `db/lake.ts` does not mistake it for a dropped connection), `cli/commands/doctor.ts` (the `lake.catalog.tls` line: the CA file the attach would trust and whether `$SSL_CERT_FILE` chose it, or the refusal it would give), `croft docs lake` and `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED`; the analyst recipe's `duckdb-reader` block carries `SSLMODE '<sslmode>', SSLROOTCERT '<ca_file>'`, which `db/lake-reader-recipe.test.ts` fills and runs (with `prefer` and an existing file, since its rig is on this machine without TLS), in DuckDB 2.0 and, when the old install is named, 1.5. `db/lake-tls.test.ts` runs a Postgres child that offers TLS with a self-signed certificate issued for `localhost` (`db/tls-testkit.ts`, made with `openssl`): `verify-full` with the right CA reads and writes, writer and reader, and the server sees both encrypted; the wrong CA, the host name `127.0.0.1` the certificate was not issued for, and a server with no TLS are each refused with the stable code and a hint that names the setting; `require`, `prefer` and `disable` behave as libpq's do; the CA file is not readable from SQL; a `PGSSLMODE=disable` in the environment of a child process changes nothing (with a control that shows the variable does reach libpq); and through croft.json, `$SSL_CERT_FILE`, a missing CA file and `croft doctor`. `project/lake-config.test.ts` pins the default by host. A lake made before this setting keeps working on a loopback host; one on another host needs the setting written once.

**D160. A store over HTTPS is checked against one CA file that croft lets DuckDB read. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D117, D118, D138; the first real-lake trial, 2026-11-02)**
- Options: leave DuckDB's file system closed and turn the certificate check off for a lake (`enable_server_cert_verification = false`); allow the machine's whole CA folder; allow one CA file by name and point httpfs at it; allow the file only (without `ca_cert_file`).
- Choice: the third. The lake modes' `allowed_paths` hold the one CA file (`modePaths`), and `SET GLOBAL ca_cert_file` names it, before the lock. The file is `lake.bucket.sslRootCert` when the project names one (relative to the project folder, `~/` for home; a name that is not a file is `CONFIG_INVALID` before anything is attached; naming one with `useSsl: false` is refused), a private authority's for example. Without it, the file is this machine's CA bundle, found by `findCaBundle` (`db/ca-bundle.ts`, the finder the catalog's TLS uses, D155): `$SSL_CERT_FILE` of the project's environment (`.env` or the shell), then the usual places (macOS, Debian, Fedora, Alpine and the others). A machine on which none is found gets `LAKE_STORE_TLS` (`no-ca-file`, with `details.looked` and the setting as the fix) when the lake's mode is made, before anything is attached. A store without TLS (`useSsl: false`, a store on this machine) allows no path.
- Reason: the trial (R2) could neither read nor write a byte: every https request failed with "Cannot read a CA certificate bundle: file system access is restricted by configuration", because the lock never let httpfs read its CA file and the suite's store was plain HTTP. Turning verification off sends the bucket key's signed requests to whoever answers; the machine's CA folder is more than the check needs. Both halves are needed [V: 2.0.0, a store served over HTTPS with a self-signed certificate]: `allowed_paths` without `ca_cert_file` still fails (httpfs looks at its default list), `ca_cert_file` without the path allowed is "Cannot access file", and a plain `SET` is lost on every connection after the first (the instance's global is what a later lease sees), so it is `SET GLOBAL`. The check is pinned, not assumed: DuckDB 2.0's `enable_server_cert_verification` defaults to false, and its httplib client then read and wrote a store with no CA and with the wrong one, verifying nothing [V: 2.0.0]; so the mode sets `enable_server_cert_verification = true` and `httpfs_client_implementation = 'curl'` (which checks regardless of that setting) globally before the lock, for every store over TLS. The CA file is the instance's, not SQL's: the gate protects it as it protects a local lake's own files (`sql/gate.ts` `lakeFiles` adds the `ca_cert_file` setting), so a query that names it, to read or to overwrite it, is `QUERY_PATH_DENIED` or `QUERY_NOT_SELECT`, and no other file of the machine is reachable; the paths a mode allows were already part of the sandbox's fingerprint. `croft backup`'s client names `rejectUnauthorized: true`, since Bun's fetch honours `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` and then reads any store [V: 1.3.14]; with it named, the variable cannot turn the check off (a backup of a store the CA does not vouch for is `LAKE_STORE_TLS` whatever the environment says), which is what refusing a mirror under the variable would have achieved, without a case for it.
- Build: `db/store-tls.ts` `storeCaFile` (the named file, else `findCaBundle`); `db/modes.ts` (`LakeBucket.caFile`, `modePaths`, `modeIdentity`, `SET GLOBAL ca_cert_file`); `db/lake.ts` `lakeMode`; `project/lake-config.ts` (`sslRootCert`); `croft backup`'s own client (`db/s3-mirror.ts`) trusts the same file (`tls: {ca}`). `db/store-tls.test.ts` serves the test store over HTTPS with a self-signed certificate (`db/store-tls-testkit.ts`, made with the openssl program, which CI has): with the CA the project names, or one found by the finder (`$SSL_CERT_FILE` set, nothing named), run, query, status, doctor, maintain and backup all work and the Parquet files are in the store; with a bundle that does not know the store's authority (named in `$SSL_CERT_FILE`, named by the project, or this machine's own) every command says `LAKE_STORE_TLS`; `storeCaFile` is tested with an injected finder (the environment's file first, then the usual places, none is `no-ca-file`); with the httplib client forced back (a prepare hook before the lock) the wrong CA is still refused and writes nothing (the test fails with the verification pin removed: the write went through); the backup mirror refuses the wrong CA with `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` set (in a child process, as the variable is read at start); the CI job `test-lake-postgres` runs it. `scripts/bench-lake-seq.ts` and the rest of the suite still use plain HTTP, which is what hid this.

**D161. Every way the store's certificate fails is `LAKE_STORE_TLS`, in every command. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D118, D141; the first real-lake trial)**
- Options: map it in each command; map it where errors leave the lake's warehouse and where a query's error is mapped.
- Choice: the second. `DuckWarehouse.scrub` (every error that leaves a lake lease) and `mapQueryError` turn DuckDB's words (`Cannot read a CA certificate bundle`, `SSL peer certificate or SSH remote key was not OK`, and libcurl's and OpenSSL's others) into `LAKE_STORE_TLS` (category environment, exit 2, never retried), with `details.kind` `no-ca-file` or `untrusted`, `retryable: false`, and the fix in words: ask the user to set `lake.bucket.sslRootCert` to the file the store's certificate is signed by; never turn `useSsl` off or skip the check. A maintenance pass that stops at such a step records the same code (a warning there, `failedPassProblem`), `croft backup`'s own client maps its fetch errors to it, and a retry is not made.
- Reason: the one failure was `INTERNAL_ERROR` ("a bug in croft") in `run`, `backup` and `doctor`, `QUERY_FAILED` ("fix the query") in `query`, and `LAKE_MAINTENANCE_FAILED` in a pass. A person or an agent that reads the code should get the fix, and the same one.
- Build: `db/store-tls.ts` (`storeTlsProblem`, `storeTlsError`, `isStoreTls`), `src/agent/docs/LAKE_STORE_TLS.md`, the registry; `db/store-tls.test.ts` checks run, query, describe, maintain, backup and doctor, with no CA, with another's and with a store certificate for another name, and that none of them says `INTERNAL_ERROR`, `QUERY_FAILED` or `LAKE_MAINTENANCE_FAILED`.

**D162. The pass flushes the assets' schema and leaves croft's bookkeeping in the catalog. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D149, D154; the first real-lake trial)**
- Options: flush every schema as `ducklake_flush_inlined_data` does by default; flush `main` only (`schema_name => 'main'`); flush the tables one by one; keep `_croft` out of inlining some other way.
- Choice: the second. A new lake's bookkeeping is never a file; a lake an earlier pass flushed keeps the files it has (they are read as before, and a rewrite and merge treat them like any).
- Reason: the pass's flush moved `_croft`, a few rows at a time and read on every run, into tiny Parquet files, and each read of it then cost 2 to 3 requests of the store (200 to 700 ms on R2) instead of one round trip to the catalog (50 to 90 ms): a run with nothing new went from 3.8 s before the first pass to 8.7 to 9.1 s after it. The bookkeeping is small and the prune (D154) keeps it small, so inlining it costs the catalog nothing worth having.
- Consequence, plainly: slice 3's drop in inlined-data tables after a pass (D149 to D152; 181 tables to 18 in the simulated week, `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-02-lake-maintenance.md`) now holds for the assets' schema (`main`) only. croft's own bookkeeping tables in `_croft` stay inlined, so the count `croft doctor` and `croft status` give ("tables of rows kept in the catalog") includes them and stays that much higher than those figures; the benchmark file was not run again, and its tables are the figures of the flush as it was.
- Build: `db/lake-maintenance.ts` (`ASSET_SCHEMA`); `db/lake-steps.test.ts` (the pass makes the assets' rows files, and `_croft` has no data file and reads back the same, on a local and a Postgres lake); `scripts/bench-lake-bookkeeping.ts` and `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-03-lake-bookkeeping.md`: with the store 100 and 250 ms away (a TCP proxy that delays each chunk, as bench-lake-seq.ts's does), a run with nothing new makes 6 requests of the store and takes 0.5 s longer at 100 ms and 1.6 s longer at 250 ms after a flush of every schema, and none after this pass.

**D163. secretsFrom, the lake's secrets and the reader recipe, as the trial found them. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D108, D138, D147)**
- Options: keep "status, query and doctor never run secretsFrom" and stop a lake project's commands running it; make the text true.
- Choice: the second. In a lake project every command that opens the lake asks for its logins and keys, so it runs the command, once, when the shell and `.env` lack a name (`run`, `preview`, `query`, `describe`, `context`, `doctor`, `delete`, `restore`, `rename`, `maintain` with `--dry-run`, `backup`, `serve`, the scheduler's runs); `status`, `validate` and `logs` do not. `croft docs secrets` says so, and doctor's one ProjectEnv per run makes it once and its line says "run once by doctor, for the lake's secrets" (or "not run: the shell and .env set every secret the lake names"), no longer "not run by doctor". `croft secrets` and doctor's secrets check list the lake block's names, used by "the lake (croft.json)". The reader recipe's placeholder is `<data_path>`, the folder exactly as `croft doctor` prints it with its one slash (`s3://bucket/trial-1/`): the old `s3://<bucket>/<folder>/` with `<folder>` written as croft.json writes it made `trial-1//`, where the catalog still answered a count and every read of a file was a 404. `lake.bucket.folder` is one folder however many slashes end it. The recipe says INSTALL fetches over plain HTTP from extensions.duckdb.org and fails behind a proxy that refuses it, and how to `LOAD` the files from the add-on instead.
- Reason: each is what the trial found, and the only change is that the text and the checks say what the code does.
- Build: `cli/commands/lake-secrets.test.ts` counts the command's runs for each command on a Postgres lake whose secrets are only in the store; `db/lake-reader-recipe.test.ts` runs the recipe with `<data_path>` from croft.json; `project/lake-config.test.ts`.

**D164. Small corrections. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D126, D134, D150, D151)**
- The run summary's "done X s" is the run's own time (`RunData.durationMs`, the whole run from its start), not its longest step's; a summary stored before it falls back to the longest step, the least the run took.
- A run that ends, failed or not, removes its staging (`.croft/staging/<run>`): a failed lake run left 7 MB for 3 days "for inspection" that nothing reads, since the error is in `croft logs` and a rerun extracts again. A run whose process died is still reconcile's, and chunks waiting for a commit are kept as before (D126, `pruneStaging`).
- `backup.json`'s `project.database` is the lake's label for a lake, not the `warehouse.duckdb` croft.json says and a lake does not have.
- `AddonView.installed` is true when the add-on's own package supplied the files (or one of them is there and wrong or missing for this machine); files from `$CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR` or the builders' cache run the mode and are not the add-on installed, and the line says so. (Gone with the add-ons, D195.)
- A failed pass says what makes the next one ("a pass is due again an hour after one that failed, and the next croft run, or the scheduler's next tick when croft schedule is on, makes it; croft maintain now makes it at once"), instead of "croft tries again within the hour", which holds only if something runs (`MAINTENANCE_RETRY`).

**D165. Doctor asks the bucket and the catalog's encryption before a first run. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D144)**
- Options: leave doctor at the lake's catalog; list the folder and read a file through croft's own locked instance; try a write to see whether the key may.
- Choice: the second, without the third. With the read-only key, in an instance that has the bucket's secret and CA file and no catalog (`LakeSpec.storeOnly`), doctor lists the lake's folder (the first object only: `glob` with `LIMIT 1`) and reads the footer of one data file (`parquet_metadata`), whether or not the lake exists, and writes nothing (the key could not, and the folder holds nothing but the lake). It says how many objects, how long, which CA file, or `LAKE_STORE_TLS` or `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` (the key refused, the store not answering in 15 s). It also says whether the connection the lake is attached over is encrypted (first by asking the catalog's server, `pg_stat_ssl` for that connection; from the client's side since D175, which replaced it): plain text to another machine is a warning (libpq's default `sslmode` falls back to it silently), to this machine a note.
- Limit found while building it: DuckDB 2.0 under croft's lock lists one page (1,000 objects) of a folder and fails on the next with `Cannot access "s3://<bucket>/"` [V: 2.0.0, a folder of 1,100 objects, `LIMIT 1` or not]. For the probe that error is proof that the first page came back, so it is reported as "the bucket answers, it holds more than 1,000 objects" with no sample file. The same limit makes `croft maintain --orphans` fail with `INTERNAL_ERROR` on a bucket folder of more than 1,000 objects (measured with 1,200 strays); it is not fixed here and is open.
- Reason: doctor said "no problems found" before a first run that could write nothing, because with no lake it touched no byte of the bucket. A write probe would put an object in a folder that must hold nothing else, and the writer's key is for commands that write.
- Build: `db/lake-probe.ts`; `cli/commands/doctor.ts` (`checkLakeStore`, `catalogEncryptionLine`); `db/store-tls.test.ts` (a lake nobody has made: the bucket answers with the CA and the folder is empty, and without the CA doctor says `LAKE_STORE_TLS` and exits 2; after a run it lists and reads a footer and the folder is as it was). The catalog's own TLS settings are the `lake-tls` branch's; the two lines are different facts (what is set, what the server sees).

**D166. Doctor's time for comparing tables scales with the lake. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D144; superseded by D180 for a lake over a network)**
- Choice: 400 ms for a file and for a lake on this machine; 8 s for a lake with a bucket (`TABLE_SCAN_LAKE_MS`), and the line that says tables were left out says the budget.
- Reason: comparing one table takes several statements, each a round trip of 50 to 700 ms, so 400 ms never fit one: the trial compared none of its 6 tables. 8 s compares a few and keeps doctor to about ten seconds on a far lake; the rest are compared by the next run of each asset, as before.

**D167. A lake block with `"enabled": false` names the lake a project moves into, and croft sets it to true as the move's last step. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "A warehouse in a lake" and §4.1; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: name the lake in the command (flags, or a file); a `lake` block that is on while a marker in the state folder says the move is pending; a `lake.enabled` key (default true) that keeps the project on its file while it is false; and for the switch, croft rewriting croft.json or the person (or the agent) editing it.
- Choice: the third, and croft makes the switch. `lake.enabled` is validated with the rest of the block (every credential by secret name, so croft.json stays committable), `CroftConfig.lake` is the lake a project is in and `CroftConfig.idleLake` the one it is not in yet, and `switchLakeOn` (`db/lake-move.ts`) replaces the one token `false` in the person's text, reads the result back through the validator and renames it over croft.json. `serverMode.enabled` and `readCopy` are refused with a lake only while it is on, so a project with server mode may carry the block, and the move is what refuses it.
- Reason: a block that is on turns every command to an empty lake at once, and the first run then builds the project again from its sources (the only history some of them keep is 90 days), where a move was meant to carry the data; a marker in the state folder would make croft.json say one thing and a machine's state another, and a second machine would read the committed file and find no warehouse. A flag cannot carry two logins and two keys by name. `serverMode.enabled` is the precedent for a switch in the config. The command is the one that knows the lake holds a proved copy, so it is the one that flips the switch, in one rename; a person told to flip it after the fact can flip it before.
- Build: `project/lake-config.ts`, `project/root.ts`, `croft.schema.json` (the key table, `config-schema.test.ts`), `project/lake-config.test.ts`. `croft doctor` warns when a file warehouse sits next to a lake nobody has written (the first run there would build the project again), and says how a switched-off block is moved into; `croft status` and `doctor` show the three states (switched off, moved in, back on the file).

**D168. The move copies from a backup in one lake transaction and proves the copy from the read-only login before it switches. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Owning the DuckDB file" and §6 "Backups of the project's data", D109; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options for the source: the live file attached from the lake's instance (refused: the sandbox allows only `files/` and the state folder, and croft never attaches the live warehouse from another database, §5); Parquet exports of each table (types are lost: HUGEINT becomes DOUBLE, D70); a clone of the file; the backup `croft backup` makes. For the copy: a transaction per table; one for everything. For the proof: counts; a hash of each table; `EXCEPT ALL` both ways; and read with the writer's login or the read-only one.
- Choice: the backup (croft's own, so the way back is also a full backup with `runs.sqlite` and the trash), attached read-only from the lake's instance in the same state folder; one transaction; counts, the columns' types and `EXCEPT ALL` of the file's rows against the lake's, read with the read-only login and key on an instance of its own.
- Reason: the backup is the one copy of the file croft already vouches for, and the clone and the backup are the same bytes (fingerprinted by a child), so nothing reads the live file and the file cannot change under the copy except by something that is not croft, which the second fingerprint finds. One transaction makes the lake hold all of it or nothing, so a kill never leaves half a project there; the cost is that a failed commit is retried as a whole (D139), and the proof cannot be in the same transaction (DuckLake 2.0.0 cannot read back a table a transaction changed, D142). The reader's key and login are what every reader will use, so a proof made with them also proves they work, and it sees Parquet as a reader does; a proof by the writer could pass on rows only the writer's connection sees. `EXCEPT ALL` is exact and costs a hash anti-join per table.
- Build: `db/lake-move.ts` (`inventoryOf`, `copyIntoLake`, `verifyLake`, `undoCopy`, `fingerprints`), `cli/commands/move-to-lake.ts`, `db/lake-move.test.ts` (both kinds of lake), `cli/commands/move-to-lake.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts`. The journey's project (6 tables and 13,429 rows over assets of every kind, 55 columns' records, a trash with versions and a run history) moves in 0.9 s into a local lake and 1.2 s into a Postgres catalog with the store (wall time of the confirmed command, macOS arm64, local Postgres: no network). When the proof finds a difference, or the second fingerprint a changed file, `undoCopy` drops the tables, empties the logs and removes the marker in one transaction, but only while the marker's tag is the lake's newest snapshot (a lake written since is left as it is, and the error says so).

**D169. A lake stores some types inexactly: the move finds them by value, the proof names the rest, and BIT and a fixed-size ARRAY join the types it refuses. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D142 and §7; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: leave it to the proof after the copy; check every column's type only (refuse a HUGEINT column outright); check the values of the columns whose types a lake changes; and for the write path, the same check or none.
- Choice: the third for the move as first built (`inexactColumns`, then the proof names whatever else differs), none for the write path. **Superseded by D174**, which refuses by type in both and makes croft's own inference choose a type a lake keeps.
- Reason: measured on DuckDB 2.0.0 with DuckLake 1.0 on a local lake, with enough rows that DuckLake writes a Parquet file (a few rows stay in the catalog and read back exactly, so a probe of two rows found nothing; the first probe of this slice did exactly that): a HUGEINT and a UHUGEINT are stored as DOUBLE (`range * 9007199254740993` came back as `9007199254740992`, and a value near the top of the range makes the whole table unreadable: "failed to cast column from DOUBLE to HUGEINT"); an INTERVAL loses the microseconds under its milliseconds (`1.000003 s` came back `1 s`); a TIMETZ comes back at offset 0 (`10:11:12+02` as `08:11:12+00`); the same inside a STRUCT or a LIST. Everything else round-tripped equal: the other integer widths and their extremes, DECIMAL up to 38 digits (so `DECIMAL(38,0)` is the exact cast for a HUGEINT), FLOAT and DOUBLE with NaN, infinity and negative zero, VARCHAR, BLOB, DATE and TIMESTAMP at their limits, every TIMESTAMP unit, UUID, JSON, STRUCT, LIST and MAP. BIT and a fixed-size ARRAY (`INTEGER[3]`) are refused by DuckLake as ENUM, UNION and BIGNUM are (D142), so `LAKE_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED` names them with their casts. A person who is moving should be told what to cast before the move starts, not after a copy.
- Build: `LAKE_VALUES_INEXACT` (project, exit 2; details.columns has each table, column, count, example and cast), `lakeRefusedColumns` and `lakeCastFix` in `db/lake.ts`, `db/lake-move.ts` `inexactColumns` (a HUGEINT is inexact when `try_cast(try_cast(x AS DOUBLE) AS HUGEINT)` is not `x`, an INTERVAL when `datepart('microsecond', x) % 1000` is not 0, a TIMETZ when its offset is not 0). **A finding for the maintainer, not fixed here:** croft's own write path does not check these, and the maintenance pass's flush (`ducklake_flush_inlined_data`, D149) turns a HUGEINT that read back exact while it was held in the catalog into a DOUBLE in a file (`9007199254740993` read back `9007199254740992` after a flush of five rows); croft made a HUGEINT column for an integer past 64 bits, so a lake project that ingested one lost digits at its first pass. Fixed in the same branch by the maintainer's decision: D174.

**D170. The way back is the setting, and the catalog mirror follows the warehouse the project is on. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §5 "Where state lives"; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: only the setting (the mirror is whatever the last command left); heal the mirror from the file at the first writing command (`reconcile`); a `--back` command; a mirror saved for each place the project has been.
- Choice: the last, kept in runs.sqlite with no warehouse opened (`history/mirror-home.ts`): `catalog.home` is the label the mirror describes, `catalog.stash` the mirrors of the other places; the first command in a project that has a lake block, on or off, puts the mirror at home with the warehouse the project is on, and the move saves the file's mirror as it is just before the switch. A project that never named a lake is not touched.
- Reason: the planner and `status` read the mirror and never the warehouse, so after a hand-switch back to the file they would decide from the lake's days over the file's data (a stale transform judged fresh, an ingest's cursor and row count of the lake's). Healing it from the file needs a warehouse open before each reader and conflicts with a process's one access mode per file (§5); a `--back` command would leave the hand edit, which is the natural one, broken. The saved mirror is the file's state to the byte, since nothing wrote the file.
- Build: `history/mirror-home.test.ts`; `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts` step e reads the project after two lake runs, goes back by editing croft.json, and compares every table, every `_croft` table, `status` and `run --dry-run` with what they were before the move (the file's bytes are the same sha256), then returns to the lake and reads its days. Each asset's last run in `status` is left out of that comparison: the run history is the project's, and a run in the lake is a run.

**D171. A move that stopped is finished by moving again: a marker in the lake and the commit's tag. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D139; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: a journal in the state folder, as `croft rename` keeps one; a marker in the lake; refuse a lake that holds anything, always.
- Choice: the marker. `_croft.meta` `moved_into_lake` holds `{v, tag, at, croftVersion, fileSha256, fileBytes, tables, bookkeeping}`, written in the copy's own transaction, and the copy's commit carries `tag` (`commitTag`, the option D139 gave tests only, now used for real). The lake is `marked` when the marker is there, and `unchanged` when its tag is the newest snapshot's; a move whose file has the marker's sha256 and whose lake is marked and unchanged is in `finish` mode.
- Refinement (the review): a lake whose marker tag is the one the record `lake.move` in `runs.sqlite` names was filled by a move that finished, and then the project was switched back to the file; moving again is refused (`MOVE_LAKE_NOT_EMPTY`, "that move finished and the project was switched back") and not run as a `finish`, because "finish" is for a move that stopped. `lake.move` gained `tag` for this. The way to use that lake again is `"enabled": true` by hand.
- Reason: the one fact that matters is whether the lake holds exactly the copy of this file, and that is in the lake, in the same commit as the data; a journal could not say it after a crash between the commit and the journal. The refusal stays for every other lake (it holds tables, or a marked copy that has been written since, or of another file), because croft cannot tell whose rows would be merged.
- Build: `CROFT_FAULT=move_after_backup|move_after_copy|move_before_switch|move_after_switch` kill the process (`tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts`, both kinds of lake): after the backup the lake is empty and the next move copies; after the copy and before the switch it is marked and the next move finishes; after the switch the project is in the lake, equal to the file. `move_touch_file` is another program writing the file just before the second fingerprint (`MOVE_FILE_CHANGED`, the copy taken out). In every case the file is the same sha256 and croft.json is either unchanged or switched, never between.

**D172. What the move refuses, what it asks, and why the whole move is one confirmation. (new, 2026-11-02; refines §6 "Destructive operations need confirmation" and "Guards aimed at agents"; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: confirm each step (the backup, the copy, the switch); confirm the move once; confirm only the switch; and for server mode, move it with its keys, or refuse until slice 5.
- Choice: the move is confirmed once, with an impact that says what moves, what stays, what does not come along and the way back (`CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` with the token, or `Proceed? [y/N]`), recounted under the project's leases and spent by `Confirmations.consume()` (a generation of the file's counts and stamps, so a token minted before a write is `CONFIRMATION_STALE`); and server mode is refused with its keys and settings left as they are.
- Reason: the steps before the switch change nothing the person has (a backup, a copy in a lake that was empty, taken out again if it does not prove), and the switch is the decision; asking for each would ask three times for one choice. Server mode over a lake is slice 5: a project with it on and a lake on is an invalid croft.json, so a move would have to turn it off, which is the person's decision about who can read what. (Refinement, D185: slice 5 made the combination valid, so server mode is no longer a reason to refuse.) A croft serve that is running would go on serving, and scheduling, for the file, so it is a refusal too, whose fix is to stop it. The skill's ask-first list gets the move, the hand edit of `lake.enabled` either way, the lake itself (never made by an agent), and a stopped croft serve; the recipe says that LAKE_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED and LAKE_VALUES_INEXACT name the columns to cast, that MOVE_LAKE_NOT_EMPTY needs a new lake, and that a stopped move is finished by running it again.
- Build: `cli/commands/move-to-lake.ts` (`refuseUnlessReady`, `preflight`, `carryOut`; `CONFIRMABLE` and `destructiveStepRan` in `cli/commands/confirm.ts` know it), `src/agent/skill.md` and §9 item 2, `croft docs lake`, the pages of the six new codes (`src/agent/docs/`).

**D173. What differs from option 07's text, slice 4. (new, 2026-11-02; refines D167 to D172; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: build the text as written (a command that takes the lake and switches the project, `croft confirm`, refuse a lake that holds tables and a second move, "going back is switching the setting back"); or build what the design and its measurements called for.
- Choice: the second, in these places. The lake is named in the block with `"enabled": false` and croft sets it (D167); the command is `croft move-to-lake`, flat like `backup` and `maintain` (D152). The copy comes from a backup and is proved from the read-only login (D168), which the text left open. A stopped move is finished (D171), where the text only said a second move is refused. The way back restores the file's catalog mirror (D170), where the text said only that writes made in the lake are not carried back. The types a lake changes are found before the move (D169). The move was estimated at 2 to 4 builder-days. The acceptance holds as written: after the move every table, row count and bookkeeping row is equal (the bookkeeping is the log's latest rows, so equal means the same latest rows, `_croft.meta` being the one table that differs on purpose: format 4, `bookkeeping = log`, the machine's record and the marker), `croft status` shows the same staleness and the next run does only what it would have done on the file, the file is byte for byte unchanged (a pending write-ahead log is folded in by `croft backup` before the move, which refuses until then), nothing is written without `croft confirm`, and a second move is refused (also after the project was switched back to the file, D171).
- Reason: each is the smaller or the safer of two readings that the findings of the build made apart (an enabled block turns every command to an empty lake at once; a copy from the live file is not allowed; a proof by the writer would not prove the reader).
- Build: the places are D167 to D172.


**D174. A lake write never changes a value: a column of a type a lake stores inexactly is refused by its type, and croft's own inference chooses DECIMAL(38,0) for integers past 64 bits. (new, 2026-11-03, the maintainer's decision on D169's finding; refines D142 and §7; option 07, slice 4)**
- Options: refuse by the column's values; refuse by its type; refuse by type and have inference choose a type a lake keeps; make the maintenance pass skip tables that hold such columns.
- Choice: the third. `refuseUnfitLakeColumns` (`db/lake.ts`, called from `load/write.ts` for every lake write: an ingest, a file ingest, a SQL transform, a TS transform, a pin's retype) raises `LAKE_VALUES_INEXACT` ("nothing was written", the cast in the hint and in `details.columns[].fix`) for a column whose type is HUGEINT, UHUGEINT, INTERVAL or TIMETZ, also inside a STRUCT, LIST or MAP; the types of D142 are told first. The fix names `DECIMAL(38,0)` (exact to 38 digits) or text for a HUGEINT, text for a UHUGEINT, an INTERVAL (or milliseconds) and a TIMETZ (or `TIME` when the offset does not matter), and `to_json` for a nested one. `evolve()` and `planColumn()` take `{lake}` (`load/types.ts`, from `inLake(tx)` in `load/cast.ts` and `load/files.ts`): where inference would create or widen to HUGEINT, a JSON or CSV or Parquet (UBIGINT) column of integers past 64 bits, it chooses DECIMAL(38,0) instead, and a stored unpinned DECIMAL(38,0) takes integers as a HUGEINT does and widens to DOUBLE for fractions under the same loss proof (a pinned one is the person's and keeps a DECIMAL's rules). A pin to HUGEINT is refused, and the fix is the pin to DECIMAL(38,0). **A SQL or TypeScript transform's top-level HUGEINT result is retyped to DECIMAL(38,0) in the batch before it is written (`widenHugeResults`, `load/write.ts`), not refused**: `sum()` and `count`-like aggregates of integers return a HUGEINT in DuckDB, so refusing it would have failed most aggregations in a lake (the first full run after the change failed 26 file-suite tests and 39 lake tests on `sum(amount)`); the cast keeps every digit, which is what the refusal was for. It leaves the column as it is, to be refused with the cast, when a value has more than 38 digits. A UHUGEINT, an INTERVAL, a TIMETZ and a HUGEINT inside a STRUCT, LIST or MAP are still refused. (A departure from the maintainer's wording, "refuse a SQL transform's HUGEINT", for that reason; to refuse instead, drop the call in `writeBatch`.) A restore of a version from the file's days with such a column is refused before the token is issued, and the move's question names those versions.
- Reason: whether a value survives depends on where its rows are kept, which changes under a table (D169: a few rows in the catalog read back exact, the maintenance flush then turns them into DOUBLEs), so a check by value passes today and corrupts tomorrow; a check by type cannot. With no such column in a lake, the flush has none to change, so the pass needs no exception (`ducklake_flush_inlined_data` was measured to change a HUGEINT, D169). DECIMAL(38,0) is the stand-in croft already uses for a HUGEINT in Parquet snapshots (D70) and in rendering (`db/values.ts`), it round-trips (measured, D169), and it holds every integer croft's inference can make up to 10^38; a HUGEINT between 10^38 and 1.7 x 10^38 does not fit and fails the loss check with the usual error (TYPE_CONFLICT) instead of being stored differently.
- Build: `db/lake.ts` (`LAKE_HUGE`, `lakeInexactColumns`, `lakeInexactFix`, `refuseInexactTypes`, `LAKE_INEXACT_WHY`; `refuseUnfitLakeColumns`, which raises either code and was `refuseLakeTypes` before it raised two), a `TYPE_WIDENED` when a transform's HUGEINT is widened and its table is made (`load/write.ts`), `db/lake-move.ts` (`inexactColumns` now flags by type and counts the values that would change as news), `load/types.ts`, `safety/restore.ts`, `db/lake.test.ts`, `load/types.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/j40-lake-exact.test.ts` (both kinds of lake: a JSON ingest of 450 rows and of 5, a CSV, a Parquet UBIGINT, a BIGINT column that later gets big integers and is rewritten, a fraction arriving, each SQL case refused with the cast and the fix running, a pin, and a maintenance pass after each, with every digit compared) and `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts` (a trashed version). The control: with the inference left as it was, the same run is refused with the cast in the hint instead of writing HUGEINT. In a file nothing changes: a HUGEINT stays a HUGEINT. A lake built by an earlier build of this branch with such a column (none was released) is not repaired.

**D175. Doctor says whether the catalog connection is encrypted from the client's side, and says only what it knows. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D159, D165; the second real-lake trial)**
- Options: keep asking the database (`pg_stat_ssl` for the connection's backend) and say nothing when it cannot be read; read libpq's own view of the connection; say what the setting makes libpq do, and for the one setting that leaves it to the server, ask the server what libpq asks first.
- Choice: the third. `lake.catalog.sslMode` `verify-full` and `require` make libpq end a connection the server will not encrypt, so the line says the connection is encrypted and why; `disable` is not encrypted because the setting says so (the words no longer say the client "fell back without saying so": it was told not to encrypt), a warning to another machine and a note to this one; `prefer` asks the server the question libpq asks first, an SSLRequest of eight bytes answered `S` or `N` (`db/lake-probe.ts` `serverOffersTls`, no login and no data), and says encrypted when the server offers TLS, a warning when it offers none, and a note ("could not be checked") when it did not answer. With `disable` the certificate line is a note (there is no certificate to check) and the encryption line carries the warning, so a lake without TLS is one warning and not two.
- Reason: the hosted catalog of the trial (a pooler in front of the database, `verify-full`, certificate checked) was reported "NOT encrypted", with a check mark on the line above that said the certificate was checked. `pg_stat_ssl` is the database's view of its own connection, and behind a pooler or a proxy that is the last hop, not the client's. libpq's view is not readable: the postgres extension links libpq statically and exposes no call for `PQsslInUse` [V: 2.0.0, its function list].
- Limit, plainly: under `prefer` with a server that offers TLS, a handshake that failed would make libpq go on in plain text; the line says "the server offers TLS and sslMode prefer takes it", which is what is known, and not that this connection was read. `verify-full` and `require` have no such gap.
- Build: `cli/commands/doctor.ts` (`catalogEncryptionLine`, `checkCatalogEncryption`), `db/lake-probe.ts` (`serverOffersTls`; the `pg_stat_ssl` query is gone). `db/store-tls.test.ts` (the line for every setting and every answer, a hosted catalog's case, never a warning for what cannot be known), `db/lake-tls.test.ts` (the question against a Postgres that offers TLS and one that does not, a server that answers something else or nothing, and doctor's line against a real TLS catalog for `verify-full` and for the default `prefer`).

**D176. A lake read is one catalog transaction, and a step reads once. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D138, D144, D145, D162; the second real-lake trial)**
- Options: fewer statements (batch the bookkeeping's reads and writes into larger ones); one transaction around everything a read lease does; a pool of connections kept between leases; settings of the `postgres` extension's pool; skip the work a run with nothing new does not need; a cache of what the catalog said, between processes.
- Choice: one transaction for each read lease, and less asked in it. A read lease on a lake is `BEGIN`, `USE lake`, the format check, the body, and a `ROLLBACK` (nothing in a read changes the lake; a rollback costs nothing to commit); a statement DuckDB refuses aborts a transaction, so `LeaseSql.recover` rolls back and begins another, and a body that goes on after a refused statement (a table that is not there, the user's query that was wrong) is as it was when every statement was its own transaction; a connection that dropped is still the lease's retry, of the whole body, in a new transaction. Then what a run with nothing new asked in them: an ingest step reads its own state (assets row, stored columns, files) in the lease that checks its config (`settleConfig`'s `alsoRead`; when settling applies a change it reads again afterwards, as before), and a table that is as its code says is not counted (`readConfigState`); doctor reads the lake's counts in the lease that reads the format and leaves the tables out (D180); the probe that asks whether a lake exists only attaches (`ReadOptions.attachOnly`); the prune is one transaction (D179). The pool settings, a pool of connections of our own and a cache between processes were measured or weighed and not done (below).
- Reason: the trial's hosted catalog was 41 ms away. DuckLake's catalog access is a Postgres transaction through the extension's pool, and each use of a pooled connection is `SELECT 1`, `DISCARD ALL`, `SELECT 1` around it: outside a transaction every statement was 3 to 5 of them, 20 to 26 round trips (0.9 to 1.1 s) for a read of one table, and a run with nothing new made 65 statements, 11 for each ingest, one after another. Inside a transaction the first statement costs the same and each one after it 4 round trips (the table's files, the inlined-delete check, the schema versions, the inlined rows), so the 11 statements of an ingest cost one snapshot, not eleven. The numbers (`docs/benchmarks/2026-11-03-lake-latency.md`, a Postgres 17 on this machine behind a proxy that holds each chunk back 20 ms each way, four assets, medians of three): a run with nothing new 18.3 s to 4.6 s (407 round trips to 94), a run in which one file changed 35.7 s to 21.5 s, a first run 35.3 s to 30.9 s, a `croft query` 7.7 s to 3.7 s, `croft describe` 13.4 s to 5.6 s, `croft doctor` 24.0 s to 5.1 s, `croft maintain` 33.3 s to 26.8 s; with no distance the commands take what they took (0.3 to 1.2 s).
- What is left, plainly. A command on a lake costs at least about 2.7 s at 41 ms that no change of croft's removes: the attach (0.8 s), the first look at the catalog (`USE lake`, 0.9 s) and the first read of croft's own inlined tables, which DuckLake reads at the older schema version they were made in and so loads the catalog a second time (1.1 s). The target was a `croft query` under about 2 s; it takes 3.7 s, and 2.6 s if its format check were skipped, which D144 requires on every read, so it is not (a query that never names `_croft` would not need it; that is a decision for whoever owns D144, not a measurement). A step that writes still takes about 7 s at that distance: a commit is 15 round trips and every scan of a table in the transaction at least 4, and the write path reads about thirty of them (the checks after a write scan the data table four times); that was not shortened. `croft maintain` is DuckLake's own calls (a `CALL ducklake_*` takes 1.5 to 4 s, most of it in its prepare).
- Not done: `pg_pool_health_check_query = ''` takes one `SELECT 1` of the three around each pooled use (about 15 % of the round trips, 0.5 s of a query), and a dead pooled connection is then found by the statement that uses it instead of by the check; croft's retry would meet it, but a server restart could take several pooled connections in turn, so the cost is resilience for a long-lived `croft serve`. `pg_pool_enable_thread_local_cache` removed nothing. A cache of the catalog between processes would answer a lake that changed.
- Build: `db/warehouse.ts` (`inLake`, `LeaseSql.recover`, `ReadOptions.attachOnly`), `load/config-change.ts` and `run/ingest.ts` (the state read once), `db/lake-maintenance.ts` (the prune), `cli/commands/doctor.ts`, `db/lake-pass.ts`; `db/delay-proxy-testkit.ts`, `scripts/bench-lake-latency.ts`, `scripts/bench-lake-bookkeeping.ts` and `scripts/bench-lake-seq.ts` (which use it). Tests are in §10.

**D177. A failed attach ends every lease that shared it with its own error, and the next lease attaches again. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D141, D118; the second real-lake trial)**
- Options: remember the failure in the warehouse and refuse every later lease with it; give the leases that shared the instance the error that stopped it, and let a later lease try again on a new instance.
- Choice: the second. connect.ts keeps, with the mark that an instance failed to start, the error that did it (`startFailure`); a lease that shared the instance with the one whose attach failed asks for it when its own connection is refused ("left part set up by a mode that failed to start") and gets that, a retry reopens through the one-open-at-a-time path (`ensureOpen`), and a later lease finds no instance and attaches again. Nothing is remembered for long, so a catalog that is fixed while a long process runs (croft schedule's ticks, a serve) is reached by the next lease.
- Reason: the trial's run had two ingests in flight; the first attach to fail (a catalog at another format, a CA that did not check) marked the instance and the second lease was told `INTERNAL_ERROR`, "report this croft bug", about the first's failure. Twice, with two different causes.
- Build: `db/connect.ts` (`startFailure`), `db/warehouse.ts` (`inLake`). `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` (three leases together and a fourth after, on a refused login, and a write: every one `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED`, none `INTERNAL_ERROR`; the test fails with `startFailure` removed), `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` (two ingests side by side, a wrong password and a foreign lake: each step fails once with its own code, attempt 1).

**D178. An attach that no waiting mends has its own code, `LAKE_CATALOG_MISMATCH`, and is never retried. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D137, D141; the second real-lake trial)**
- Options: more words in `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED`'s hint; `retryable: false` on it for these causes; a code of its own that says the database holds another lake.
- Choice: the third. DuckLake's refusals "catalog version mismatch: catalog version is 0.3, but the extension requires version 1.0. To automatically migrate, set AUTOMATIC_MIGRATION to TRUE" (an older lake) and "catalog version is '1.1', which is newer than the requested version '1.0'. Cannot downgrade" (a newer one, as DuckDB 2.0's default makes) are `details.kind: "format"`, and `DATA_PATH parameter ... does not match existing data path in the catalog ...` (the lake's files are in another bucket folder) is `details.kind: "data_path"`. The message says the database holds another lake and croft never migrates one or overrides a data path; DuckDB's advice (`AUTOMATIC_MIGRATION`, `OVERRIDE_DATA_PATH`) is in neither the message, the hint nor the details; the fix is the user's: a database of croft's own, or the tool or version that made this one. `retryable: false`, so a run does not retry it and does not call it temporary. The other permanent refusals were already `retryable: false` with their own hints (`details.refused` for a login, a key, a database or role that does not exist; `details.tls`; `details.notCreated`); they and this are the cases `LAKE_ATTACH_FAILED` keeps for a catalog that may come back, and it says so.
- Reason: the trial's database held another tool's lake at 0.3; `croft run` retried it three times over 154 s (30 s and 2 min apart), called it temporary, and `doctor` hinted at the host and the login.
- Build: `db/modes.ts` (`catalogMismatch`, `lakeFailure`), `core/errors.ts`, `src/agent/docs/LAKE_CATALOG_MISMATCH.md`. `db/lake.test.ts` (DuckLake's three messages word for word, and the refusals that are not this), `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` (a real 1.1 lake made by another DuckDB, and a lake under another folder: reader and writer, no retry), `db/modes.test.ts` (the 1.1 case of D137 now has this code), `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` (the CLI, with doctor).

**D179. croft's bookkeeping that an older pass moved into files is found by doctor and brought back into the catalog by the first step of a pass. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D154, D162; the second real-lake trial)**
- Options: warn and document the limit; a pass that rewrites `_croft` back inline; both.
- Choice: both. DuckLake has no way to take rows back from a file, but the rows can be copied out, deleted and inserted again in inserts small enough to stay in the catalog (its inlining limit, 10 rows by default; the lake's own option if one is stored). That is the second half of `pruneBookkeeping`: in the one transaction of the prune, each `_croft` table with live data files (`bookkeepingInFiles`, read from the catalog's own tables, with the row ids each file covers) has up to `REINLINE_MAX_ROWS` (1,000) of the rows that are in files copied out, deleted by row id and inserted again; a table with more in files than that (`_croft.writes_log` grows with every write) comes back over several passes, a batch each, and the step's line says how many tables are still partly in files (`did.leftInFiles`). The pass that moves a file's last rows leaves it with every row deleted. The file is then read by nobody, and the pass's own `rewrite` step drops it (all its rows are deleted) and `cleanup` deletes it from the store [V: 2.0.0: after the prune alone the file is still live with its rows deleted; after `ducklake_rewrite_data_files` it is gone]. `croft doctor` counts the files in the same statement as the lake's other counts (`LakeStats.bookkeepingFiles`) and, when there are any, warns with `LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES` naming the tables, files and bytes, and `croft maintain` as the fix. The prune is one transaction now (it was one DELETE for each of five logs, each its own commit), which also costs a lake at a distance one commit and not six.
- Reason: the trial's first lake had been maintained by croft before D162: every command read `_croft` from Parquet files over the network, a run with nothing new took 9 s, and no line said why. A large single insert (a file ingest that retires 200 files in one `INSERT ... SELECT`) can put a log in a file in a new lake too.
- Build: `db/lake-maintenance.ts` (`pruneBookkeeping`, `bookkeepingInFiles`, `LakeStats.bookkeepingFiles`), `cli/commands/doctor.ts`, `cli/commands/maintain.ts` (the step's words), `src/agent/docs/LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES.md`. `cli/commands/lake-reinline.test.ts` (a local and a Postgres lake: a history of runs, DuckLake's flush of every schema as the old pass made it, doctor warns, `croft maintain` brings the tables back, the files are gone after the pass, every view reads as it did, and the next run goes on), a table over the cap is left and said.

**D180. Doctor on a lake with a catalog over a network compares no table unless asked, and reads the lake's counts in the one lease. (new, 2026-11-03; supersedes D166)**
- Options: more time for the comparison (D166's 8 s); the first table only; sample; in parallel; none by default and `--tables` for all.
- Choice: the last. `croft doctor --tables` compares every table with croft's record, with no budget, on a file and on a lake; without it a file keeps its 400 ms and a lake on this machine its 400 ms, and a lake over a network compares none and says "tables: not compared with croft's record on a lake (each table costs the catalog's round trips); croft doctor --tables compares them, and the next run of each asset compares its own". The lake's counts (snapshots, files, the expiry options, the bookkeeping in files) are read in the lease that reads the format, not in a second one.
- Reason: comparing one table takes several statements of the catalog's round trips each, so D166's 8 s compared 1 of 4 tables and doctor took 22 s on the trial's hosted catalog, 2 to 3 s of it the comparison of a table that a run compares again anyway. What the comparison finds is a table changed by another tool that has the writer's login, which is rare, and the next run of each asset compares its own table whatever doctor did.
- Build: `cli/commands/doctor.ts` (`lakeScanMs`, `DoctorDeps.allTables`, `checkTables`), `cli/commands/index.ts` (`--tables`), `safety/out-of-band.ts` (`TableScan.notCompared`). `cli/commands/lake-doctor.test.ts` (a Postgres lake: left out and said; `--tables` compares), `cli/commands/doctor.test.ts` (on a file, `--tables` lifts the time).

**D181. validate checks the CA files the settings name. (new, 2026-11-03; refines D159, D160)**
- Choice: a file named by `lake.catalog.sslRootCert` (with `verify-full`) or `lake.bucket.sslRootCert` that is not there is `CONFIG_INVALID` in `croft validate`, as it is in the command that attaches; a machine with no CA bundle of its own is doctor's line, since another machine may have one. Doctor does not repeat it in its asset count (it has its own lines).
- Reason: validate said all was well for a project whose next query failed on a missing catalog CA file.
- Build: `cli/commands/validate.ts` (`lakeFileProblems`); `cli/commands/validate.test.ts`, `db/lake-tls.test.ts` (the CLI).

**D182. Small corrections. (new, 2026-11-03)**
- doctor's `secretsFrom` line printed the program's path twice when the command was an absolute path; it prints it once (and, for a program found on the PATH, where).
- The lake-exists probe that `croft maintain` and the scheduler's passes make attaches and asks no more (`ReadOptions.attachOnly`): no transaction, no `USE`, no format check; the pass's own lease checks the format. At 41 ms that was 3 s of a pass.
- A step that settles nothing reads its own state in the lease that checked its config (`settleConfig`'s `alsoRead`), and a table as its code says is not counted at all (`readConfigState` counts rows only for a change or a lossy pin); a run with nothing new took two leases and a scan of every table per ingest before, and one lease per ingest now.

**D183. Server mode over a lake is the lake engine asked for the readers' features, and there is no copy. (new, 2026-11-04; refines §5 "Server mode, apps and GUIs", D118, D119, D125, D143; option 07, slice 5)**
- Options: the readers' engine on a copy of the lake (a lake is not a file, so a copy would be a second store to keep equal to the first, and the point of a lake is that many processes read it); a third engine; the lake engine with `serve` in its process's open message.
- Choice: the third. `serve/lake-engine.ts` with `serverMode.enabled` does what the readers' engine does for the copy (`serve/readers.ts`): the keys file is read on its poll and sent to the process (D126), Quack's address is checked before it starts (D131), a Quack sign-in or query reaches `onQuack`, a Quack query past the deadline ends the process (D127), a key's query is sent with its tables (`shared`) and answered with them, and `status().serverMode` is there (`copy` is `null`, `swaps` 0, `copyCost` null). Without `serverMode` the engine is D143's, unchanged, and a key is still refused (`SERVE_KEY_NEEDS_SERVER_MODE`). The process (`serve/worker.ts`, `open` with `lake` and `serve`) attaches the lake with the mode `lakeReadersMode(lake.mode("read"))`: `lake-readers` (httpfs, postgres, ducklake, quack: D118's "lake readers" profile, which slice 1 built and tested at the connection) for a Postgres catalog and a bucket, and `lake-local-readers` (httpfs, sqlite, ducklake, quack) for a SQLite catalog and a local folder, which slice 1 had not needed, because a local lake is how the journeys of the suite run on every machine. Both run under the serve profile only, refuse a read-write lake, and need the extension files of both modes (D195). The hooks and the listener are registered in `prepare`, before the lock, as for the copy (`serve/quack-listener.ts`); the views, the as-of view and Quack's catalog are made after it, on the process's admin connection. A key's connection works in the in-memory database (`USE memory`), where the views are, and the app token's in `lake` (`USE lake`); the gate and its catalog snapshot are the readers' (D123), loaded for each query because a lake changes under a process (D143). `serverMode.enabled` is no longer an error with a `lake` (`project/root.ts`).
- Reason: a lake is built for many readers, and a copy of one would give away both the freshness and the reason for the lake. The engine's other half is the same code the copy's engine runs: a second copy of it would drift (D112's reason for one gate). Over a bucket the process's wall against a write is three, not two: the read-only attach, the read-only login of the catalog and the bucket key that cannot write, which the tests prove one by one.
- Build: `serve/lake-engine.ts`, `serve/worker.ts` (`LakeServe`, `syncLake`), `serve/query-worker.ts`, `db/modes.ts` (`lake-local-readers`, `lakeReadersMode`), `project/root.ts`. `serve/lake-serve-mode.test.ts` (HTTP, over a local lake and over a Postgres catalog with an S3-compatible store: a key reads the shared tables and the answer says which snapshot it could have read; the whole attack list, with the lake's own (`lakeAttacks`) and the lake readers' (`lakeReaderAttacks`: the lake's own names, a shared table through `lake.main`, USE, DETACH, ATTACH again, CREATE SECRET, COPY into the folder, `ducklake_*` procedures), is refused with a key and nothing is written to the project or to the lake's folder, nor a snapshot added; a CTE named after a hidden table answers as one named after nothing; a removed key is a 401; 100 queries during a 10 s write step all answer from the last snapshot; a stuck query ends the process and a write beside it completes; stopping ends the process first), `serve/lake-quack.test.ts` (a DuckDB 2.0 client in a process of its own: attach, read with the filters pushed down, the attack list, the catalog texts as their exact bytes, a removed key's open session refused within a second, a wrong or removed key at sign-in, a kill, the deadline, the address rules), `serve/lake-serve-lockdown.test.ts`.

**D184. The views follow the lake by looking at its newest snapshot, and an answer says which one. (new, 2026-11-04; option 07, slice 5)**
- Options: remake the views on a timer for as long as the server runs; look before every query that is answered and, for Quack, on a timer while a session is signed in; make the as-of view read the lake's `snapshots()` when it is read; remake the views inside Quack's authorization hook.
- Choice: the second. `syncLake` asks `SELECT id FROM lake.current_snapshot()` (one catalog call); if the snapshot is the one the views were made for it is done, else it reads that snapshot's time from `lake.snapshots()`, makes every shared table's view again in one transaction (`CREATE OR REPLACE`, so a Quack session mid-sync never finds a name gone; a shared table the lake lacks has no view, one it lost loses its view), refreshes Quack's catalog (`QuackAccess.setCatalog`), bumps the epoch (a query that failed while the views were made runs again, once, as after a swap, D129) and tells the engine the snapshot's time (`snapshot` message: `/health`, `/status` and `croft doctor` show it). One look runs at a time and one waits: a caller that arrives while one runs shares the next, which starts after it arrived, so a table made before a query is there for it. While a Quack session is signed in (`QuackAccess.signedIn`) a timer does the same every `LAKE_SYNC_MS` (250 ms, the copy's poll); a server nobody is signed in to asks the catalog nothing. The as-of view stays a static one-row view (D125), remade by the sync with the snapshot's time, so it is never newer than the data a client has read, as the copy's was never newer. The HTTP answer's `asOf` is the time of the snapshot the query's own look found.
- Reason: the hook must decide at once (D123), so it cannot look at the lake; and an idle server on a hosted catalog that never sleeps costs its owner money (a poll every 250 ms would keep a catalog that suspends when idle awake for ever). What the views read needs no look at all: a view over a DuckLake table reads its new rows and its new columns as they are committed, and only a table that is created or dropped changes which views can exist [V: 2.0.0, a local lake: 3 rows then 4 after an INSERT through the same view, a new column visible at once, `Catalog Error: Table with name t does not exist` after a DROP].
- What it costs a DuckDB client: a client lists a server's tables when it attaches [V: 2.0.0: after a run made a shared table, the attached session said `Table with name extras does not exist`, a query sent as written with `quack_query` read it, and a new `ATTACH` listed it], so a session in use keeps the list it had and reads on; a table made later is there for an `ATTACH` made after the next look. The docs say so. It is the same for a shared table the first copy lacked, which no Quack test of the copy's time covered.
- Build: `serve/worker.ts` (`syncLake`, `lookAtLake`, `LAKE_SYNC_MS`), `serve/lake-engine.ts` (`onSnapshot`), `serve/quack-listener.ts`. `lake-serve-mode.test.ts` (a commit is in the next query for the key and the token, and `asOf` moves; a table a run makes appears, a column is read at once, a table dropped by another writer is gone), `lake-quack.test.ts` (the same for a session; the as-of view follows within a look; many commits under two DuckDB clients and the HTTP API lose no query and each answer is a whole snapshot's; with a Postgres catalog a client holding a transaction does not stop it).

**D185. What server mode over a lake turns off, and what a move does with it. (new, 2026-11-04; refines D119, D121, D172)**
- Options: keep a lake with server mode an invalid `croft.json`, as D172 had it; allow it and keep the read copy and its policy (the 1 GB question) for a lake; allow it with no copy at all.
- Choice: the third. `config.readCopy` is `readCopy || (serverMode.enabled && !lake)`, so a lake project has no copy to refresh, no copy policy (`assessCopyPolicy` is not run by `croft run`, `status` or `doctor`: the 1 GB question and `SERVER_MODE_COPY_COSTLY` are the file's), and `"readCopy": true` is still `CONFIG_INVALID` with a lake. The words follow: `croft serve`'s banner says `server mode over lake …: answers from the lake's last snapshot, read-only, and never waits for a run`, `data.serverMode.readCopy` is `null` (the schema allows it) and `asOf` is the newest snapshot the server has seen; `croft status` and `croft doctor` say server mode is on and whether croft serve is up, with no copy line; `croft serve key add` says the views are the lake's. `croft move-to-lake` no longer refuses a project with server mode on: D172 refused it because a project with a lake and server mode was an invalid `croft.json`, which it is not now. Its keys and `serve.sharedTables` are unchanged by the move, the copy it made on the file stays on disk (read-only, no longer refreshed), and only a read copy asked for by name (`"readCopy": true` in the file, which a lake refuses) is a reason (`MOVE_BLOCKED`).
- Reason: the copy is the file's way of letting readers not wait; a lake's readers never wait. Keeping the combination invalid would leave a project that wants keys over a lake with nothing to turn on.
- Build: `project/root.ts`, `run/runner.ts`, `cli/commands/serve.ts`, `status.ts`, `doctor.ts`, `serve-key.ts`, `move-to-lake.ts`, `serve/types.ts` (`serverMode.copy` may be null). `project/lake-config.test.ts`, `project/config-schema.test.ts`, `cli/commands/move-to-lake.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts` step c (the move carries server mode and its keys over, and no copy is made after), `tests/e2e/j32-server-mode.test.ts` (a lake journey: no copy, croft serve answers from the snapshot, a run's rows are in the next query, SIGTERM stops it clean), `j33-keys.test.ts` and `j34-quack.test.ts` (the key and Quack journeys run on both lakes of CI).

**D186. What the lockdown does not refuse past the gate, and what differs from option 07's text, slice 5. (new, 2026-11-04; refines D118; option 07, slice 5; the last point refined by D204)**
- Options: ask the lock to refuse more, by name (`quack_serve`, `ducklake_flush_inlined_data`); leave the lock as D118's profile built it and name what only the gate holds.
- Choice: the second. DuckDB has no setting that refuses a function by name (D204 looked for one), and what the lock, the read-only attach, the read-only login and the read-only key refuse is already everything that writes. With the gate left out (`serve/lake-serve-lockdown.test.ts` opens the same instance, loaded and locked, and sends it SQL): a write to a table, a column or a schema is refused by the read-only attach; the catalog's `postgres_execute` DROP, DELETE and CREATE by the read-only login (`permission denied`); a COPY into the folder, a nested path of it and `COPY main.orders` by the store, with a 403, because the bucket key cannot write; another folder, another bucket, an `https://` URL, the state folder, `files/`, the project's `.env`, `/etc/hosts` and every local path by the lockdown (`Permission Error`); and SET, INSTALL, LOAD of what is not loaded and a remote attach by the lock. A `ducklake_flush_inlined_data('lake')` is not refused by name: on a bucket it tries to put a Parquet file and gets the 403, on a local lake it says `Cannot append to a readonly database`. **Not refused by the lock: `quack_serve`.** The lake's secrets are made before the lock, so the secret manager is up, and past the gate `quack_serve('quack:127.0.0.1:<port>', token = '…')` starts a second listener [V: 2.0.0, the readers' lake instance: the port accepted a connection]; the copy's instance, which makes no secret, refuses it. The gate refuses `quack_*` in every key's SQL (the attack list over HTTP and over Quack, both kinds of lake), which is the wall, and `quack_serve` needs the gate bypassed. What such a listener is worth, and why it is accepted, is D204.
- Reason: three independent walls stand under the gate for a write (the attach, the login, the key), each proved by a test of its own, and a read of the lake is what a process attached to it can do whatever the gate says; the one thing past the gate that the lock does not close is a listener, and it is bounded by D204.
- Differences from the text: a local lake (SQLite) is supported as well as a Postgres one, since the suite's journeys run on both (`lake-local-readers`); the key-queries, quack and readers' suites of option 06 are not run unchanged on a lake but have lake versions that keep their cases (`lake-serve-mode.test.ts`, `lake-quack.test.ts`) and the three journeys j32 to j34 run on the lake jobs, because a case about the copy (its swap, its read-only file, a stray WAL, its policy) has no meaning there; the as-of time is the snapshot's, and on a Postgres lake the cases that need a bucket (acceptance 5) run only there; no case ran against a real R2 or a hosted Postgres, so the key's refusal is proved against the test store, which enforces a read-only key the way S3 does (an `AccessDenied`, 403), not against Cloudflare's.
- Build: `serve/lake-serve-lockdown.test.ts`, `db/modes.test.ts` (`lake-local-readers`).

**D190. No macOS job in CI. (new, 2026-11-04; refines §10 item 8, D155)**
- Choice: the `test` job's matrix drops `macos-15` (both Bun versions, both shards) and its Postgres step loses the `brew install` branch. Linux x64 and arm64, the lake journey jobs, the Alpine and Windows smokes and the release workflows are as they were. macOS stays tier 1 in the support list (§2): its code and tests (the boot id from `/usr/sbin/sysctl`, `cp -c`, the LaunchAgent) stay and run wherever the platform matches, on a Mac that runs `bun test`.
- Reason: GitHub's hosted macOS runners kept dropping the jobs after 15 minutes unstarted ("not acquired by Runner of type hosted", a capacity shortage), which blocked merges; a Mac check that never starts says nothing about the change.
- Cost: nothing in CI runs on macOS now, so a macOS-only break shows up on a person's Mac and not in a pull request.
- Build: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `tests/workflows.test.ts` pins the two operating systems.


**D191. A pull request waits for one run of the suite and a smoke per platform; the rest runs after a merge and daily. (new, 2026-11-04; refines §10 item 8 and "Test strategy", D155, D190; the suite's seven shards are dealt by time since D196, not turn by turn)**
- Options for a pull request's wait (26 minutes wall for the last run on main, run 41886964033): leave the matrix and add shards (the same work in four times the jobs, more than the plan runs at once); run the suite once and give every other platform and Bun a smoke; run the suite on one platform and nothing on the others. For the log run: all of it, a hand-kept list of files, a selection made from what the files say. For the post-merge run: a push to main only, or a push and a daily schedule.
- Choice: on a pull request, `test` is the whole suite on `ubuntu-24.04` and Bun 1.3.14 in seven shards, the typecheck in shard 1. `smoke` (`scripts/smoke.ts`) runs on Linux x64 with `bun@latest` and on Linux arm64 with both Bun versions: install, a project's pipeline and a query, `croft serve` in server mode answering a key and stopping, and the platform's pinned DuckDB extension files loading (what differs per platform: the pins are per platform, and the native DuckDB library is too). The two lake journey jobs stay on every pull request, in four and five shards. The Alpine and Windows smokes stay as they were (musl pins no extension files, and Windows is unsupported, so neither can run the pipeline smoke). The log run keeps two shards and runs only the test files that name the bookkeeping (`_croft`, a word `bookkeeping` in any case) in their own text, leaving out the journeys (they already run on a log, in a lake, in the lake jobs) and the files named `lake-*` (a lake's bookkeeping is always a log, so the switch changes nothing for them). The rule is a script that reads the files (`scripts/bookkeeping-tests.ts`), so a new test that touches the bookkeeping is in the run the day it is written, and it fails, not empties, when it chooses nothing (`bun test` with no filter would run everything).
