It cannot see a test that reaches the bookkeeping only through code and not through a name; the full log run after a merge does. On a push to main, on tags, by hand and on a daily schedule (09:17 UTC) everything that left the pull request path runs: the suite on the other three platform and Bun combinations (`test-platforms`, four shards each), and the whole log run in two shards. The concurrency group names the event, so the daily run, which is on main's ref, and a push to main do not cancel each other. The shard counts keep a pull request at eighteen jobs of over two minutes (plus seven of under a minute): the free plan runs twenty hosted jobs at once for the whole organization, and a job that waits for a slot is a wait.
- Reason: croft is the same TypeScript on every platform and Bun, and what differs is the native DuckDB library, the extension files (pinned per platform) and the process model, which the smoke exercises where they differ; the suite on the other combinations repeats the rest. Measured (per-file wall times from a probe run of the pull request's jobs, run 41896841977): the suite's 251 files add to 2,667 s, the journeys to 1,280 s on a local lake (41 files) and 1,840 s on a Postgres lake (44 files, with the HTTPS and DuckDB 1.5 files), and the 58 files the log rule chooses to about 526 s, 6,300 s in all, about 350 s a job over eighteen. Bun deals the sorted files out in turn, and the heavy files are not spread by it: with eight shards the suite's slowest was 8 minutes against a 4-minute fastest, and with three the local lake's was 14 minutes against 5 (run 41894249472). Dealing the same files by their measured times would bring the slowest to about 6 minutes, but it needs a table of times that goes stale, so the shard counts are chosen for the turn-by-turn deal instead: the largest shard of each job comes to about 8 to 9 minutes (the suite about 530 s over seven, the local lake about 350 s over four, the Postgres lake about 490 s over five), and a job's setup and teardown take about 30 s.
- Cost: a break that shows only on Linux arm64 or on `bun@latest` in the suite (and not in the smoke) is found after the merge, by the push to main, and not in the pull request; a break in a test that touches the bookkeeping only indirectly, through code and not through a file the rule can see, is found after the merge too. More jobs run at once on a pull request (the free plan allows 20 at a time), so a pull request's wait is not the sum of anything but it can grow when the queue does.
- Build: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `scripts/smoke.ts`; `scripts/bookkeeping-tests.ts` and `tests/bookkeeping-selection.test.ts`; `tests/workflows.test.ts` pins the jobs of each trigger, the shard counts' bounds and the log run's two steps; `tests/shards.test.ts` pins Bun's split for seven and four shards and for a list of files.

**D192. `croft maintain --orphans` lists a folder of any size, by letting its two warehouses name the bucket's root. (new, 2026-11-04; refines D149 to D152, D118)**
- Found in the real-lake trial against R2: on a lake folder holding more than 1,000 objects the command failed with `Cannot access "s3://<bucket>/" - file system operations are disabled by configuration`. DuckLake finds the files it does not own by listing the folder (`read_blob('s3://<bucket>/<folder>/**')`), and DuckDB's listing walks it a folder at a time and asks for each page past the first (S3 and R2 send at most 1,000 entries to a page) at the bucket's root, which a locked instance, whose allowed directories are the lake's folder alone (D118), refuses. Measured with DuckDB 2.0.0's httpfs against the test store: 1,000 objects list, 1,001 do not, and the same listing without the lock works. It is DuckDB's request, not a missing loop in croft.
- Options: add the bucket's root to every lake connection's allowed directories (it would let a person's SQL name any object in the bucket the key reaches); list the folder in croft with the store's API and hand DuckLake the names (a second implementation of what its function does, and its delete would still list); allow the root only in the two warehouses that run `ducklake_delete_orphaned_files`.
- Choice: the third. `LakeBucket.listsBucket` (db/modes.ts) adds `s3://<bucket>/` to the mode's directories and to the instance's identity; `listOrphansOf` and `deleteOrphansOf` (db/lake-pass.ts) ask for it through `lakeOption(project, env, { listsBucket: true })`. Those two warehouses run croft's own CALL and nothing a person wrote, in a process that ends with the command; every connection that runs SQL a person wrote keeps the folder alone.
- Cost: for the length of `croft maintain --orphans` an instance of croft's own may name any object of the bucket; the key's rights are what bound it there.
- Build: the test store (`db/s3-store-testkit.ts`) pages a listing the way S3 does when it rolls keys up under a delimiter (a key or a folder is one entry, `max-keys` entries to a page); before, it paged the keys first and sent a folder once per page, so a listing past one page repeated every file. `cli/commands/maintain-orphans-bucket.test.ts` plants 1,150 stray files in a Postgres lake's folder and runs the real command: the list, the confirmation and the delete.

**D193. In server mode over a lake the engine looks for a changed keys file every 250 ms. (new, 2026-11-04; refines D126, D183)**
- Option 06 promises that a removed key's open Quack session is refused "within one second", and the file engine sends the readers' process the keys every 250 ms. The lake engine used its one poll, `LAKE_POLL_MS` (1,000 ms), for the keys as well, so a removal could take a full second to reach the process, and the promise left no time for the process to refuse.
- Choice: the engine's look (`tickMs`) is `LAKE_KEYS_POLL_MS` (250 ms) when server mode is on and `LAKE_POLL_MS` otherwise; how long a lake nobody has written waits before the next attach (`pollMs`) stays a second, so the catalog is not tried four times a second. A `pollMs` given to the engine sets both, as before.
- Build: `serve/lake-quack.test.ts` "the engine's own poll" starts the engine without a `pollMs`, adds a key, removes it at once and checks that the process was told within 1,000 ms; it measured 1,000 ms before the change and about 250 after.

**D194. `croft move-to-lake` reads croft.json the way the loader does, byte-order mark included. (new, 2026-11-04; refines D172)**
- `readCopyByName` read croft.json with `JSON.parse` on the raw text, which refuses a leading byte-order mark, and answered false for a file it could not parse; the loader strips the mark (`parseConfig`). A croft.json with a mark and `"readCopy": true` passed the move's check, and the project failed CONFIG_INVALID after the switch ("`readCopy` does not apply to a lake").
- Choice: `withoutBom` (project/root.ts) is the one function that strips the mark, used by `parseConfig`, by `readCopyByName` and by `croft init --claude`, which reads the time zone for the Claude files and fell back to the detected one when the mark made the parse fail. It is not the only place a mark is stripped: the user tick (`schedule/user-tick.ts`) is a script that runs without croft's modules, so it strips its own when it reads `stateDir`.
- Build: `cli/commands/move-to-lake.test.ts` "a read copy is refused in a croft.json that starts with a byte-order mark"; `project/init.test.ts` "reads the time zone from a croft.json that starts with a byte-order mark".

**D195. DuckDB's extension files are fetched from DuckDB's own servers; nothing but croft is published. (new, 2026-11-04, the maintainer's decision; replaces D134 and D135 in how files reach users; refines §2, §5 "Pinned extensions", D117; option 06 slice 5)**
- Options: optional add-on packages on npm, 2 add-ons and 16 per-platform extension packages (D134, D135); the files bundled in every croft install; croft fetches each file from the extension repository DuckDB itself uses, checks it against the checksum it pins, and keeps it on the machine.
- Choice: the third. The maintainer, 2026-11-04, shown the 18 packages: "i don't think we should be publishing something that is already published". The files are DuckDB's, signed by DuckDB, and DuckDB publishes them; croft publishes only itself, and DuckDB's own notices travel with DuckDB's files because croft redistributes nothing.
- How it works: `db/extension-fetch.ts` downloads `https://extensions.duckdb.org/v2.0.0/<platform>/<file>.duckdb_extension.gz` (`$CROFT_EXTENSION_REPO` for a mirror or a test's stand-in), unpacks it in memory, compares size and sha256 with the pin (D117) and only then writes it, to a `.part-<random>` file, opened exclusively and renamed into place, in the folder of §5 "Where the files come from" (`$CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR`, else `~/.cache/croft/extensions`). The body is read with a cap of the pinned size plus 1 MB and unpacked with a cap of the pinned size, so a server cannot fill memory or disk (either overrun is the same mismatch, `details.bytes: null`). A download that differs from the pin is `EXTENSION_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH` with `details.kind: "download"` and nothing is written; a fetch that cannot finish is the new `EXTENSION_FETCH_FAILED`. DuckDB's signature check stays on (`allow_unsigned_extensions` is set nowhere; a test reads the source for it) and croft still never runs `INSTALL` or autoloads: a file is loaded by absolute path, after the pin and then DuckDB's own signature check at `LOAD`.
- When it fetches: on first need, in `prepareMode` (`db/modes.ts`) for the files a mode needs that are absent, called by `connect` for an instance that is not locked yet (so always before the lockdown, and a locked instance never fetches); and on `croft fetch-extensions [names] [--all]`, the explicit command for a machine that has no network when croft runs, which also works outside a project and replaces a file that fails its check. `croft validate`, `croft doctor` and `croft status` never fetch: they report `EXTENSION_MISSING` (`details.kind: "file"`, `details.missing`, `details.mode`) with `croft fetch-extensions <names>` as the fix, which an agent can run; `data.extensionFiles` (was `data.addons`) and the doctor check `extensions.<mode>` (was `addon.<name>`). A file that is there and wrong is refused at the mode's start, not replaced behind the user's back. `$CROFT_NO_FETCH=1` turns the first-use fetch off. The readers' process fetches in its own process, so the parent's wait for its first open includes the download (about 2 s on the machine below; there is no separate timeout on that wait).
- Deleted, with no shim: `.github/workflows/publish-addons.yml` and the `npm-addons` environment it named, `db/addons.ts` (`ADDONS`, `MODE_ADDONS`, `ADDON_VERSION`, the package names), `db/addon-testkit.ts`, `scripts/addon-packages.ts`, `scripts/build-addons.ts`, the licence-notice machinery nothing else uses (`scripts/notices.ts`, `scripts/check-notices.ts`, `scripts/notices/`, `scripts/build-source-owners.ts`, `scripts/elf-files.ts`), `ModeSpec.projectRoot` and every caller that passed it, `croft docs addons` (replaced by `croft docs extensions`), `tests/addons.test.ts`, `db/addons.test.ts`, `cli/commands/addons.test.ts` and `addons-lake.test.ts` (their checks moved to `cli/commands/extension-status.test.ts`), and the workflow tests for the add-on publish. `db/addon-status.ts` became `db/extension-status.ts`; `AddonView` became `ExtensionFilesView`; `ExtensionView.source` is gone (there is one place a file is). The builders' cache folder is `~/.cache/croft/extensions` (it was `test-extensions`) and `scripts/fetch-extensions.ts` fills a folder with the same code, for CI, which therefore also exercises the real fetch on Linux.
- Reason: the add-on packages would have published DuckDB's own files a second time, 18 packages with every DuckDB version, each publish on the maintainer's word, for a download DuckDB already serves signed. The checksum pin (D117) already made the registry as untrusted as the folder, so it makes no difference to safety where the bytes come from; only DuckDB's servers are one hop less.
- Cost, accepted: a project's first use of either mode needs the network and DuckDB's servers (a download of about 21 MB for server mode and 34 MB for lake mode, about 66 MB and 109 MB on disk once unpacked, on macOS arm64; Linux files are larger; once per machine and DuckDB version); an air-gapped host fetches elsewhere and copies the folder (`$CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR`). If DuckDB removed a version's files the mode would fail with `EXTENSION_FETCH_FAILED` (404), and the fix is a newer croft that pins a newer DuckDB. Plain croft with no mode on stays offline and unchanged, and the install is the same size (`tests/pack.test.ts` still asserts no extension file is packed).
- Build: `db/extension-fetch.test.ts` (a stand-in repository on 127.0.0.1 with small files pinned in place of DuckDB's: layout, fetch once, a tampered file and a one-byte change refused with nothing written, 404, 500, unreachable and not-gzip answers, a wrong file replaced by the explicit fetch and not by the first-use one, two fetches of one file made once, no fetch when `$CROFT_NO_FETCH` is set), `db/modes.test.ts` "a mode fetches what the folder lacks from DuckDB, before it locks" (the stand-in serves DuckDB's real files, and DuckDB loads them with its signature check on; a locked instance reopened with its files deleted asks the repository for nothing; a mode that does not fit its profile downloads nothing), `db/extension-files.test.ts` (the fix is the command, several missing files are named in one), `cli/commands/fetch-extensions.test.ts` and `extension-status.test.ts` (the missing-file report and its fix, run, then validate clean), `tests/golden/g04-schedule-serve.test.ts` (the command's envelope against its schema), `tests/workflows.test.ts` (only `publish-npm.yml` publishes, nothing names an add-on). No test reaches DuckDB's servers: `tests/preload.ts` sets `CROFT_NO_FETCH=1` and points `CROFT_EXTENSION_REPO` at a closed port, and the e2e harness and `cliEnv` do the same for the processes they start.
- Real fetch (2026-11-04, macOS arm64, DuckDB 2.0.0, Bun 1.3.14): `croft fetch-extensions --all` into an empty folder, outside a project, from `https://extensions.duckdb.org`: httpfs 19.7 MB, quack 46.4 MB, postgres 45.9 MB and ducklake 43.2 MB unpacked, 2.2 s in all, each matching its pin; `croft fetch-extensions sqlite` likewise (41.9 MB). `db/modes.test.ts`, `cli/commands/extension-status.test.ts` and `cli/commands/server-mode.test.ts` then passed (76 tests) against that folder, so DuckDB loads the fetched files with its signature check on. The Linux platforms' downloads were pinned from the same server on 2026-11-01 and are fetched by CI through `scripts/fetch-extensions.ts` on its runners; croft's own fetch was not run on Linux by hand.


**D196. A release publishes what main's CI already tested; the pull request's shards are dealt by time. (new, 2026-11-04, the maintainer's request; refines §10 item 8 and "Test strategy", D191, D155)**
- Options: the release as it was (the tag runs `ci.yml` again, and `publish-npm.yml` runs the typecheck, the whole suite in one job and the site test, a third full run of one commit); a release that refuses unless main's CI passed at the tagged commit and runs no suite; a release that skips the check and trusts the tag. For the shards: Bun's turn-by-turn deal with more shards; the same deal with the heavy files named by hand; a deal by the measured seconds of each file.
- Choice: the second and the third. The release of 0.5.0 ran the suite three times on one commit (main's push, the tag's `ci.yml` and the `pack` job), about 40 minutes of runner time for no new information. `ci.yml` no longer runs on `croft-v*` tags (`phase-*` tags still run it). `publish-npm.yml`'s `pack` job keeps the tag-equals-version check, the already-on-npm check, the typecheck, `npm pack`, the tarball checks, and the `publish` job keeps the manifest dry-run refusal, OIDC trusted publishing and provenance, with no npm token; it loses the extension files, Postgres, `bun test` and the site test (the site job is part of `ci.yml`'s run on main), and gains `actions: read` and one step, `scripts/release-gate.ts`, which lists `ci.yml`'s runs for the tagged commit with `event=push` and `branch=main` through the API and passes only on a completed run with conclusion `success` in which every job succeeded and each kind of croft job (the suite's shards, the after-merge platforms, the log run, both lake journeys and the smokes) is there as many times as `ci.yml` has it (D202). A push whose change detector finds only the site, docs or infrastructure skips every croft job and still ends `success`: a docs-only commit B on top of a croft commit A whose own run failed, or was cancelled by a newer push, would release A's untested code, so a run with a skipped job does not count. A manual run of `ci.yml` on main (workflow_dispatch, which always runs everything) at the tagged commit counts like the push run, and is the way to get a full run at such a commit: the refusal prints `gh workflow run ci.yml --ref main`, which tests main's tip, so the tag must be on it. A run still queued or going is waited for, every 30 seconds up to 45 minutes (main's push run takes about 25; a release tagged after main's CI is green waits for nothing); a run that failed or was cancelled, or none after a few minutes, stops the release with the reason. The daily run, a pull request's run and a tag's run do not count. A tag on a commit that was not the tip of a push to main has no run and is refused: tag the commit main's CI ran on. The pull request's seven shards are dealt by `scripts/shard-files.ts` from `tests/shard-times.json` (longest file first, to the shard with the least so far), instead of Bun's `--shard`.
- Reason: measured on four runs of the `test` job (pull request runs of three branches and the push to main of the 0.5.0 merge, 251 files, 2,420 to 2,710 s of tests in all). Bun's deal gave the shards 194, 259, 279, 300, 493, 535 and 361 s of tests in the first of them (the job of shard 6 took 9.3 minutes against 3.7 for shard 1), because the sorted files are dealt in turn and the heavy ones are not spread by that: the one file `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` takes 200 s alone. Dealing the files of each run by the mean of the other three runs gave 311 to 385, 349 to 403, 350 to 446 and 338 to 382 s (the longest shard in each, against an even split of 345 to 390), so the longest suite job comes to about 7.5 to 8 minutes with its 30 s of setup, against 9.3; the committed table is the mean of all four and deals an even 369 s a shard. The shard count stays seven, so a pull request still runs eighteen jobs of over two minutes (D191). D191 declined this deal because a table of times goes stale; it is taken now because staleness is harmless by construction (the script deals every file it finds, the unknown at the median weight) and refreshing it is one command, and the next refresh is due when the slowest suite job is 1.5 times the others.
- Cost: a release trusts the CI run on main: nothing is tested again at the tag, which is the same commit, and a commit whose run on main is gone (GitHub keeps runs for 90 days by default) is refused until main is tested again. The wait for main's CI runs on a hosted runner and spends its minutes; it is zero when the tag follows a green main, which is the order of the release steps. `tests/shard-times.json` is a file to keep: a new heavy test weighs the median until the table is refreshed, and the shard that gets it runs longer. The lake journey jobs (four and five shards) are still dealt in turn, and the local lake's fourth shard (8.2 minutes in the run measured above) is now the pull request's longest job.
- Build: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (no `croft-v*` tag; the `test` job lists its files first, so that a script that fails stops the step and `bun test` is not left with no filter), `.github/workflows/publish-npm.yml`, `scripts/release-gate.ts`, `scripts/shard-files.ts`, `scripts/shard-timings.ts`, `tests/shard-times.json`. `tests/workflows.test.ts` pins that `ci.yml` has no release tag, that the pack job runs no test, extension fetch or Postgres, that the gate runs after the version and already-published checks and before the pack with the job's token and `actions: read` as its only addition, that the publish job holds the OIDC token and no more, and that the gate passes a successful push or manual run on main at the commit in which every job succeeded, and stops a failed, cancelled, missing or other-event run, a run with skipped jobs or without a kind of croft job, and a manual run on another branch (judged on stubbed runs and jobs; also run once by hand against the 0.5.0 merge commit, which it passed, with the real API). `tests/shards.test.ts` pins that the script finds the files Bun runs (a tree with `.test`, `_test`, `.spec` and `_spec` files of every extension and look-alikes in `node_modules`, dot folders and `.d.ts` files), that a list of `./` paths runs exactly those files, that the deal is a partition for 1 to 7 shards with a new file and a gone file in the table, and that the committed table splits the package's files within 10% of even.

**D197. A lake's bookkeeping is written in inserts that stay in the catalog, and the move's copy is one of them. (new, 2026-11-05, found dogfooding the move; refines D154, D168, D179)**
- Options: leave the copy as it was and let the first `croft maintain` mend it (D179); run the bring-back as the move's last step; write the bookkeeping inlined in the first place, in the adapter every insert of a SELECT goes through.
- Choice: the third. The log adapter's `insertSelect`, when the warehouse is a lake, keeps the SELECT's rows in a temporary table and writes them in inserts of the lake's inlining limit (`inliningLimit`, now in `db/bookkeeping.ts`, the option the lake stores or DuckLake's default of 10), numbered in order from the log's highest `seq`. Up to `INLINE_MAX_ROWS` (1,000, the number a pass of D179 brings back) rows go in that way; a table with more is written in one insert for the rest, which a lake puts in a file and `croft maintain` brings back a pass at a time. A lake with an inlining limit of 0 is written as before. A file warehouse is untouched.
- Reason: the move's copy wrote each bookkeeping table in one `INSERT ... SELECT`, and DuckLake writes an insert of more rows than its inlining limit as a Parquet file. A real move of 11 tables left five of the `_croft` logs in files straight away (`croft doctor` warned LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES, and every command read them over the network until a pass mended it). D179's bring-back cannot be the move's last step inside the copy's transaction (DuckLake 2.0.0 cannot read back a table a transaction changed, D142), and as a step after the commit it would be a second write the equality proof (D168) does not cover; inlining the rows in the copy keeps them inside the one transaction the proof already reads. The adapter is also where a restore's rows go, so a restore's copy stays in the catalog too; `remove`, `update` and `rekey` of more than 10 rows were other statements, which this did not change and which could still write a file (D198 chunks them too). The cap is the cost of a lake at a distance: an insert is a round trip to the catalog, and a long history is a thousand of them at most.
- Doctor's words: LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES no longer says an older croft's pass left the files. It cannot know (a large insert does it too); it says what it found, in how many files and bytes, and that `croft maintain` is the fix.
- Build: `db/bookkeeping.ts` (`insertSelect`, `inliningLimit`, `INLINE_MAX_ROWS`), `db/lake-maintenance.ts` (`REINLINE_MAX_ROWS` is `INLINE_MAX_ROWS`), `cli/commands/doctor.ts`, `src/agent/docs/LAKE_BOOKKEEPING_IN_FILES.md` and `lake.md`. `db/lake-move.test.ts` (a local and a Postgres lake: after the copy no `_croft` table has a file, the proof is equal and the log's `seq` are distinct; a table of 1,200 rows has its first 1,000 in the catalog and the rest in one file, which a pass brings back), `tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts` step c (doctor has no bookkeeping warning after the move).

**D200. The scheduled job carries the shell's extension settings; doctor says when they differ. (new, 2026-11-05, from the review of D195; refines D195, §8 "Turning it on")**
- Options: leave scheduled runs on the default folder and fetching (the OS job passes only `HOME` and `PATH`) and document it; record the four settings in croft.json; copy them from the shell that runs `croft schedule on` into the job.
- Choice: the third, and doctor compares. croft.json is committed and shared, and a folder or a switch for fetching is one machine's (an image with the files baked in, a host that must stay offline); the job is one per user, like the shell that installs it.
- How it works: `schedule/register.ts` `jobSettings` takes `CROFT_EXTENSION_DIR`, `CROFT_NO_FETCH`, `CROFT_EXTENSION_REPO` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` (`EXTENSION_ENV`, `schedule/user-tick.ts`) from the environment `croft schedule on` ran in, those that are set, a folder made absolute. On macOS they are keys of the plist's `EnvironmentVariables`; on Linux they are `NAME=value` assignments before the command on croft's crontab line (not lines of the crontab, which would reach the user's other jobs). The tick script passes them to each project tick (`TICK_PASS_ENV`, template 3), and the tick passes its environment to the runs it starts. `ensureJob` is as idempotent as before: the same environment is no rewrite, a different one rewrites and reloads the job, and a shell with none of them removes them. `croft schedule on` names the settings it carried (`job.extensionSettings`, names only: a mirror's address may hold a login, and the plist is readable by the machine's other users).
- Doctor: for a project with a mode on and scheduling through the OS job, `scheduling.extensions` is a warning when this shell's settings are not the installed job's (`installedSettings` reads the plist, or `crontab -l`), saying which differ and that `croft schedule on` from the right shell rewrites the job. Silent when they agree, with no mode, with scheduling off or through `croft serve`, and when no job can be read. It has no code of its own: it is not a problem with a fix an agent can apply without choosing which shell is right.
- Cost, accepted: two shells with different settings that each run `croft schedule on` take turns owning the job, and the last one wins; the warning is how the other one finds out.
- Build: `schedule/register.test.ts` (the plist and the crontab line, quoting, reading back, idempotence, a table from before this change), `schedule/user-tick.test.ts` (the settings reach the tick's child), `cli/commands/extension-status.test.ts` (the warning on macOS and Linux, and each silent case). No test installs a LaunchAgent or a crontab: every one uses a fake runner and a fake home (`CROFT_FORBID_OS_JOBS`).

**D201. A killed fetch is cleaned up after, and a file that cannot be stored is a croft error; the doctor and the modes read one list of files. (new, 2026-11-05, from the review of D195; refines D195)**
- Options for the `.part-` file a killed fetch leaves: leave it, remove every `.part-` file beside the target, or remove those older than a minute. Options for the two lists (`MODE_FILES` in `db/extension-status.ts`, `MODE_EXTENSIONS` in `db/modes.ts`): a test that they agree, or one derived from the other.
- Choice: the third, and the second. A fetch that is killed between its write and its rename leaves a file of the pinned size, and nothing removed it. Another croft may be between its own write and rename, so only a leftover of this file's name that is older than a minute is removed, by the next fetch of it. `MODE_FILES` takes its extensions from `MODE_EXTENSIONS` (`readers` for server mode, `lake`), so `validate`, `doctor` and `status` cannot say a mode's files are fine when the mode would fetch others.
- A file that downloads whole and passes its checksum but cannot be put in place (a folder at the path, a read-only folder, a full disk) was a raw rename error. It is now `EXTENSION_FETCH_FAILED` with `details.kind: "write"` and `details.path`, not retryable, and a manual fix: what is in the way is the user's, and retrying the download does not help.
- Build: `db/extension-fetch.test.ts` (stale and young `.part-` files, a folder where the file goes), `cli/commands/fetch-extensions.test.ts` (the same through the command), `db/modes.test.ts` (the two lists agree; a fresh instance works after croft's fetch with fetching off and the repository a port nothing listens on).

**D198. A lake's bookkeeping is also appended in inserts that stay in the catalog by `remove`, `update` and `rekey`, and a failed chunk reports its own error. (new, 2026-11-05, follow-ups of croft PR #31; refines D197)**
- Options: leave the three to a pass of D179; chunk each of them where it is written; give the log adapter one append that every write which reads rows of the log and writes them back goes through.
- Choice: the third. `LogBookkeeping.appendRows` (`db/bookkeeping.ts`) takes a SELECT and whether its rows close their keys, keeps the rows in a temporary table in a lake, and writes them in inserts of the lake's inlining limit, up to `INLINE_MAX_ROWS` and one insert for any more, as D197 did for `insertSelect`; `insertSelect`, `update` and `remove` call it (`rekey` is an `update` and a `remove`). A file, and a lake with an inlining limit of 0, run the one statement they ran. Its `finally` drops the temporary table, and when the insert failed it swallows a failure of the drop: the failed statement had aborted the transaction (`TransactionContext Error: Current transaction is aborted`), the drop threw over the error that did it, and the person was told about the drop. The rollback takes the table.
- Reason: a file ingest retiring many files, a restore of an asset with many columns, a rename of an asset with many files, and any `update` of a table's rows wrote more than 10 rows in one INSERT, which DuckLake puts in a Parquet file; every read of the table then goes to the store until a pass brings it back (D179), and nothing says so until `croft doctor` does. The chunks cost no catalog round trip more than the one insert did (the rows are read from the log once, into the temporary table, which is local), measured by `scripts/bench-lake-latency.ts`: a run with one file changed was 475 round trips before and 477 after.
- Build: `db/bookkeeping.ts`. `db/bookkeeping.test.ts` (in a local lake: 40 rows removed, updated and renamed leave no file in the store and read as they should, a change of 1,100 rows reads right, and a chunk that cannot convert its value fails with its own error and leaves the next transaction to write; all but the 1,100-row one fail on main).

**D199. A lake's format is stamped where the catalog is loaded, so a query that names no croft table does not read croft's tables. (new, 2026-11-05, follow-ups of the dogfood; refines D144, D176)**
- Options: leave it (D176 measured what is left and called the format check the one removable part, "a decision for whoever owns D144"); skip the check for a query that names no `_croft` table (weakens D144); turn off the `postgres` pool's health check (`pg_pool_health_check_query = ''`); stamp the format in the catalog and check that.
- Choice: the last. `ensureState` writes, in the transaction that writes `format_version` and before its rows (DDL first), a comment on the lake's `_croft.meta` table, `croft format <n>`, only when the stamp differs; `checkFormat` in a lake reads it from `duckdb_tables()`, which is in the catalog a connection loads as it begins, and answers from it when it names a format this croft reads. No stamp (a lake no croft that stamps has written; the next write of state puts it), or a format this croft does not read, is answered from the rows of `_croft.meta` exactly as before, so the refusal of a newer lake (`DB_NEWER_FORMAT`, with the croft that wrote it) is unchanged. The rows stay the source of truth; the stamp is a copy croft writes in the same transaction. A file warehouse is untouched.
- Reason: where an attach spends its round trips (a `croft query` on a four-asset lake, 40 ms away, 76 round trips, 3.8 s): `ATTACH` 17 (the connection with its SCRAM login, DuckLake's version and metadata reads, and `SELECT 1` / `DISCARD ALL` around each use of a pooled connection), `USE lake` 20 (DuckLake loads the whole catalog as the first statement of a transaction), the format check 28 (6 for the table, 22 because DuckLake reads inlined rows at the schema version they were made in and so loads the catalog a second time, D176), the query 8, the end of the transaction 2. The secrets and the extensions cost no round trip (0.04 s of this machine's CPU). Only the check was croft's to remove, and a second connection of the same process pays 4 for `USE lake` and 3 for a table, because DuckLake keeps what it loaded, so the first look is what is dear. After the stamp the same query is 53 round trips and 2.7 s; a command that reads croft's own tables anyway (every other command) pays the second load at its first read of them, as before. Not done: the pool's health check is 7 of the round trips (17 to 12 in the attach), and `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` "reconnects by itself" and "a Postgres that restarts between leases" fail without it (a connection ended between two leases is found by the statement that uses it, and DuckLake's error is not one croft's retry mends), so it stays (D176's "Not done" stands). `lakeExists` (a read-only attach before `croft maintain` attaches again to write, 17 round trips of 590) and the lookup of a lake's data path in the query gate (1 round trip) were left: they are small, and each guards a decision (a lake nobody has written is not made by a pass; a local data folder is never SQL's to name).
- Cost, accepted: a lake carries one more catalog change per format bump (the comment is a snapshot, once for a lake that had none), and a croft older than this one ignores the comment and keeps reading the rows. A lake whose rows say a newer format than its stamp does is read as the stamp says: only a hand edit or a croft that writes `format_version` outside `ensureState` could make one, and the first is not croft's to guard against; the second is the rule this decision sets (a writer of `format_version` writes the stamp with it).
- Build: `db/state.ts` (`lakeStamp`, `checkFormat`, `ensureState`). `db/lake-warehouse.test.ts` (the first read of a stamped lake whose meta rows are of an older schema version costs the catalog 20 or more round trips less than the same lake with the stamp taken off, and the next write of state puts the stamp back once; a lake of a newer format is refused with the stamp a newer croft writes and without it). `scripts/bench-lake-latency.ts` and `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-05-lake-start.md` hold the numbers.

**D202. The release gate counts each kind of croft job by its own name; the daily run is checked, not changed. (new, 2026-11-05, from the review of D196; refines D196)**
- Options for the gate's job kinds: a word in the name of each kind (what D196 built: "shard", "smoke"); an anchored name per kind with the number of jobs it has; the job ids from the API (they are not in the jobs of a run's listing).
- Choice: the second. `JOB_KINDS` in `scripts/release-gate.ts` is eight kinds (the suite's 7 shards, the after-merge platforms' 12, the log run's 2, the local lake's 4 and the Postgres lake's 5, the platform smokes' 3, the Alpine smoke, the Windows smoke), each a name matched from its start to its end and a count, and a run passes only if every job succeeded and each kind has exactly its count. `tests/workflows.test.ts` expands `ci.yml`'s matrices (the product of the dimensions less `exclude`, or the `include` list; `${{ matrix.x }}` filled in) and checks that its croft jobs are exactly these kinds, each matched by one kind and counted, so a job added, renamed or resharded in `ci.yml` fails there until the gate is changed with it.
- Reason: "shard" is also in the after-merge, log and lake jobs' names, and "smoke" in the Alpine and Windows jobs', so a deleted or renamed suite job went unnoticed as long as another job said "shard" (stubbed: a run with no job of the suite's seven shards, no Alpine and no Windows job, and one job of each other kind, passed the old check and fails the new one with every short kind named). A job a run skipped still fails first, as before: GitHub does not fill in a matrix job's name when it skips the job, so it keeps `shard ${{ matrix.shard }}/7` (seen in the run of this change's pull request, and in a probe: a matrix made empty by `fromJSON` of `[]` fails the run instead, so the name stays and is explained in a comment in `ci.yml`). Run against the 37 jobs of a real full run (a manual run of this branch, 42056028512) the gate passes.
- Not changed: the gate still counts a push or a manual run on main only, and not the daily run, though the daily run is a full run of main's tip; counting it would let a release follow a green night without a green push at its commit, which is a decision of its own.
- The daily run (found 2026-11-05 that it had not run): the schedule (`17 9 * * *`) reached main with PR #25 on 2026-11-04 at 19:54 UTC, so its first run was due on 2026-11-05 at 09:17 UTC, and none had been made by 14:40 UTC. Nothing in `ci.yml` keeps a scheduled run from being made: the `on:` block lists it, the workflow is active on the default branch, Actions is enabled on the public repository, and a job's `if` only skips the job (the run is still made). A manual run of the branch ran all 37 jobs of a full run (the `changes` job answers `true` for any event that is not a push or a pull request, and `test-platforms` and the log run's full step run for any event that is not a pull request), which is what the daily run runs. So the file is right and the cause is GitHub's side, which documents that scheduled runs can be delayed or dropped under load; unverified until the run due on 2026-11-06 at 09:17 UTC shows (`gh run list --event schedule`). If it is still missing then, the minute is the next thing to move.
- Build: `scripts/release-gate.ts` (`JOB_KINDS`, `fullRun`), `tests/workflows.test.ts` (`jobNames`, "ci.yml's jobs, matrices expanded, are exactly the kinds", "the gate refuses a run missing, short of or renamed in any one kind"), `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (a comment), `scripts/smoke.ts` (the server it starts is stopped when an assertion fails after that; the exit handler sends SIGINT; before, `fail` ended the process with the server running, shown by a probe that failed after the key read and left `croft serve` behind).

**D203. The independent kill -9 faults of j37 run side by side. (new, 2026-11-05; refines "Test strategy", D191)**
- Options: leave j37 in order (200 s alone in CI, the longest file); run its independent tests with `test.concurrent`, as j16's are since PR #30; share one lake rig between them (measured and dropped in "Test strategy": a start is 0.4 to 0.6 s); split the file in two.
- Choice: the second. Of the 27 tests, the faults a, b, e and f of each lake kind (10 on a local lake, 10 on a Postgres lake) are concurrent; c (Postgres restarted and its connections ended under a running command), the credentials tests d and the two attach-failure tests stay in order, since c's restart is felt by every test on that rig and the others take 1 to 5 s. Each fault already builds a project of its own (`shop()`: a folder, a route on the mock API, a lake: a SQLite catalog in the project or a database and a bucket folder in the rig, `createLakeDatabase` taking turns since PR #30), kills only the croft process it started (`CROFT_FAULT` is that child's environment) and reads only its own project's rows and lock, so nothing of the test changed but the route of c, which was found by a counter shared with the other tests and is now the one its shop returned. All 300 assertions are kept (27 tests, 300 `expect()` calls before and after).
- Reason, measured: on the maintainer's laptop (a shared machine, 28 cores) the file took 112.7, 118.9 and 119.5 s in order and 59.0 and 50.9 s with the faults side by side; the ten Postgres-lake faults ran together against one rig (60 connections allowed) without a refusal. In CI (four vCPUs, the file's time in the jobs that run it; run 42043410666 on main before, the manual run 42056028512 of this branch after) it went from 206.6 to 163.2 s in suite shard 1, 201.3 to 164.2 in the log run's shard 1, 242.2 to 158.0 on the local lake's shard 2, 258.2 to 170.2 on the Postgres lake's shard 3, and 221.7, 221.4 and 191.2 to 119.5, 141.1 and 96.5 s in the after-merge shards. The gain is smaller than on a laptop because a fault is mostly croft processes starting, which the runner's four cores run four at a time.
- Cost: on a runner with fewer cores the tests run longer each (the twenty concurrent tests have 300 s each: the longest took 34 s with twenty at once on a busy laptop, and about 100 s on a CI runner; three copies of the file at once on a laptop timed out every concurrent test together at the earlier 180 and 240 s); a failure of one fault prints in the middle of the others' output. `tests/shard-times.json` was refreshed from the two full runs of this branch (the file's weight 198.7 to 165.9 s, and the files PR #30 sped up have their new times: `lake-gate` 67.6 to 56.3, `store-tls` 60.4 to 47.3), which deals the seven shards an even 384 s each; the old table dealt 360 to 422 s by the new times.
- Build: `tests/e2e/j37-lake-faults.test.ts` (`test.concurrent` on a, b, e and f; `shop()` returns its route; the comment at the top says why c stays alone), `tests/shard-times.json`.

**D204. A second Quack listener past a gate bypass is accepted: the lock cannot refuse it, and what it is worth is bounded. (new, 2026-11-05; refines D131, D186, D118)**
- Options: a DuckDB setting that refuses or constrains `quack_serve` after the lock; refusing the function at the instance; a macro of croft's named `quack_serve` in the in-memory database; leave it, with the gate as the wall, and record what a listener started that way is worth.
- Choice: the last. [V: 2.0.0, quack build `f96420ed46`] Quack's settings are cache sizes, timeouts, `quack_server_max_connections` and the names of the authentication and authorization functions, and debug switches: none refuses a listener, fixes its address or counts the servers of an instance, and two `quack_serve` calls on one instance listen side by side. DuckDB has no setting that disables a function by name. A macro `memory.main.quack_serve` shadows an unqualified call, and `system.main.quack_serve(…)` still reaches the real function, so a macro would be a second gate and not a wall. What a listener started that way is worth is proved in `serve/lake-serve-lockdown.test.ts` ("a second Quack listener started past the gate"): the authentication and authorization functions are DuckDB settings of the instance (D125), so the second listener runs croft's hooks; the token it was started with signs no one in; a listed key signs in and is refused the tables the first listener refuses. It differs from the first in its address, which the caller picks: D131's loopback rule is a check croft makes before it starts its own listener, so a bypass can bind every interface, without TLS (`allow_other_hostname`, `disable_ssl`), where the listed keys and the shared tables are all that stand.
- Reason: it needs a bypass of the gate, which refuses `quack_*` in every key's SQL (the attack list over HTTP and over Quack, both kinds of lake), and a bypass already has SQL in a process attached read-only to the lake, which reads all of it; the listener adds a door on the network to a service that still asks for a listed key and refuses what a key may not read, and gives the caller no data it could not already read. Only the lake readers' instance can start it (the copy's makes no secret and refuses). Revisit if DuckDB gives an instance a way to refuse a function or a listener.
- Build: `serve/lake-serve-lockdown.test.ts` (the test above, on a local and a Postgres lake), `serve/lake-serve-testkit.ts` (`lakeSession` takes a listener and can let people sign in).

**D205. `croft query` keeps changing the process's folder to the project's, because DuckDB's sandbox cannot do without it. (new, 2026-11-05; refines §4.3 "query", D112; found checking the follow-up of croft PR #30)**
- Options: pass the project root to the gate and let DuckDB find relative paths through `file_search_path`; rewrite the relative path literals of the SQL to absolute ones in the gate before DuckDB sees them; keep the change of folder (`inDirectory`, which takes turns).
- Choice: the third. [V: 2.0.0, the query sandbox: `allowed_directories` the project's `files/`, external access off, configuration locked, `file_search_path` the project root] Run from any other folder, `FROM 'files/x.csv'`, `read_csv`, `read_text` and a glob all fail with "Cannot access file files/x.csv": the sandbox checks the path as written against the process's folder, and `file_search_path` is only consulted afterwards, so it cannot stand in for the folder. Without the sandbox it is a fallback too: a file that exists under the process's folder wins over the project's, so a gate that resolved against the project root and a DuckDB that opened the folder's file would read different files. Rewriting the literals in the gate (the AST gives each constant's `query_location` and length) would work, with a re-parse to check the rest of the statement did not change, but it is a new mechanism in the security gate, DuckDB's own error text would name absolute paths, and it buys nothing in a real run: the launcher changes into the project root before it starts the project's croft ("The launcher"), so `inDirectory` is a no-op there (`before === dir`) and only a caller inside one process (the tests, `main` with `io.cwd`) ever changes the folder.
- Reason: the change of folder is serialized (croft PR #30), so two projects asked at once in one process each see their own, and it is restored afterwards. Build the rewrite if croft is ever run as a library with several projects in one process at once, or if the sandbox starts to resolve against a folder of its own.
- Build: none; `cli/commands/query.test.ts` "inDirectory" (projects asked at once take turns) stays.

## Open questions for the user

Decided on 2026-09-22:

- **Name:** croft, published as `@zabaca/croft` (D52).
- **Desktop notifications** on scheduled failures: on by default.
- **Scope:** v1 is all 5 phases, about 14.5 engineer-weeks (13.5 before D53 added `croft serve`).
- **App access:** `croft serve` (reading through croft serve, D119) instead of a default read copy; the read copy is opt-in, for GUIs (D53).

Open since the build (2026-09-23):

- **Overlapping file exports:** the latest-loaded file owns a key (D58, shipped), or the export that sorts last wins (rebuild-invariant, and a re-exported old file would not override newer rows).

Open since phase 2 (2026-09-24):

- **Paid rows lost on a failed attempt:** a chunked TS transform loses, and re-bills, the chunk it was filling each time its code fails (a 429 from an LLM after `http`'s retries, a timeout). In one test run, rows 501–699 were billed three times across three attempts (§3e, §8). The alternative is to commit the rows already yielded, with the position before the failing row, before retrying or failing: the code asked past each of those rows, so their outputs are complete.

## Appendix A: Changes after review

**From the non-data-engineer review:**

- `@zabaca/croft/read` now ships as built JavaScript, because it crashed under Node/Next.js. It locates the project explicitly, and `init` inside an app repo creates `data/` without touching the app's files.
- The Bun floor was raised to 1.3.14 and is enforced, with CI on `bun@latest`. The earlier "1.3 or newer" was false.
- `SELECT *` over an asset no longer collides with `_loaded_at`: reserved columns are excluded automatically.
- CSV handling:
  - globs use `union_by_name`, fixing a silent column drop;
  - UTF-8 falls back to latin-1;
  - money and thousands separators parse;
  - date format is decided once per column;
  - file ingests get a `map()` hook;
  - duplicate rows across files and deleted files are reported.
- Long runs detach automatically off a TTY; lock waits cap at 90 s.
- Paid per-row TS transforms are incremental by template, protected by a cost guard, and capped in preview.
- Scheduling uses one per-user job with a registry and a verified heartbeat, and diagnoses privacy protection, WSL idle, missing Bun and moved projects. `Bun.cron` is no longer used.
- The Stripe journey is taught correctly: typed epoch cursors with `unit` and `lookback`, newest-first cursor pagination, and a rule for records that change after creation.
- NULL-only placeholders are typed from the column name, and `NULL_ONLY_COLUMN` maps binder errors to a pin fix.
- Cut: incremental SQL, `--step`/`--to`, `checks/` files, `copy`/`--database`, `query --write`, `initial`. Merged: `plan`, `history`, `trash` and `drop` into other commands. The result is 19 commands (20 after D53 added `serve`) and 7 concepts.
- Synced and WSL-drvfs folders get automatic database relocation.
- Secrets: "edit `.env`" is the primary instruction, `--stdin` is supported, and `.env` values are redacted from output (the build narrowed redaction inside command data, D54).
- `INPUT_NOT_BUILT` handles validation of SQL over never-run ingests.

**From the Claude Code operator review:**

- `query` became a sandboxed single SELECT. A READ_ONLY connection had overwritten the warehouse via `COPY TO`. All user SQL is gated, and every instance is sandboxed.
- `--allow-shrink` is a destructive operation (trash + confirmation) whose fix requires a human.
- Confirmation tokens via `croft confirm` replace `--yes`. The impact is recomputed at confirmation, destructive commands never appear in `next`, and one permission rule gates them all.
- The scheduler hold (`SCHEDULE_HELD`) keeps half-finished edits away from real data.
- A backfill matrix replaces silent duplication and truncation. `--from` accepts relative dates and converts to the cursor type.
- Type safety:
  - casts are whitelisted, with a round-trip loss check;
  - pin changes that alter stored values need confirmation;
  - `TYPE_WIDENED`, `COLUMN_STOPPED_ARRIVING` and `JSON_KIND_CHANGED` report drift;
  - `TYPE_CONFLICT` fixes are reordered.
- `restore` marks downstream stale. `delete --where` replaces `query --write`. `OUT_OF_BAND_CHANGE` detects outside writes. The safety principle is reworded to what is enforced.
- Proxy-guarded rows raise `UNKNOWN_INPUT_COLUMN`, and generated input types move into v1 (phase 5).
- `rename` and `ASSET_RENAMED` stop file renames from refetching history.
- Preview semantics are defined: partial inputs, capped TS transforms, no lock held during user code, and `--rebuild` for drift.
- JSON contracts are specified for `query`, `run`, `wait`, `status`, `describe`, `validate` and `context`, along with exit precedence and the meaning of `ok`.
- Replace became a diff that keeps `_loaded_at`; bare `run` has a defined meaning.
- The skill was rewritten with an "ask the user first" list and operating recipes.
- Checks are parsed as single expressions and executed via `prepare()`. This closes statement injection.
- JSON is canonicalized for unchanged-row detection.
- `logs --failed`, `problems[].runId`, and the skipped-because-input-failed state were added.

**From the technical review (transformation and scheduling):**

- Incremental SQL is cut (D7).
- Dependencies come from the AST plus the unoptimized plan (D45). Catalog prefixes, file reads, volatile functions and reserved-keyword asset names are reported.
- SQL bodies are checked with `extractStatements` and run through a temp view with a `COLUMNS` filter, which tolerates trailing `;` and `--`.
- Keyed replaces and SQL rebuilds are diff-MERGEs that keep `_loaded_at` on unchanged rows.
- Incremental TS transforms get composite positions, ordered snapshots, chunked commits, staged-chunk reuse and no-progress timeouts (D46).
- TS values round-trip as ISO strings, and HUGEINT is snapshotted as DECIMAL(38,0) (D48; the build stores it as text, D70).
- Every open goes through `DuckDBInstance.fromCache` with one mode per process.
- The tick plans and spawns, with a singleton. `croft serve` spawns a fresh tick per minute (D47).
- DST fire rules are defined; the time zone is part of every fingerprint; one connection factory sets it.
- Leases carry process start time and boot id.
- Stale transforms are picked up by the tick. Deterministic failures wait for the next fire time.
- The DDL-before-DML invariant is enforced.
- Estimates are revised to about 13.5 weeks (14.5 after D53), and the phase-3 OS-registration spike gates scheduling.

**From the technical review (storage and ingestion):**

- **A second instance in the same process is invisible to the OS lock** (the blocker). A second read-write instance lost committed data, a second read-only one served stale data, and closing either, or closing any `fs` descriptor on the file, released the first instance's lock [V]. The fixes:
  - every open goes through `fromCache`;
  - `@zabaca/croft/read` reuses a loaded runtime's lease;
  - `validate` rejects imports of the binding or `@zabaca/croft/read` in assets and `lib/`;
  - ingests get `ctx.query()`;
  - the foreground scheduler loop (now part of `croft serve`) spawns subprocesses;
  - copies are made by a child process.
- **Casts** read JSON text, the loss check compares exact decimals, and `PIN_ROUNDED` and `DECIMAL_PRECISION_UNSUPPORTED` were added. The claim that JSON staging keeps fractional text exact was corrected: integers stay exact, fractions become doubles.
- **DDL before DML** is enforced by the Sql wrapper (`DDL_AFTER_DML`), and restore uses `CREATE OR REPLACE`.
- **Positions** come from SQL values, never `Date`, and naive timestamps round-trip as strings.
- **Names** are cleaned and resolved case-insensitively in the JS writer before `read_json`. Source `_loaded_at`/`_file` columns are renamed, every generated identifier is quoted, and `ROW_NOT_OBJECT`, `UNSERIALIZABLE_VALUE` and `DUPLICATE_OUTPUT_COLUMN` were added.
- **CSV:** header-less all-text files fail with `CSV_HEADER_AMBIGUOUS` instead of losing a row; `union_by_name` and encoding handling were confirmed.
- **Secrets** are parsed by croft with Bun's loading off, so `.env.local` and the working directory no longer matter.
- **Query sandbox:** extension autoinstall and autoload are off, allowed directories are narrowed to `files/` for `query`, and `QUERY_PATH_DENIED` was added.
- **Preview** snapshots its inputs to Parquet instead of attaching the live file.
- **Readers:** the write-intent handshake stops direct app readers from starving writers. D53 later extended it to `croft serve`.
- **Copies:** the read copy uses `CHECKPOINT` plus a child-process clone under the write lease. The pre-upgrade backup includes the WAL and reads the "newer engine" version from `runs.sqlite`.
- **Cursors:** the "inclusive start" claim was replaced by a 1-second default lookback; lookback renders in the saved value's own form; resumable first loads (monotone partial commits) moved into v1 (D50).
- **Staging and schema:** `_croft_seq` orders dedupe; per-row absence means NULL (with post-v1 `partial: true`); the real schema is read from `duckdb_columns()`, with `TABLE_MODIFIED_OUTSIDE_CROFT`; Parquet types are normalized.
- **Platforms:** native Windows is unsupported in v1 (use WSL on ext4).
- **Rejected:** deferring incremental TS transforms (D51).

## Appendix B: Verification ledger

All spikes ran on macOS arm64 with `@duckdb/node-api` 1.5.5-r.5 (DuckDB 1.5.5), under Bun 1.3.14 unless noted. They live in the design scratchpad (`spike/`), and they are recorded here so implementation can turn each into a test.

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Runtime | node-api loads under Bun 1.3.0–1.4.2; `JSON.rawJSON` and reviver `context.source` exist on all of them; `Bun.cron` is absent before 1.3.11; `Bun.cron.parse` ignores tz on 1.3.14 and honors it on 1.4.2; the built `@zabaca/croft/read` works on Node 24.3/24.20, while a `.ts` export under `node_modules` fails on Node |
| Locking | a second process cannot open a file held read-write, even READ_ONLY; the error names the holder path and PID; open+close is 3–6 ms; lock handoff is about 57 ms; overlapping readers delayed a writer 2.4 s; two instances on one file in one process lost data |
| Sandbox | a READ_ONLY connection executed `COPY TO` over the warehouse, leaving 4 bytes and an unopenable file; `allowed_directories` + `enable_external_access=false` + `lock_configuration=true` blocked `COPY TO` the warehouse, reads outside allowed dirs, and re-enabling; `DETACH` + read-write `ATTACH` of an already-attached path still worked; `json_serialize_sql` rejects COPY, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and PIVOT, accepts DESCRIBE/SUMMARIZE, and reports 2 statements for `select 1; select 2`; a multi-statement `run()` executed an injected `DROP TABLE` |
| SQL assets | dependency extraction through CTEs, subqueries, EXISTS, UNION and 3-part names; quoted file paths appear as BASE_TABLE; `query_table()`/`query()` hide their tables; dynamic PIVOT fails to serialize and prepare, while PIVOT with an IN list works; `prepare()` yields output columns; the AST fingerprint (without `query_location`, lowercased names) is stable across formatting and case |
| Reserved columns | the `SELECT q.*, stamp AS _loaded_at` wrapper kept the upstream `_loaded_at` and added `_loaded_at_1`; `INSERT BY NAME` raised `Duplicate column name`; `EXCLUDE` of a present column works, and of an absent one is a binder error |
| Writes | DDL is transactional (CREATE, ALTER ADD/TYPE, CREATE OR REPLACE); MERGE with duplicate source keys applies one to matched rows and inserts both for unmatched ones, and fails with a PK; `MERGE … WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` gives UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT actions and keeps an unchanged row's stamp; `INSERT BY NAME` fills missing columns with NULL; kill -9 inside a transaction rolls back; committed data before checkpoint survives via the WAL |
| Types | the sniffer types mixed-offset and mixed-fraction timestamps as VARCHAR; JSON staging keeps integer text exact (fractions become doubles); `json_type` classification; `1.7` into BIGINT stores 2; `'1.5'::BIGINT` is 2 even via `try_cast`; `+02:00`→TIMESTAMP drops the offset; `'02134'`→BIGINT gives 2134; a VARCHAR pin sorts `9 > 100 > 10`; STRUCT insert drops an extra field; the lossless proof catches 2^53+1; a VARCHAR NULL-only column breaks `date_diff`, comparisons and `COALESCE`; JSON `IS DISTINCT FROM` is text-based (key order, whitespace, `1.0` vs `1`); `->>` on a JSON string returns NULL |
| CSV | the sniffer flips day/month order depending on the rows; a glob without `union_by_name` drops later columns; latin-1 files fail as UTF-8 and load with `encoding='latin-1'`; money strings parse to DECIMAL; `strptime` with a pinned format works; a read-only instance can query CSV globs |
| Time | `SET TimeZone` after connecting works, as an instance option it fails; `::DATE` of TIMESTAMPTZ yields project-zone days; `getRowObjectsJson` renders TIMESTAMPTZ in the process-local zone |
| TS code | the `Bun.build` fingerprint with `identifiers: false` is stable under comment edits, detects `lib/` changes, and costs about 0.5–1.2 ms; with identifier minification it changed on a comment edit; Proxy rows guard unknown columns, including destructuring, at 17 ms per 2M reads, but break `structuredClone`; a detached child outlives its parent |
| Stripe shape | against a newest-first mock, the keyset loop got stuck after 2 requests, and a `starting_after` loop fetched all 250 records in 3 requests |
| Trash | an ATTACH copy preserves HUGEINT, JSON, TIMESTAMPTZ and DECIMAL in 1 ms; one transaction cannot write two databases; restore from a read-only attached file works in one transaction; APFS `COPYFILE_FICLONE` clones in 0.1–0.2 ms |
| Process locks | `fs.openSync`+`closeSync` on the held file released DuckDB's lock (a child then wrote); opening and closing a second read-only instance in the same process did the same; `statSync` and APFS `COPYFILE_FICLONE` did not; `DuckDBInstance.fromCache` shares one instance across realpath and case-variant paths and refuses a different configuration; a byte copy without `CHECKPOINT` missed 500 WAL rows, and with it was complete |
| Transactions | DELETE or UPDATE followed by ALTER on the same table failed at COMMIT; ALTER before DML, including MERGE, worked |
| Dependencies | the unoptimized bound plan found `query_table`, `query()`, table macros, PIVOT with IN, and correct CTE shadowing; the optimized plan dropped scans under `WHERE false` and `LIMIT 0`; `current_date`/`current_timestamp` are COLUMN_REF nodes in the AST; the 75 reserved keywords break `FROM <name>` |
| SQL wrapper | a temp view plus `COLUMNS(lambda c: c <> '_loaded_at')` handled `SELECT *` over assets, trailing `;` and `--`; `extractStatements` counts statements; a failing check after CREATE OR REPLACE rolled back cleanly |
| TS positions and values | stream order of a merged input was not stamp order, and a max-stamp position skipped 3 of 5 rows; a naive TIMESTAMP passed through `Date` came back as TIMESTAMPTZ shifted 8 h without microseconds; HUGEINT became DOUBLE in Parquet and survived as DECIMAL(38,0) within 38 digits (the build stores text, D70); a cache-busted `import()` kept the old `lib/` module |
| Scheduling math | wall-clock matching skips 02:30 on 2026-03-08 and doubles 01:30 on 2026-11-01 in Los Angeles; `TimeZone` is per connection and changes `::DATE` keys |
| Staging precision | `read_json` into JSON columns re-rendered `3.14159265358979323846` as `3.141592653589793` and `1.50` as `1.5`; integers beyond int64 kept their digits; JSON→DECIMAL(18,2) gave `1.00` for `1.005` while text gave `1.01`; TRY_CAST of JSON `1.7` to BIGINT gave 2 |
| Staging names | `read_json` matched keys case-sensitively (`ID` loaded NULL into `Id`), failed with "Duplicate struct entry name" for `Id` + `id`, and rejected an empty key |
| CSV header | a header-less all-text CSV lost its first data row, with or without `all_varchar`; numeric files were detected correctly |
| Secrets | `bun --no-env-file` disables `.env` loading (default loading read `.env` from the working directory) |
| Server handoff | a read-only server that closed its instance on seeing `.croft/write-intent` let a writer in within 10–23 ms (5 writes) while answering 2,226 queries in 6 s |
| Serve handoff hazards | an instance closed with an idle connection kept the lock (20 s); disconnecting before an interrupted query settled kept it indefinitely, and the promise never settled; interrupt, then await, then disconnect, then close let a writer in within about 20 ms; one shared intent file locked out a second writer 3 of 3 times, and per-holder files let it in after 505–615 ms; macOS `fs.watch` missed short-lived files (0 of 100 seen at 0–1 ms hold); a reopened read-only instance saw commits, including WAL-only ones after a writer's kill -9 |
| Throughput | a 200k-row batch merged into a 2M-row, 20-column table in 327 ms including checks |
| Storage | 30 hourly full rewrites doubled a 9.8 MB file to 19.3 MB; 10% merges stayed at 9.5 MB; the sandbox blocks `read_text('.env')` and https; spilling works under the sandbox; Unicode identifiers work unquoted |
| Build findings (2026-09-23, recorded in the code's tests) | Bun's `realpathSync` and `realpathSync.native` open the file on macOS, and closing that descriptor released DuckDB's lock, while `lstat`, `readlink` and realpath of a directory did not; the sandbox always lets a connection read its own database file, WAL and `.tmp` folder; `enable_logging` changed a locked READ_ONLY instance; `lock_configuration` refuses a later per-session `SET TimeZone`; a TEMP table shadows `t` and `main.t`; inside a write transaction a TEMP table created by it scanned about 4.5× slower than a view (1,247 vs 417 ms, 1M × 5); the `DECIMAL(38,18)` loss formula gave 11,218 false losses among 40,011 random doubles; DuckDB refuses a zoned time without seconds, and `read_json` rejects unpaired surrogates; 30 of the 35 `type_function` keywords also break `FROM <name>`; under Bun, `node:http` and `fetch` sent `127.0.0.1` requests through `HTTP_PROXY`; Bun spawns children with the environment it started with, `.env` values included, unless given one |
| Build findings (2026-09-24, phase 2, recorded in the code's tests) | `PRAGMA disable_optimizer` works on a connection whose configuration is locked, while `SET enable_optimizer` is refused; the unoptimized plan's scan nodes carry `extra_info.Table` as `catalog.schema.table` with DuckDB's quoting, and an unused CTE's table is never scanned; a CTE's body sees only earlier CTEs, so a non-recursive `WITH orders AS (SELECT * FROM orders)` reads the table, and a recursive CTE sees itself only in its recursive part; `json_serialize_sql` writes `1e400` as a bare `Infinity`, which is not valid JSON; `PIVOT … IN (SELECT …)` also becomes two statements; `DESCRIBE`, `SUMMARIZE` and `SHOW` prepare with `statementType` SELECT, and `DESCRIBE`'s plan scans nothing; a view renames a repeated `_loaded_at` to `_loaded_at_1`; a prepared statement's column types drop the `JSON` alias inside nested types (`VARCHAR[]` for `JSON[]`), while a view's `duckdb_columns()` keeps it; the parse error of a bare keyword column points past it (`SELECT id, order FROM t` fails at `FROM`, `WHERE order > 1` at `order`); DuckDB's "Did you mean" can name a system view (`pg_constraint`); a missing column is "Referenced column "x" not found in FROM clause!", and `g.x` is "Table "g" does not have a column named "x"", both with candidate bindings; Parquet writes HUGEINT as DOUBLE (rounding 2^127 − 1), and `DECIMAL(38,0)` cannot hold its 39-digit values; DuckDB marks `current_localtime` and `current_localtimestamp` consistent within a query, not volatile |

AS SELECT *` from it in a transaction of its own works for every type that is kept; `ducklake_snapshots()`'s `commit_message` of the newest snapshot is the tag a write was given; a view of an attached log-adapter file binds its own log table (it reads the file's rows, not the attaching database's), and the move reads the log table anyway to break ties by row id; a project of 13,429 rows over six tables moved in 0.9 s (local lake) and 1.2 s (Postgres catalog and store), and the file's sha256 was the same before and after in every journey, also after a kill -9 at each of four points |

SET DATA TYPE DECIMAL(38,0)` of a temp table inside the write transaction keeps every digit (an `abs()` of the HUGEINT minimum overflows, so the check for a value past 38 digits compares both bounds); `BIGINT` to `DECIMAL(38,0)` and `DECIMAL(38,0)` to `DOUBLE` are not DuckLake promotions and are made by the rewrite; `CAST(row AS VARCHAR)` of a table's row prints a float's shortest round-trip text, `-0.0` as `-0.0` and NaN as `nan`, which `EXCEPT ALL` by value does not tell apart from `0.0`; a `-0.0` written to a lake comes back `-0.0` |

Cannot downgrade a DuckLake catalog" for a newer lake and `DATA_PATH parameter ... does not match existing data path in the catalog ...` for a lake under another folder; a Postgres answers an SSLRequest with `S` when it has TLS on and `N` when it has not, and the `postgres` extension exposes no call that tells whether a connection is encrypted; `DELETE FROM` every row of a table whose rows are in a file leaves the file live with the deletes inlined (gone for a log table, live for `_croft.meta`, whose rows had been merged), and `ducklake_rewrite_data_files` then drops it (`files_processed: 1, files_created: 0`); an insert of up to 10 rows stays in the catalog |

**Unverified [U]:**

- OS job registration on Linux (crontab), and macOS privacy-protection behavior for background jobs on other Macs. The macOS LaunchAgent itself was verified on 2026-09-24 (§8).
- WSL idle shutdown.
- Linux reflink, and the copy policy's clone probe on Linux (D121): it was run on macOS only, and on Linux through a `cp` script that refuses the strict flag. What a plain copy costs on ext4, the 2 to 40 s at 5 GB in D121, is an estimate; no Linux machine measured it.
- Server mode (D119) on Linux and on the CI runners: the readers' process, the swap and the e2e journey ran on macOS arm64 only. The same holds for keys (D122): the views, the key journey `j33` and the refresh child's signal handling (D124) ran on macOS arm64 only.
- Quack (D125 to D127) on Linux and on the CI runners: the listener, the hooks and the attack list ran on macOS arm64 only. The pinned quack files for the other three platforms were never loaded. A reverse proxy that terminates TLS in front of Quack was not run (a recording HTTP proxy was); that a client behind Cloudflare Access can attach with the service-token headers is tested only as far as the headers arriving on every request. The DuckDB command line 2.0 as a client was not tried. A query that streams a large result slowly to a slow client counts as `active` for as long as Quack reports it so, and is ended at the deadline; not tested.
- Lake bookkeeping against a Postgres catalog and a bucket (D132, D133): the lake tests and the benchmark used a SQLite catalog and a local folder, so the timings are the statements' own and not a network's, and croft's own writes were not run against Postgres or R2. The suite on the log adapter ran on macOS arm64 only; the CI step that runs it (one Linux job) has not run on GitHub's runners.
- A warehouse in a lake (D137 to D147) ran against a Postgres 17 and an S3-compatible store (the test rig) on this machine, and a local SQLite lake, on macOS arm64, and in CI on Linux (`test-lake-local` and `test-lake-postgres`, which also fetches DuckDB 1.5.5 and its extension files from DuckDB's repository, checked against pinned checksums; D190, D191). Two real-lake trials (2026-11-02 and 2026-11-03, D160 to D162 and D175 to D182) ran it on Cloudflare R2 with a remote Postgres catalog, the second with the catalog 41 ms away; the suite's distance is still simulated with a TCP proxy that delays bytes (no loss, no jitter, no bandwidth limit). A lake written by DuckDB 2.0 was read by DuckDB 1.5.5 only through the recipe's one table, read-only. Two machines writing one lake was not tried beyond the record that tells them apart (D144); croft cannot stop it. The lake process of `croft serve` was killed and restarted but not run for days. A write that rewrites a table twice, or rewrites it after another change of the table (a pin that retypes together with a placeholder that gets values, or a key conversion confirmed with one), is `LAKE_UNSUPPORTED` (D142).
- A file moved into a lake (D167 to D173) ran against a Postgres 17 and an S3-compatible store (the test rig) and a local SQLite lake on macOS arm64, and in CI on Linux (`tests/e2e/j39-lake-move.test.ts`); one real project (11 tables, 51,085 rows) was moved into a lake on R2 with a remote Postgres catalog on 2026-11-05 (D197). No warehouse bigger than that was moved (the proof is an `EXCEPT ALL` per table, so its cost on a warehouse of hundreds of millions of rows, and a copy in one transaction of that size over a network, were not measured). The set of types a lake changes was measured on DuckDB 2.0.0 with DuckLake 1.0 and a local catalog; a Postgres catalog was not probed for it (the type mapping is the extension's, not the catalog's). A move of a project whose file sits on a filesystem that cannot clone copies it in full (D121) and holds the file's lock for that long. The way back was tested through a hand edit and the mirror's restore, not with a `croft serve` or the scheduler running across the switch.
- Lake maintenance and backup (D149 to D153) ran against a Postgres 17 and an S3-compatible store (the test rig) and a local SQLite lake on macOS arm64 only: no remote Postgres and, but for the orphans listing past 1,000 objects (D192, run 2026-11-04 on 1,100 strays in a real R2 bucket shared by two lakes: all listed, none of the other lake's files), no real R2; no Linux or CI runner, and no lake of more than a few thousand snapshots (the month measured 3,693), so the cost of a pass on a lake of millions of files, of a catalog far away (D145: every statement is a round trip) and of a bucket mirror over a real network is unknown. R2's HTTP 500 to a bulk delete is simulated by the rig's fault (the message DuckDB gives for it is the rig's, not R2's). `pg_dump` against other server versions was not run (a mismatch is detected from its message, not tried), nor was the hard link across filesystems (the fallback to a download is code that did not run), nor a mirror of a folder over 1,000 files against a real store (the rig's listing pages are tested). A pass while `croft serve`'s lake process is reading was probed (100 reads, no failure) but a reader in the middle of a scan of a file the cleanup deletes could fail once; its next read is fine. The month's catalog size shows what Postgres has not given back, which `VACUUM` would.
- The TLS of a lake's catalog (D159) ran against a local Postgres 17 with a self-signed certificate, on macOS arm64 only (LibreSSL's `openssl` made the certificates). No real hosted catalog (Neon's certificate chain is the case it exists for), no Linux machine and no CI run has checked it; that `sslrootcert=system` trusts the operating system's store on 2.0.0 is not shown, and croft does not use it. The CA bundle search order was written from the usual places, not checked on each system.
- The second real-lake trial's fixes (D175 to D182) ran against a Postgres 17 behind a TCP proxy that delays bytes (no loss, no jitter, no bandwidth limit; a new connection costs one round trip, not the several of a TLS handshake) with an S3-compatible store on this machine, and a local SQLite lake, on macOS arm64 only. No hosted catalog behind a pooler was asked the SSL request (D175 rests on the protocol: `S` or `N` before anything else), no Linux machine ran it and no CI job has. The numbers of `docs/benchmarks/2026-11-03-lake-latency.md` are round trips and the time they take at a simulated 40 ms; a real network adds what a proxy cannot (jitter, TLS records, a pooler's own wait). The write path of a step was not shortened: a step that writes still takes about 7 s at 40 ms, mostly DuckLake's own work (a commit is 15 round trips, a table's first scan in a transaction at least 4).
- The fetch from DuckDB (D195) was run by hand on macOS arm64 only. The macOS x64 and Linux files were downloaded from DuckDB's servers and checked against the pins on 2026-11-04, and the Linux files are loaded only in CI (`scripts/fetch-extensions.ts` on its runners); the macOS x64 files were never loaded. Croft's own first-use fetch (`prepareMode` in a readers' process, `croft fetch-extensions` outside a project) was not run on Linux, nor behind a proxy; a download interrupted half-way was tested only as a failed answer, not as a dropped connection mid-body. The add-on packages that D134 and D135 measured were never uploaded and are deleted. The licenses of what the extension binaries link were read once from the binaries (D135, superseded) and are no longer shipped by croft: DuckDB's own files carry DuckDB's notices.
- musl and Windows runtime behavior.
- Power-loss durability.
- Claude Code permission-rule matching beyond a command prefix, and the validate hook inside a live Claude Code session. Its input and exit codes are verified against the documentation, and its command through a real `sh -c` (§9 item 7).
- The CI workflow on GitHub's runners (Linux x64, `bun@latest`, Alpine, Windows): GitHub Actions is blocked by the organization's billing, and the gates ran locally on macOS arm64 and Linux arm64 (§10 item 8).
- The mode tests (D117, D118) on Linux and on the CI runners: they ran on macOS arm64 only. The CI steps that fetch the extension files and find Postgres (`ubuntu-24.04`'s preinstalled PostgreSQL 16 under `/usr/lib/postgresql`; on a Linux image without it, `apt-get install postgresql` with a `policy-rc.d` that stops the service starting, as on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` if it lacks Postgres; the macOS branch (`brew install postgresql@17`) went with the macOS job, D190) have not run on GitHub's runners. The pins for osx_amd64, linux_amd64 and linux_arm64 were taken from the repository and never loaded on those platforms. `detectMusl` was tested with stubbed probes only, never on a real Alpine or a glibc Linux.
- `secretsFrom` against a real store (D108): the tests use a Bun script that prints dotenv. What `sops -d --output-type dotenv` prints for nested keys, which age key file sops reads under a scheduled run's environment, and `op inject` were not run.
